decisions.name: Opus 5 carry
decisions.research_notes:
CHECKED: July payrolls (released Fri 2026-08-07), Fed hike odds pre/post-print, week's equity/bond tape, DXY and EM debt flows, Brent/Hormuz, VIX, JAAA flows and AAA CLO spreads, NLY Q2 results, PFF.

WHAT CHANGED — the exact premise I sized on last week broke. On 2026-07-30 I concentrated JAAA 16 -> 40 and zeroed EMLC/EMB/NLY explicitly because the 29-July hawkish hold (three dissents to hike) put a September hike at ~60-65% and floating-rate CLO carry was the only leg whose coupon rises on a hike. On 2026-08-07 July nonfarm payrolls came in at -23,000 vs +80,000 expected, June revised down to +20,000, and average hourly earnings decelerated to 3.2% y/y — the lowest since May 2021. Markets took a September hike off the table. That single print removes the entire differentiating kicker behind a 40% JAAA weight while simultaneously un-blocking the three mandate legs I had zeroed.

TAPE: S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed at record highs, strongest week since April (Nasdaq ~+5%, S&P ~+3.5%), Treasury yields fell across the curve. VIX closed 14.88, near cycle lows, down from ~18 when I sized SPYI. DXY at four-year lows in the mid-90s (dollar sold off hard, partly on Fed-credibility questions after Chair Warsh's presser). EM fixed income split cleanly: local-currency sovereigns +0.95% on the week vs hard-currency -0.07%, with weekly inflows into EM local the heaviest since the late 2010s. Brent ~$84-86, off the ~$100 spike as an Iran-Oman Hormuz transit arrangement moves toward (but has not cleared) Iran's parliament.

LEG-LEVEL: JAAA ~$25bn AUM, distribution now 4.73% and taking inflows ($381m/5d, $935m/1m) — healthy, but 4.73% against 4% cash is only ~73bp of pickup for credit and liquidity risk, and that pickup compresses if SOFR drifts lower rather than higher. JPMorgan flags AAA CLO spreads as tight with unclear growth drivers and 2027 issuance guided down ~20%. NLY Q2 was strong and is the leg most directly helped by hike risk coming off: dividend raised to $0.75 from $0.70, EAD $0.79 (105% coverage), book value +1.7% to $20.15, 5.5% economic return in the quarter, net interest spread +8bp to 1.50%, economic leverage a conservative 5.6x. PFF screened as a possible tenth leg and I rejected it — 5.47% forward yield is barely above cash, 60-70% bank/insurer concentration, and near-universal call provisions cap the recovery I would be buying it for. BTC ~$64,940, +2.8% on the week and up on the jobs print itself; still ~40% below its Jan-2025 high while equities make records.

CAVEAT I SIZED FOR: this is not a one-way dovish trade. Some strategists are sticking with 75bp of hikes this year starting in September, June CPI was 3.5% y/y, and the next CPI lands ~2026-08-12 — a hot print snaps hike odds back and hits EMLC/EMB/NLY together. So I barbelled rather than rotated: ~28% in newly-added duration/FX-bearing carry against ~32% still in zero-duration floating-rate CLO paper, plus 11% cash.

decisions.reason: I sized this book on a specific, stated macro call — that a September hike at ~60% odds made floating-rate CLO carry uniquely privileged — and Friday's payroll print (-23,000 vs +80,000 expected, earnings growth down to 3.2%) took that hike off the table. When the reason for a 40% weight disappears, the weight should not survive it. Two things follow mechanically. First, JAAA's coupon-upgrade optionality is gone, leaving a 4.73% distribution against 4% cash — about 73bp for credit and liquidity risk, and shrinking if SOFR drifts lower — so 40% is no longer justified and comes down to 20% (still the largest leg, because zero duration is exactly the insurance I want if CPI on the 12th reverses this). Second, the three mandate legs I zeroed on 29 July purely because a hawkish Fed made them uninvestable are now the best carry on my board: EMLC with DXY at four-year lows, EM local sovereigns +0.95% on the week and record inflows; EMB collecting hard-currency sovereign spread with duration now a tailwind instead of a tax; and NLY, the leg most leveraged to hike risk receding, which just raised its dividend to $0.75 on 105% EAD coverage with book value up 1.7% and spread widening 8bp. I am deliberately barbelling rather than rotating — 28% new duration/FX carry against 32% still floating-rate — because a hot 12-August CPI would hit all four new-regime legs together. I also trim the two legs whose premium got thinner rather than richer this week: SPHY, because ~285bp of already-crowded high-yield spread got crowded further in a record-high tape, and SPYI, whose entire case was writing calls at VIX 18 — VIX closed 14.88, so the premium I am collecting is roughly what I said was too thin to size. AMLP trims 16 to 14 only because Brent fell from ~$100 to ~$85 on Hormuz de-escalation, removing the windfall leg of the thesis while leaving the fee-based, volume-linked core intact. The BTC perp short goes 5 to 3 — back to the mandate's stated 3% margin — because its macro leg (hawkish Fed, ETF outflows) just weakened materially while its financing-arb leg (perp shorts pay 0% funding here versus ~7% all-in drag on an equity short) is untouched; I keep it small rather than kill it because BTC is the one asset refusing to participate in a record-high tape, and I tighten the stop to -50% so the whole hedge cannot cost more than ~1.5% of NAV. I am not shorting into the gold-miner or leveraged-semi complexes at all, which is where 12 of 17 stop-outs have happened.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to breach; the distinct expression here is a barbell that funds a cut in zero-duration floating-rate CLO carry into EM local-currency FX carry, EM hard-currency sovereign spread and agency-MBS-versus-repo carry — the three sleeves priced off a September hike that the market has now removed — while keeping the only short as a small unfunded perp rather than a borrow-paying equity short.

positions.thesis: Still the anchor, but sized for what it actually is now rather than what a hike would have made it. AAA CLO paper at SOFR+~120bp with effectively zero duration, a 4.73% distribution, thirty years without a default including 2008 and 2020, LSTA trailing loan defaults down to 3.5% from 4.3%, and $935m of inflows over the past month. The 40% weight was justified by one thing only — that its coupon rises if the Fed hikes — and Friday's payroll miss removed that. What remains is a ~73bp pickup over cash that compresses if SOFR falls, against JPMorgan's warning that AAA spreads are tight with issuance guided down ~20%. So it stays the largest position, because zero duration is precisely the hedge I want against a hot 12-August CPI reversing this week's move, but it stops being half the book. Wide -10% stop: the only real risk is a liquidity gap, and a tight stop would just whipsaw me out of the safest income I own.

Real-asset cash yield and the book's main inflation-linked leg. 7.8% distribution just raised to a record $1.03 per quarter, every top holding raised in H1, coverage guided through 2027, revenue fee-based and volume-linked with LNG exports at capacity and data-center power demand adding multi-year throughput, and midstream contracts escalate with CPI. Trimmed from 16 for one honest reason: Brent has fallen from ~$100 to ~$85 as the Iran-Oman Hormuz transit arrangement advances, so the windfall part of my thesis — a shock that pays this leg rather than punishing it — has largely paid out and reversed. The core case is unharmed, because $85 crude is nowhere near the sub-$60 level that would choke producer activity, but I should not keep paying for optionality that has already expired.

The single cleanest beneficiary of the payroll print and the leg I zeroed on 29 July for a reason that has now inverted. EM local-currency sovereign carry pays high single-digit local coupons, and the return has two engines that just both turned on: DXY at four-year lows in the mid-90s after a sharp dollar sell-off, and US hike odds collapsing, which is historically the trigger for EM local outperformance. The tape confirms it rather than merely predicting it — EM local sovereigns returned +0.95% on the week while hard currency was -0.07%, and weekly inflows into EM local are the heaviest since the late 2010s. I express the FX-bearing version larger than the hard-currency version because the dispersion this week was entirely FX, not spread. -10% stop because local-currency drawdowns come through the exchange rate and can be fast; this is the leg that hurts most if CPI on the 12th revives the hike.

BBB/BB CLO mezzanine at roughly 9% floating — the same improving loan collateral as JAAA, paid for taking subordination rather than duration. Trimmed only modestly from 15 while JAAA is halved, because the case here never depended on the hike: at a ~9% coupon there is five points of cushion over cash, so a lower SOFR path erodes far less of the edge than it does at JAAA's 4.73%. The offsetting negative is real and is why it does not get raised — a payroll print of -23,000 with government and retail shedding jobs is a mild negative for leveraged-loan borrowers, even with defaults still falling toward 3.5%, and mezzanine subordination gaps wider in a risk-off well before the collateral actually deteriorates.

Agency MBS versus repo — the mandate leg most directly geared to the risk that just came off the table, re-added after being zeroed for hawkish-Fed reasons. mREIT book value is destroyed by rate volatility and hike shocks, so removing a live September hike removes the specific thing that made this uninvestable two weeks ago, while a front-end rally with anchored policy is the exact curve shape agency carry wants. The fundamentals are not a recovery bet, they are already delivering: Q2 dividend raised to $0.75 from $0.70 on EAD of $0.79 (105% coverage), book value +1.7% to $20.15, 5.5% economic return in the quarter and 6.9% in the first half, net interest spread +8bp to 1.50%, and economic leverage a conservative 5.6x with $9.6bn available for financing. Sized at 8 rather than larger because that same leverage cuts both ways on any hike repricing, and the -15% stop respects it.

Plain-vanilla US high-yield corporate spread at roughly 7% with short duration, supported by defaults falling toward 3%. I called this the richest and most crowded carry on the board at ~285bp; a week in which the S&P and Nasdaq closed at record highs and posted their best week since April has made it richer and more crowded still, which is a reason to take size down rather than up. It keeps a place because the carry is genuine and short duration limits the damage from a CPI-driven rate reversal, but I am not paid to add credit beta at the tights into a tape where VIX is at 14.9.

EM hard-currency sovereign spread, re-added as the non-FX half of the EM barbell. It pays roughly 6% in dollars with no exchange-rate risk, and its seven-ish years of duration flipped this week from a liability under a hiking Fed to an asset under a Fed the market no longer expects to move. Deliberately sized below EMLC because the entire week's EM dispersion came through the currency — local +0.95% versus hard currency -0.07% — so the FX engine is where the return is; EMB is here as the version that still works if the dollar stops falling but rates stay anchored, which is the middle scenario neither of my other new legs covers.

Equity variance risk premium, cut again for the same reason I halved it last week, now confirmed by the tape. My stated case was that writing index calls at VIX 18 collects a materially richer premium than at VIX 14 — VIX closed Friday at 14.88, near cycle lows, so I am now collecting almost exactly the premium I said was too thin to size. The structure is long index beta with capped upside into a market at record highs, which is the worst configuration a covered-call fund can have. It survives at 5% because the mandate calls for an equity-premium sleeve and monthly distributions still clear cash comfortably, but I will not pay up for compressed volatility, and I did not add SVXY for the same reason — buying short-vol carry at cycle-low VIX after a 3.5% melt-up week is selling insurance at the cheapest possible price.

Cut from 5% margin back to the mandate's 3% because half the thesis weakened and half did not. The financing edge is untouched and is the real reason this leg exists in perp form: perp shorts are charged 0% funding in this engine while longs pay 10% APR and an equity short would cost 3% borrow plus 4% forgone cash yield, so short beta here is roughly seven points a year cheaper than any alternative expression. What did weaken is the macro leg — the hawkish Fed I was leaning on is gone, the dollar is at four-year lows, and BTC rallied ~2.8% on the week and again on the jobs print. What keeps it alive is that BTC at ~$64,900 is still ~40% below its January-2025 high and conspicuously failed to participate while the S&P and Nasdaq made records, which is the profile of an asset with its own problem rather than a macro discount. 9% of notional hedging an 86% gross risk book. Stop tightened from -60% to -50% so the entire hedge cannot cost more than ~1.5% of NAV; liquidation would still need a ~32% rally at 3x and the stop fires long before that. Take-profit at +45% (roughly a 15% BTC decline) so a working hedge gets banked rather than round-tripped. Note this is not a short in gold miners or leveraged semis, where 12 of the 17 standing orders ever fired in this experiment were shorts being stopped out.

decisions.research_notes:

MY ATTRIBUTION: NAV $990.09, -0.99% since 08-03 entry, max DD -1.96%. Decomposed: the 24% SPY + 13% QQQ hedge cost -1.54%; the 61% long book contributed only +0.57%, i.e. the basket averaged roughly +0.9% against SPY +3.6%. That is the whole story — the screen has selected into names whose *realised* beta is far below 1 (my own theses cite HUM 0.35, CF -1.4≈0, OXY ≈0), so the book behaved as if net-beta-flat-to-short even while running a +24-point net-long notional tilt. Neither the tilt nor the hedge paid.

NAME-BY-NAME CHECKS (all longs, nothing broke):
- MRNA: PDUFA cleared 5 Aug. mFLUSIVA approved for adults 50+, the FIRST mRNA influenza vaccine ever approved in the US; unlocks the combo and pandemic resubmissions. Initial fade (~-4%) then +7.5% to $59.35 on 7 Aug. The dated binary I bought it for is now resolved to the upside.
- OXY: Q2 on 5 Aug was a blowout — adj EPS $2.40 vs $1.87 est (+823% y/y), revenue $8.33bn vs $7.18bn est (+57%), Midstream & Marketing pre-tax $961m above the top of guide, production above guidance, $1.9bn of debt retired in one quarter against the $10bn target. Stock +3.9%. Thesis strengthened.
- CF: Q2 5 Aug, mid-cycle EBITDA target lifted to $2.9bn, nitrogen tightness guided through 2030, dividend +20% to $0.60. Stock +55% YTD. Gas feedstock down 11% y/y. Thesis strengthened.
- HUM: Morgan Stanley upgrade to Equal Weight 4 Aug on better cost trends, following Piper to Overweight 30 Jul and Barclays PT to $407. The utilisation debate is turning my way at the margin.
- COF: UBS PT to $280 (Buy) 3 Aug, $0.80 dividend declared. Credit costs fell sharply sequentially in Q2. No change.
- PYPL: ~$59, set first-ever revenue targets for its three core units; Cantor PT to $60, Truist to $59 (Hold). Genuinely two-sided — exactly what a scatter asset should be.
- QCOM: the one real negative. Apple modem revenue will decline FASTER than guided starting fiscal Q4 as Apple's in-house modem share rises; stock -13% YTD. Offsets: price increases from 1 Sept, $5bn AI-datacentre revenue target FY27 / $15bn FY29. Kept — this is idiosyncratic risk, which is the mandate, not a broken thesis.
- DLTR: Section 301 forced-labour tariffs (10% or 12.5% across 60 economies, 99.4% of US imports) were finalised 23 July effective 24 July, replacing the expiring universal Section 122 tariffs — already in the price when I entered on 3 Aug, so not new information. Tariff refunds are arriving (Bernstein: not a big boost). Q2 print is the next dated catalyst.
- RCL: ~$320-327, record bookings, FY guide $17.73-17.87, offset by fuel/airfare and Med/West-Mexico itinerary softness. No change.

NEW-NAME SCREEN (three adds to restore the mandate's twelve):
- BA: 777X certification is the largest purely company-specific binary in US large cap, first delivery promised 2027 and slipping; Q2 had a record $715bn backlog, 171 deliveries (most since 2018) and +$631m FCF after four quarters of burn. BNP upgraded to Outperform, JPM PT $290, RBC trimmed to $265 on cert conservatism — genuinely two-sided. Zero AI-factor loading.
- CHTR: at a record low ~$111 after -18% in a session in April; Q2 lost 172k broadband subs but added 406k mobile lines (12.5m, +15.5%), and the $34.5bn Cox deal closes this summer. Enormous residual vol, no index analogue, no AI loading.
- GM: -1.4% on the week to $87.58 while SPY rose 3.6%. Guidance raised to $12-14 adj EPS, $500m tariff refund after the Supreme Court struck the IEEPA tariffs, against $2.5-3.5bn gross tariff cost and $1.5-2bn of commodity/DRAM cost. Note the DRAM line: GM's cost base is hurt by the same memory squeeze that is lifting the AI complex, so it is a rare *negatively* correlated leg to the dominant factor.
- REJECTED: NEM/gold miners. Correlation-wise ideal, but the complex has gone parabolic (+12.7% in two sessions) and the prompt's own tape note flags this as the most violently squeezed complex in the experiment. Buying the third day of a parabola is not a residual-vol trade.

decisions.reason: Three mandate deviations had compounded and this week's tape priced them. (1) The book had drifted to nine conviction-sized longs totalling 61% against a 37% hedge — a +24-point net-long notional tilt my mandate never authorised — and it still lost 0.99% in a week SPY rose 3.6% and QQQ 5.2%, because the screen has selected into names whose realised beta is far below one. So the tilt bought me none of the upside while the hedge charged me the full 1.54%: I was paying for direction and receiving none. (2) Nine names weighted 5.5-7.5% is a conviction book wearing a dispersion label. The mandate specifies twelve equal-weight names because the edge here is the law of large numbers over many independent residuals, not sizing skill on a few — and the loss this week was exactly a concentrated-residual loss. Twelve at 4.5% adds three uncorrelated return functions (777X certification, a cable subscriber/M&A workout, and an auto tariff-and-DRAM cost book) and cuts the variance contribution of any single one. (3) Both index shorts carried take-profits at +7% and +9%. That is a structural defect, not a tuning choice: a hedge that self-liquidates into a market drawdown would leave me 54% net long at precisely the moment the hedge exists to work. Removed. On the hedge mix itself I am changing nothing directional — the SPY:QQQ ratio goes 64.9:35.1 to 63.6:36.4, i.e. untouched. I re-cut that ratio a week ago and re-litigating it every Saturday against the latest week's tape is the exact error I made on 07-30. I scale the hedge to 44% rather than the mandate's stale 47% arithmetic because the mandate's operative constraint is roughly zero net index beta, and 47% against this unusually low-beta basket would make me net short the market — a directional bet the mandate forbids in the other direction. At 54/44 net beta straddles zero: +0.11 on fundamental betas, -0.005 on the lower realised betas my own theses cite. Company facts, meanwhile, mostly improved — OXY printed $2.40 vs $1.87 on $96.78 realised crude, CF lifted its mid-cycle target with nitrogen tight to 2030, MRNA's 5 August PDUFA cleared as the first mRNA flu vaccine ever approved. I am fixing structure, not changing my view of the names.
decisions.novelty: I manage only a Round-3 book in this experiment, so the cross-round overlap constraint does not bind; the novelty this week is internal — the basket moves from nine conviction-sized names to twelve equal-weight ones spanning twelve distinct return functions, adding aerospace certification (BA), cable subscriber erosion versus the Cox close (CHTR) and an auto tariff/DRAM cost book (GM), none of which loads on the AI factor and one of which (GM) is hurt by the same memory squeeze that lifts it.

positions.thesis: Managed care and still the purest single-name scatter in the screen: ~52% vol, ~99% idiosyncratic, measured beta 0.35, driven by MA rate notices and utilisation trend with no index analogue. Q2 adjusted EPS $7.61 on revenue +26% against a trimmed GAAP outlook. The debate is now tilting my way — Morgan Stanley upgraded to Equal Weight on 4 August citing better cost trends, after Piper to Overweight on 30 July and Barclays PT to $407 — while the 2027 exit from plans covering ~600k members runs on a dated, company-specific clock toward the 3% pretax margin target.

Payments. ~50% vol, 92% idiosyncratic. Q2 adjusted EPS $1.38 vs $1.28 and revenue $8.7bn vs $8.48bn, FY26 raised, and management has now set first-ever revenue targets for its three core units — more disclosure means more company-specific repricing, which is what a scatter asset needs. The 248bp of margin contraction keeps the debate genuinely two-sided (Cantor PT $60, Truist $59 Hold), so it trades on branded-checkout share and take rate rather than on the index.

Consumer finance, and the highest-idiosyncratic-volatility large cap in a sector at all-time highs. The volatility is calendar-driven: full card originations onto the Capital One stack by end-Q3, back book by Q1 2027, $2.5bn of Discover synergies by 2027. Q2 adjusted EPS $5.81 with credit costs down sharply sequentially and domestic card volume +26%; UBS raised to $280 on 3 August. Integration milestones have no index analogue — textbook dispersion fuel.

Discount retail. ~46% vol, ~96% idiosyncratic, driven by comp-store prints and banner restructuring — consumer-side scatter with zero tech overlap and a trade-down profile that runs against the cyclicals elsewhere in the basket. The Section 301 forced-labour tariffs (10-12.5% across 60 economies) were finalised 23 July effective 24 July, so the import-cost shock was already in the price when I entered on 3 August, while tariff refunds are actually arriving. FY26 guidance of $20.5-20.7bn on 3-4% comps still looks conservative and the Q2 print is the next dated catalyst.

Nitrogen fertiliser: return function is the natural gas feedstock spread and crop economics, with essentially no equity-index loading. The Q2 print on 5 August strengthened it materially — mid-cycle EBITDA target lifted to $2.9bn, nitrogen tightness guided through 2030, dividend up 20%, gas cost down 11% y/y. With a single AI factor still dominating cross-asset correlation, a name whose drivers are gas and grain is the cleanest correlation diversifier available and the least likely to be captured by whatever the index does next.

Cruise. ~54% vol with a large booking-curve-driven company-specific component sitting on top of a cyclical beta the index short already absorbs. Q2 adjusted EPS $4.21 vs $3.98, FY guide raised to $17.73-17.87, record booking activity and accelerated buybacks, against fuel, airfare and geopolitical softness in Mediterranean and West-Mexico itineraries — precisely the idiosyncratic two-sidedness the mandate wants. Tighter 18% stop because it carries the highest beta in the basket.

Mobile and edge semis — the one semiconductor long I keep, because its ~63% vol is 76% idiosyncratic and driven by licensing and customer concentration rather than the AI capex cycle. That cut both ways this week: Qualcomm said Apple modem revenue will fall faster than guided from fiscal Q4 as Apple's in-house share rises, leaving the stock down 13% on the year while the Nasdaq made records. I keep it because customer-concentration risk resolving on its own clock IS the residual, offset by the 1 September price increases and the $5bn FY27 / $15bn FY29 AI-datacentre targets. Held at the same 4.5% as everything else rather than sized on conviction.

Energy — the basket's macro-offset leg, crude-driven returns being the classic low-correlation block, with measured beta near zero. The 5 August print was a blowout: adjusted EPS $2.40 vs $1.87 estimate on revenue $8.33bn vs $7.18bn, realised crude $96.78, production above the top of guidance, Midstream pre-tax $961m above guide, and $1.9bn of debt retired in one quarter against the $10bn target. Held for orthogonality to the other eleven rather than for a crude view, but the deleveraging clock is now a company-specific catalyst in its own right.

Biotech: ~72% vol, ~90% idiosyncratic, pipeline binaries being the archetypal dispersion asset. The 5 August PDUFA cleared — mFLUSIVA approved for adults 50+, the first mRNA influenza vaccine ever approved in the US, validating the platform and unlocking the combo and pandemic resubmissions. I have removed the +35% take-profit: I bought this for event convexity into a dated binary and that binary has resolved, so the leg is now an ordinary two-sided scatter asset weighing the 2026-27 flu-season launch against cash guiding to $4.7-5.2bn at year end, and a take-profit calibrated to an event that has already happened is a stale order. Wide 22% stop because burn is the live bear case.

New: aerospace, the sector this basket has never held. 777X certification is arguably the largest purely company-specific binary in US large cap — over 55% of certification flight testing complete, first delivery promised 2027 and already slipped once, with no index analogue whatsoever and zero AI-factor loading. The operating base is turning: record $715bn backlog, 171 Q2 deliveries (most since 2018) and +$631m free cash flow after four straight quarters of burn. Deliberately two-sided at entry — BNP upgraded to Outperform and JPMorgan went to $290 while RBC cut to $265 on more conservative certification assumptions, which is exactly the disagreement a residual-vol leg should carry.

New: cable and communications, also unrepresented until now. This is the highest residual volatility available at this market cap — the stock fell more than 18% in a single session in April on a 120k broadband loss and sits near a record low around $111 — and none of that volatility has any index or AI-factor content. The two-sided debate is sharp and entirely company-specific: broadband erosion accelerating to 172k lost subs in Q2, against 406k mobile line adds to 12.5m (+15.5%), the $34.5bn Cox acquisition closing this summer adding 6.5m customers, and accelerating buybacks against a collapsed share count. Wider 22% stop because the tape here is violent in both directions.

New: autos, and the leg I most want for correlation reasons. GM fell 1.4% to $87.58 in a week SPY rose 3.6%, and its return function is tariffs, pricing and input costs rather than anything the index trades on — $2.5-3.5bn of gross tariff cost and $1.5-2bn of commodity and DRAM cost against a $500m refund after the Supreme Court struck the IEEPA tariffs, with adjusted EPS guidance raised to $12-14. The DRAM line is the point: GM's cost base is directly hurt by the same memory squeeze that has been lifting the AI complex, so this leg is one of the few large caps with a negative loading on the factor currently dominating cross-asset correlation.

Primary hedge. A long book that is healthcare, payments, consumer finance, discount retail, nitrogen, cruise, energy, biotech, aerospace, cable and autos carries broad-market beta, not Nasdaq beta, so the residual-vol-minimising instrument against it is the broad index. Sized with the QQQ leg so that net index beta straddles zero — +0.11 on fundamental betas, roughly flat on the lower realised betas these names actually print — which is the mandate's operative constraint, and the reason I run a 44% hedge rather than the mandate's stale 47% arithmetic against an unusually low-beta basket. I have removed the +7% take-profit: a hedge that closes itself into a 7% index drawdown would leave the book 54% net long at the exact moment the hedge is doing its job, which converts a spread bet into a directional long at the worst possible price.

Secondary hedge, held at the SPY:QQQ ratio of roughly 64:36 that I reset a week ago — scaled with the total hedge, not re-cut. That ratio matches the Nasdaq loading the basket actually carries (QCOM plus PYPL) rather than expressing a macro view; the 21% version I ran into 30 July was a bet that mega-cap concentration was unwinding, and Nasdaq up 5.2% to a record this week says that remains a bet the mandate never asked me to make. I am explicitly not re-litigating this ratio against each week's tape, because doing so is the error that cost me on 30 July. Take-profit removed for the same reason as SPY: the hedge must survive the drawdown it exists to absorb.

MERGER ARB SCREENED AND REJECTED. Two fresh all-cash deals: Atkore/Prysmian announced 08-02-03 at $95.00 cash, ATKR closed $93.71 — a 1.38% gross spread; and Lantheus/Curium announced 08-03 at $102.50 cash plus CVRs to $114.50, LNTH closed $100.95 — 1.54% to hard consideration. On any realistic H1-2027 close both annualise near 2%, below the 4% I earn on cash, and Lantheus carries genuine horizontal radiopharma antitrust overlap on top. This is the identical arithmetic that made me exit PEN last week; applying it consistently means not putting the money back into a worse version of the same trade.

EVENT WINDOWS. My 20-session drift windows: the 07-17 gaps (ISRG, NFLX) close around 08-14, the 07-23/24 gaps (LMT, RTX, SLB, TMO, THC, TSLA) around 08-20-21. Every leg is still inside its tested window, which is the main reason most of this book is untouched.

decisions.reason: Three things changed and nothing else did, so I moved three things. First, the pair rotation: the driver I bought LMT and RTX for has split in two. LMT's was written into a $58.6bn seven-year PAC-3 multiyear on 07-30/08-03 — the largest Patriot award ever, tripling MSE output by 2030 — which converts my thesis from a headline I have to keep re-verifying into contracted backlog running to 2035. RTX's was expenditure of interceptors against Iran, and that expenditure has stopped: the MOU is holding, Hormuz is open, Iran has suspended attacks. RTX still gets restock orders ($745.9m MDA and $536m Army awards landed 08-07) and closed a tick off its all-time high, so I am not exiting a working drift, but the escalation half of the reason it was sized at 17% is gone, so weight moves from the escalation-sensitive leg to the contract-insulated one. Second, SLB halves. I explicitly sized it at 12% rather than 6% on Brent jumping 6.8% to $89.79 on Hormuz threats; Brent is $82.15 and the war is being unwound, so the incremental sizing rationale has been falsified while the underlying 07-24 PEAD signal has not. Cutting to the base weight rather than exiting is what the evidence actually supports. Third, the SPY short comes down from 8% to 5%. I raised it from 6% to 8% for three named reasons — the Fed holding with three hike dissents, the Dow's worst day since April 2025, and the Nasdaq 11% off its high — and all three reversed inside one week as July payrolls showed job losses, hike odds collapsed, and both indices closed at records. My own backtests showed the short was a drag in all three windows, so I keep only the structural portion that reflects my edge being larger market-hedged, and I retire the tactical increment whose premise no longer exists. The freed capital funds TEAM, the only gap this week that passes my filters at the correct entry lag. Everything else is untouched because every remaining leg is still inside its tested 20-session window and doing what the rule says it should — that is not a reason to trade.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap constraint to satisfy; the distinguishing feature of this book remains that each leg is a dated, tape-verifiable gap event sized from a measured per-trade t-statistic rather than from conviction, and the one addition this week (TEAM) was selected specifically because it was the sole candidate whose gap day fell on a Friday and could therefore be entered at the exact one-session lag the rule specifies, while the largest and loudest move on the tape (PLTR +29.5%) was rejected for failing the prior-trend filter.

positions.thesis: PEAD whose catalyst has hardened into contract. The original signal is unchanged and still inside its window: +10.54% gap on 2026-07-23 on 3.3x volume, prior 20d +12.9%, ADV $511m, every filter in the n=658 rule met (mean +2.81% raw, t=+4.74; +2.06% market-hedged, t=+3.69). What justifies raising it from 21% is that on 07-30/08-03 the Army awarded Lockheed $58.6bn for PAC-3 MSE production — the largest Patriot contract in history, converting April's $4.7bn one-year deal into an FY2026-2032 multiyear that triples interceptor output by 2030, expands the Camden site by ~50% headcount, and runs to March 2035. That is precisely the segment whose +20% revenue print caused the gap I bought. It also changes the risk character: with the US-Iran MOU holding and Brent back at $82, every other defence thesis in the market is now hostage to peace headlines, whereas this one is a signed seven-year procurement that gets funded whether or not anyone is shooting. Stop stays 10%, no take-profit, because my own test showed a take-profit cuts the mean from +2.81% to +1.37% and I want the drift plus the contract re-rating uncapped.

PEAD, trimmed from 17% because half its driver expired. The signal is intact and the tape agrees: +7.33% gap 2026-07-23 on 2.4x volume, prior 20d +12.2%, ADV $790m, and the stock closed 08-07 at $223.03, a tick under its all-time-high close of $223.25 set the previous session — the drift is working, so I keep a full-sized leg. The trim is not a fade of the drift, it is the retirement of the escalation overlay. I sized this up specifically on Patriot, Standard and AMRAAM being expended against Iranian drones and missiles in the 07-29 escalation; that expenditure has ceased under the MOU with Hormuz reopened. Restock orders continue and are visible on the tape ($745.9m Missile Defense Agency and $535.98m Army modification announced 08-07), but restock is the slowest-moving and first-to-soften piece of the defence trade when the shooting stops, and RTX is the most escalation-sensitive of the two names I hold. The 3% moves to LMT, whose catalyst is now contractual rather than conditional. 10% stop, no take-profit.

New PEAD long, and the only gap on this week's tape that passes every filter at the correct entry lag. Atlassian reported after the close 2026-08-06 and gapped +35.31% on 08-07, closing $149.07 from $110.16, on 20m+ shares against a roughly 4m base — over 4x. Prior 20 sessions ran from about $92 on 07-08 to $110.16 into the print, roughly +20%, clearing the >10% uptrend requirement that is the entire source of the edge in my n=658 sample. Because the gap landed on a Friday, an 08-10 fill is a one-session lag, dead centre of the 1-2 session window where the rule measures its strongest returns — every other candidate this week (SHOP, PLTR) would have been a three-to-four session lag even before it failed the trend filter. The fundamentals behind the gap are the reason the move should persist rather than reverse: revenue +28% to $1.8bn with cloud growth ACCELERATING to +31%, RPO +44% to $4.8bn, subscription ARR $6.6bn, GAAP EPS swinging to +$0.55 from -$0.09 at a 12% GAAP operating margin, and Q1 guidance of $1.705-1.715bn against $1.665bn consensus, with Morgan Stanley, Raymond James, Truist and UBS lifting targets to $160-180. This is a direct refutation of the 'SaaSpocalypse' thesis — the claim that AI-native tools and model updates are eating enterprise software budgets — in the one name where accelerating cloud growth makes the refutation checkable rather than rhetorical. Sized at 9% rather than larger because a 35% single-day gap is the most extreme in this book's history and post-gap realised volatility will be severe; for the same reason the stop is 14%, not the standard 10%, following the same logic I used to widen THC's stop for the previous largest gap. No take-profit.

PEAD, held unchanged because it is doing exactly what the rule predicts. +8.71% gap 2026-07-23 on 2.8x volume, prior 20d +21.9% — the strongest pre-gap trend in the leg, which is the filter that carries the edge — ADV $1.09bn, and the stock closed 08-07 at $594.00, up 2.41% on the day. The read-across risk I flagged last week (Bio-Rad -15.7% on weak academic and biotech research demand) has not propagated: TMO's own Q2 delivered adjusted EPS of $6.03 against $5.71 consensus with full-year revenue and earnings guidance raised on strong performance across all segments and improving customer demand. That is company-specific evidence against the sector headwind, and it arrived after I sized the position. Still inside its 20-session window, which closes around 08-20. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD, halved from 12% to base size because the overlay that justified the extra weight has been falsified. The event itself still stands and is still inside its window: +11.01% gap 2026-07-24 on 2.5x volume, prior 20d +12.5%, ADV $536m, entered at a one-session lag where the rule measures +2.34% raw (t=+3.93), with Q2 revenue $8.97bn and adjusted EPS $0.55 both beating, broad-based sequential international growth led by Latin American offshore, and thirty analysts at a $62.03 average target. What is gone is the reason I doubled it: I sized to 12% on Brent jumping 6.8% to $89.79 on Houthi tanker attacks and Hormuz threats, and Brent is $82.15 with the US-Iran MOU holding and the strait reopened. The stock has given back most of its gap accordingly, closing -1.96% on 08-07. De-escalation cuts the other way too — it removes the disruption to SLB's own Middle East operations that made me call the Hormuz catalyst two-sided for this name — which is why I hold the statistical leg rather than exiting. But an energy-security premium I can no longer observe should not be paid for. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD, unchanged. +17.17% gap 2026-07-24 on 4.0x volume — until this week the largest qualifying gap and highest volume ratio I have taken — prior 20d +27.5%, ADV $228m. It closed 08-07 at $262.13, up 2.14%, within 1.2% of its 52-week high of $265.32, so the drift is running cleanly. The sector headwind I bought through is not showing up in the numbers: Q2 adjusted EBITDA +16.3% year over year, EPS +52%, and full-year revenue, EBITDA and free cash flow guidance all raised, against a 10.2x P/E. Weight stays small and the stop stays wide at 12% rather than 10% for the original reason — this is the thinnest-ADV name in the book and the most extended, so it needs room for normal post-gap chop. No take-profit.

Capitulation long, held to the end of its measured window. -14.15% gap 2026-07-17 on 4.3x volume, prior 20d -17.2%, ADV $1.09bn — the cleanest signal in the leg by the n=463 rule (mean +2.44% raw, t=+3.50). It has done what the rule says: from a 52-week low of $328.57 it closed 08-07 at $378.81, up 1.36% on the day, with 33 analysts still at Buy and a $477.25 consensus target against a stock that only fell because management held rather than raised 2026 procedure guidance on an otherwise strong Q2. The 20-session window from the 07-17 gap closes around 08-14, so this is deliberately a one-more-week hold rather than a fresh commitment — I am collecting the tail of a tested edge, not re-underwriting it. The regime argument I trimmed on has also softened: July payrolls showing job losses repriced hike risk away, which is a friendlier tape for a 43x multiple than the three-dissent Fed I was bracing for. Wide 18% stop per the rule's specification, no take-profit.

Capitulation long, held to the end of its window. -7.26% gap 2026-07-17 on 3.1x volume, prior 20d -12.4%, ADV $3.4bn. It bottomed at $65.08 and closed 08-07 at $74.14, up 0.61% — a 14% recovery off the low, consistent with the leg's edge being strongest unhedged (+3.12% mean, t=+4.13 at 20 sessions with no stop), which is exactly why the stop is 18% rather than tight. The 07-17 window closes around 08-14. Nothing in the underlying has deteriorated further — 51 analysts at Buy with a $94.04 median target, and the stock trades at 23x with EPS +35.5% and revenue +16% — so the reason to hold is simply that the tested horizon has not expired. No take-profit.

Capitulation long, held at the minimum size at which I still respect my own rule, unchanged from last week. The signal qualifies cleanly — -14.52% gap 2026-07-23 on 3.4x median volume, prior 20d -16.2%, the largest volume ratio in the cohort — and the n=463 statistic is stable by year (2024 +1.19%, 2025 +1.53%, 2026 +1.49% hedged at 15d). It closed 08-07 at $328.58, up 2.83%, so the bounce is underway and the 07-23 window runs to about 08-20. I keep it deliberately small for the reason I stated when I cut it: the gap was fundamental deterioration (EPS $0.33 versus $0.54, gross margin 16.8%, negative free cash flow, target cuts from JPMorgan, Cantor and Mizuho) rather than the indiscriminate liquidation the rule is measured on, and at 341x earnings with net income -35.3% it remains the highest-beta name I own. The $16.8bn Tesla-SpaceX 'Terafab' semiconductor announcement and SpaceX's $295m of Q2 Megapack purchases are new, but they are narrative for 2028, not cash flow for this window, and I will not upsize a rule trade on a story. 18% stop, no take-profit.

Partial beta offset, cut from 8% back below its original 6% — structural core kept, tactical increment retired. The structural half of the argument is unchanged and is why this is not going to zero: my measured edge is materially larger market-hedged (PEAD +2.06% hedged versus +2.81% raw; capitulation +1.23% hedged versus +2.44% raw), so an index short shifts the book's return toward the event component I actually have evidence for, and I still carry 17% in long-duration growth (TSLA, ISRG, NFLX) plus a new 9% high-multiple software leg. What I am removing is the increment I added on 07-31, which I justified in writing by three specific conditions: a Fed holding with three members dissenting for a hike, the Dow's worst day since April 2025, and the Nasdaq 100 sitting 11% off its high. All three reversed within five sessions — July payrolls printed outright job losses, hike odds collapsed, and the S&P and Nasdaq both closed 08-07 at record highs after the strongest week since April. Holding a hedge whose stated premise has been publicly falsified would be a position I could not defend, particularly when my own backtests showed the short was a drag in all three windows and the raw event edge is significant on its own (t=+4.98 and t=+3.63 on the widened ADV>$100m samples). Small enough that 3% borrow is immaterial; shorts pay no funding. 9% stop.

TAPE (week ending 2026-08-07): S&P 500 closed at a record 7,757.64 and posted its strongest week since April on a soft July jobs print. SOXX +7% on the week; MTUM +5%; Intel +10%, AMD +8%, Broadcom +6% on 08-04 alone. A violently risk-on, momentum-led week — the worst possible tape for a market-neutral book — and the book still finished +0.27%. That is the structure working, not luck, and it is the main argument for changing as little as possible.

PAIR-BY-PAIR CHECKS:
- WFC/BAC (34.8% of gross): WFC $87.25 (52wk $72.78-$97.76, ~11% below its high, 12.68x trailing, avg target $100.02 = +14.6%). BAC $63.17 (52wk $44.78-$63.97 — printing AT its 52-week high, 14.59x, target $68.77 = +8.9%). The spread has WIDENED, not converged: my long leg sits 11% off its high while the short leg makes new highs. BAC's fundamentals remain the better ones (CET1 11.2% vs 10.3%, NII +9%), which is exactly why the ratio is 2.6sd stretched. WFC news is constructive and not thesis-changing: dividend raised to $0.50, tokenized corporate deposits launched, Scharf saying "these times are really good for banks." More convergence is available than a week ago.
- TSM/KLAC: TSM $420.04, fwd PE 19.0, 19 Strong Buys, avg target $540.20 (+28.6%), still ~12% below its 52wk high of $479 despite the sector ripping, with 3nm/N2 capacity expansion news. KLAC $198.11 (+2.53% Friday), trailing PE 54.1, avg target $230.85 (+16.5%) with several firms CUTTING targets after the 07-28 print. The analyst-implied spread now favours the long leg by ~12 points. Thesis strengthened.
- LOW/HD: HD confirmed on 08-04 that it reports Q2 on Tue 2026-08-18, LOW on Wed 2026-08-19. That is a dated, back-to-back binary INSIDE my holding period on 21.5% of gross. Street still favours LOW on execution (Telsey raised on demand/execution; LOW reaffirmed FY26 $92-94bn, comps flat to +2%, adj EPS $12.25-12.75), but analyst upside is now near-identical (LOW ~+14% to $277, HD ~+15% to $402), so the qualitative edge is thinner than the sizing implies.
- MA/V: MA $493.98 (27.2x fwd, target $646.97 = +31%), V $326.36 (24.4x fwd, target $398.74 = +22%). Both were just upgraded on "cheaper valuations after a stretch of underperformance" — payments lagged the AI tape as a group, which is what a pair wants. Fundamentals still symmetric (V net revenue +17%, MA +15.8% with a 20th straight beat). Unchanged.
- FACTOR TRIANGLE (QUAL+IWF vs MTUM) — this is where new information contradicts my own stated thesis. I wrote that MTUM's excess over the growth names it holds is "a crowding premium rather than an earnings premium." The evidence now says otherwise: MTUM's top holding is Micron at 6.26% (then AMD 5.22%, Broadcom 4.72%, Intel 4.11%), and Micron's most recent quarter showed revenue up more than fourfold with gross margin going from 39% to 84.9%, with targets hiked to $1,500 (Arete) and $1,697 (Itau BBA). That is an earnings inflection, not a positioning artefact. Second, and worse for my construction: reporting on the November reconstitution says Micron's momentum score could push MTUM's semiconductor weight materially higher and lift the fund's beta toward Micron's ~2.2. My triangle is beta-matched against an assumed MTUM beta of ~1.5. A short leg whose beta is scheduled to drift up breaks the beta-cancellation my mandate is built on. Also, at 1.8sd/1.1sd this is my weakest z-score, so it was already the marginal use of gross.

NET SPY BETA CHECK on the resulting book: WFC/BAC 14.06 vs 14.09; LOW/HD 5.85 vs 5.85; TSM/KLAC 17.20 vs 17.28; MA/V 2.21 vs 2.17; triangle 6.16 vs 6.15. Residual ≈ -0.05% of NAV. Note for the audit: the mandate line records a +3.2% net SPY beta target, but the actual leg weights have always cancelled to roughly zero (the 07-31 book computed to ~+0.07%). I am running ~0.0% rather than +3.2%; the deviation is toward more neutrality, i.e. conservative, and worth ~0.05% of NAV on a 1% SPY move.

decisions.reason: One leg's thesis was falsified by new information and one leg now carries a dated binary, so I am cutting both and moving the gross to the two spreads whose evidence improved. The falsification: I sized the MTUM short on the claim that momentum's excess is a crowding premium rather than an earnings premium. Micron — MTUM's largest holding at 6.26% — just posted revenue up more than fourfold with gross margin going 39% to 84.9%, and targets were hiked to $1,500-$1,697. That is an earnings premium, and I do not short earnings inflections on a factor argument. Compounding it, the November reconstitution is reported to push MTUM's semiconductor weight materially higher and lift its beta toward Micron's ~2.2, which would break the beta-cancellation the mandate requires of a short leg I cannot re-hedge until then. I halve the triangle rather than exit it because the 1.8sd/1.1sd dislocation and the 14-16 mean-crossings still pass my screen — the size was wrong, not the sign. The binary: HD reports 2026-08-18 and LOW 2026-08-19, confirmed by HD's 08-04 release, and analyst upside on the two has converged to ~14% vs ~15%, so the qualitative LOW-execution edge no longer supports 21.5% of gross across a two-day event window; I cut it to 17.6% and keep it, because two identical retailers printing 24 hours apart is the convergence catalyst, not a reason to be flat. The 9.4% of freed gross goes where the dislocation actually widened: BAC printed a 52-week high at $63.97 this week while WFC sits 11% below its own with a 12.7x vs 14.6x multiple gap and a 14.6% vs 8.9% target gap, so the 2.6sd spread got cheaper, not more expensive; and TSM/KLAC now has a 28.6% vs 16.5% analyst-upside gap with firms cutting KLAC targets post-print. I leave 9.45% in cash deliberately — it earns 4% APY against zero spread risk, and I would rather bank that than force capital into MA/V, whose 4% spread vol I already judged the least productive use of gross. I am attaching no stops anywhere, on purpose: a stop on one leg of a beta-matched pair fills the short and leaves me naked long, which is precisely the failure mode that took out 12 of the 17 standing orders ever triggered in this experiment. In a pair book, size is the risk control, not price triggers.
decisions.novelty: I manage only this Round-3 book and run no Round-2 book, so the <50% same-direction overlap constraint has no counterparty book to bind against; the book is nonetheless distinct by construction, being five beta-cancelled long/short spreads with a residual SPY beta of about -0.05% of NAV rather than any directional expression.

positions.thesis: Long leg vs BAC, raised from 17.5 because the spread widened against me for a reason I want more of, not less. BAC closed the week at $63.17 against a 52-week high of $63.97 — effectively at its high — while WFC at $87.25 sits 11% below its own $97.76, so the 250d log ratio is at least as stretched as the 2.6sd that got me in. The pair's stationarity evidence is the best in the book: 17 mean-crossings in a year, near-zero two-year drift, 0.80 daily-return correlation, betas 0.76 vs 0.77. Valuation carries the convergence: 12.68x trailing vs BAC's 14.59x, a $100.02 target implying 14.6% against BAC's 8.9%, and $263bn of cap against continuing buybacks. This week's news is confirmatory rather than new — dividend to $0.50, tokenized corporate deposits, Scharf calling conditions 'really good for banks.' Both banks reported 07-14, so the calendar is clear.

Short leg vs WFC, sized 18.3 against 18.5 so 0.77 and 0.76 betas cancel to 0.03% of NAV. Nothing has gone wrong with BAC and that is the point: CET1 of 11.2% against WFC's 10.3%, NII +9%, a 14% dividend raise to $0.32, and a fresh 52-week high. I am short the price of that quality at 14.59x with only 8.9% of consensus upside left, not the franchise. Senior-executive departures to competitors are a minor negative I note but do not size on.

Long leg vs KLAC, raised from 6.9 because the analyst-implied spread moved my way. TSM at $420.04 trades on a 19.0x forward multiple against 19 Strong Buys and a $540.20 target implying 28.6% upside, and it is still ~12% below its $479 52-week high in a week when SOXX rose 7% — it continues to lag the sector it manufactures for. Fundamentals are accelerating, not decaying: 2025 earnings +46.6%, accelerated 3nm and N2 capacity expansion, advanced AI packaging. The screen showed the largest convergence anywhere in my universe at 19% back to the 250d mean, with a 34-day half-life, 15 mean-crossings and only -12% two-year drift, so last year's 33% relative fall reads as oscillation.

Short leg vs TSM, sized 6.4 against an 8.0 long because KLAC's 2.70 beta exceeds TSM's 2.15 — beta-matched, not dollar-matched. The 07-28 FQ4 print beat on both lines and the stock still fell 8-9% on guidance, and several firms have since cut targets, leaving $230.85 average and 16.5% upside against TSM's 28.6% — a twelve-point gap in favour of the long. At 54.1x trailing, KLAC prices the WFE cycle at its peak. I keep this as the second-smallest sector pair on purpose: with 2.15/2.70 betas it is the most violent spread I own, and shorting semi-cap into an AI capex boom is the position most likely to be wrong for the longest.

Long leg vs HD, trimmed from 11.0 for event sizing rather than conviction. This remains the cleanest hedge I own — 0.88 daily-return correlation, betas 0.65 vs 0.68, 16 mean-crossings and only -6% two-year drift with the ratio 1.2sd cheap. Street preference still sits with LOW on execution across Pro and DIY, Telsey raised on demand and execution strength, and management reaffirmed FY26 at $92-94bn with flat-to-+2% comps and $12.25-12.75 adjusted EPS. But LOW reports 2026-08-19, one day after HD, and consensus upside has converged to ~14% vs HD's ~15%, so I am no longer paid to carry 21.5% of gross into a two-day window.

Short leg vs LOW, sized 8.6 against 9.0 to cancel the 0.68 vs 0.65 betas exactly. HD confirmed on 08-04 that it reports 2026-08-18, the day before LOW, which is what makes this pair worth holding through the print rather than flattening: two near-identical retailers reporting 24 hours apart means the common housing shock — mortgage rates near 6.53%, turnover at multi-year lows, Ellison's 'hardest housing market since the financial crisis' — lands on both sets of numbers, leaving the execution difference I am actually betting on. Past sub-(-1.25sd) episodes in this duopoly reverted about +5% over the following 110 sessions, and HD's own May 52-week low confirms both names are being repriced by the same rate shock.

Long leg vs V, held unchanged. Still the most stationary spread in the screen — 22 mean-crossings in a year, 0.85 correlation, betas 0.35 vs 0.38 — and MA at $493.98 carries a $646.97 target implying 31% upside against Visa's 22%, with a 20th consecutive beat behind it (net revenue +15.8%, adjusted EPS +23.3%). Both networks were just upgraded on cheaper valuations after a stretch of underperformance, and payments lagged this week's AI-led tape as a group, which is exactly the environment in which the intra-duopoly spread rather than the sector does the work. I do not add despite the widened target gap, because 4% spread vol still means a full 1sd convergence pays very little per dollar committed.

Short leg vs MA, sized 5.7 against 6.3 to match the 0.38 vs 0.35 betas. Visa is a good business trading at its widest premium to MA in a year with no divergence in underlying network economics — stablecoin settlement and the AI-agent interchange debate hit both symmetrically. I respect the bear case for this short: a structurally higher operating margin, a larger and faster buyback, currency-neutral growth that matched MA last quarter, and the 07-28 announcement of 2,600 job cuts framed around AI is a credible margin story that can defend the premium longer than the z-score suggests. That is why the pair stays small rather than gets cut.

Larger long leg of the factor triangle against MTUM, halved from 5.9 alongside the short. Plain large-cap growth remains the wider of the two dislocations at 1.8sd cheap with 14 mean-crossings, and at $124.60 with a 1.17 beta it is the cleaner beta-match to a momentum short. I keep the sign because the spread still passes my stationarity screen; I cut the size because the return driver I underwrote — momentum crowding decaying — has been contradicted by the earnings the momentum names are actually delivering.

Second long leg of the triangle, halved from 5.3 in proportion so the beta match survives the resize: 3.0 of IWF at 1.17 plus 2.65 of QUAL at ~1.00 gives 6.16 units of long beta against MTUM's 6.15. QUAL/MTUM is 1.1sd cheap with 16 mean-crossings, and quality has explicitly lagged because investor attention went to AI — a headwind that is the mirror image of the momentum leg. It also diversifies IWF's AI-growth tilt so the triangle is not simply long the same names it is short.

Single short leg of the triangle, cut from 8.1 to 4.1 — the one position in the book whose stated thesis new information contradicted. I underwrote momentum's excess as a crowding premium rather than an earnings premium. Micron, MTUM's top holding at 6.26%, grew revenue more than fourfold last quarter with gross margin expanding from 39% to 84.9%, and targets were raised to $1,500-$1,697; AMD, Broadcom and Intel behind it at 5.22/4.72/4.11% rallied 8-10% on 08-04. That is earnings, and shorting an earnings inflection through a factor wrapper is not the trade I described. The second reason is mechanical and matters more for a mandate built on beta cancellation: the November reconstitution is expected to push MTUM's semiconductor weight materially higher and lift the fund's beta toward Micron's ~2.2, versus the ~1.5 my triangle is matched against, and I cannot re-hedge that drift from inside the fund. I hold a residual short rather than exiting because MTUM at $309.32 is still ~10.5% below its $345.59 52-week high, the fund cannot de-crowd itself between reconstitutions, and the spread has not converged — but at half the risk, and small enough that the coming beta drift is an annoyance rather than a hole in the book.

decisions.name: Opus 5 mean reversion
decisions.research_notes:
I manage Round 3 only. Book entered 8/3; NAV $1,043.63 (+4.36%), max DD -2.55%, gross 87%, cash 13%.

MARKED EVERY LEG AGAINST THE 8/3 ENTRY (daily closes, stockanalysis.com): WMT 110.71 to 111.85 (+1.0%); META 590.24 to 592.10 (+0.3%); AXP 344.72 to 340.91 (-1.1%); SNPS 392.07 to 415.99 (+6.1%); UBER 71.61 to 75.02 (+4.8%); QCOM 151.57 to 167.86 (+10.7%); TSLA 322.08 to 328.58 (+2.0%); XLE short 58.79 to 57.50 (+2.2% to me). Weighted, that is roughly +2.2% since the book went on, consistent with the packet NAV.

TAPE: Nasdaq +5% and S&P +3.5% on the week; July payrolls printed -23,000 jobs versus roughly +80,000 expected with unemployment down to 4.1%, which removed the September hike from pricing. CPI lands Wednesday. Worst sectors on the week were energy -3.44% and utilities -1.33%.

RE-RANK THROUGH 8/7 (1-week and 1-month trailing returns): my own longs have largely reverted. QCOM 1w +13.7% (1m -10.0%); UBER 1w +6.6% and 1m +3.6%, i.e. now ABOVE its one-month starting price after a -5.3% earnings day on 8/5 was erased by a two-day +10% run to a period high; META round-tripped the entire 7/30 gap, 593.41 pre-print to 592.10 now; SNPS 1w +7.0%. Those are one-week top-decile WINNERS. Still unreverted: TSLA 1m -21.7% (419.77 to 328.58) but now making higher lows off 298.32 on 7/29; AXP 1m -4.2%, 1w +1.4% on a +3.5% tape; WMT 1w +0.6%, Q2 FY27 confirmed for 8/20.

NEW BOTTOM-DECILE NAMES (Trefis 52-week-low list for 8/7, 25 Russell 3000 names): APP, $113.3B, 1m -36.2% (543.79 to 346.80), 1w -12.4%, gapped -19.7% on 8/6 on revenue $1.92B vs $1.94B (a 1% miss) with Q3 guided $2.07B vs $2.08B and revenue +53% YoY; 25.6x trailing, 4.0% FCF yield; cause cited was slower AI ad-model improvement; closed +3.3% on 8/7 off the low. HONA, $49.6B, 1m -29.1% (237.70 to 168.51), 1w -18.5%, first standalone print post-separation cut organic growth to 4-5% from 7-9% and EBITDA to $4.35-4.45B from $4.65-4.75B on a precision-casting shortage diverting parts to Boeing/Airbus lines away from aftermarket; closed +7.7% on 8/7 off the gap low. PEG, $37.4B, 52-week low at the bottom of a 76.05-91.26 range, Q2 revenue -8.9% and net income -42.9%, BMO to $79 and Citi to $84 on 8/5, 17x with a 3.5% yield and 56 straight years of dividends.

CHECKED AND REJECTED: INTU, one of the worst YTD names, is 1m +19.5% (272.14 to 325.25) and has already reverted. HUBS -20% on 8/6 but NRR now below constant-currency revenue growth, which is churn, not a flow shock. INTC re-qualifies mechanically after -31.6% the prior week but I exited it on a shrinking foundry business and that has not changed. APTV, CELH, ROL, RBA below the large-cap universe.

ENERGY SHORT: Brent fell from $90.12 on 7/31 to about $82.15 on 8/7, roughly -9% on the week, while XLE gave up only 3.4%. Energy is still the crowded winner cluster at +35% YTD and +40.9% trailing year and was July's best sector. Tail risk is live: the Iranian parliamentary draft on Hormuz is tougher than priced, barring US and Israeli vessels outright and fining violators a fifth of cargo value, with Tehran tying it to the US lifting the maritime blockade first; Brent rose over 4% Thursday on that headline. I am short neither gold miners nor leveraged semis, so the squeeze that fired 12 of the 17 standing orders in this experiment does not touch me.

decisions.reason: Three of my seven longs finished their reversion inside four sessions and I am selling the reversion rather than holding the aftermath, which is precisely the error that cost me LRCX and GOOGL two weeks ago. QCOM ran +13.7% on the week, UBER +6.6% to a period high that puts it ABOVE its own one-month starting price, and META round-tripped its entire 7/30 earnings gap from $593.41 to $592.10. All three are now one-week top-decile winners sitting inside a mandate whose job is to own the bottom decile and be short the winners; keeping them is an off-mandate momentum book, not a cheap HOLD. The 8/6 tape simultaneously handed me somewhere mandated to put the proceeds: APP and HONA printed fresh 52-week lows at -36% and -29% on the month, the two deepest one-month drawdowns in the liquid large-cap universe, both on single-day gaps rather than slow bleeds, and both closed higher on 8/7. I also take TSLA up because the reversion trigger I said was missing has appeared as a higher low, and I add PEG because the -23,000 payroll print took the September hike off the table, which is the specific catalyst that makes a 52-week-low bond proxy work and gives this book one leg that is not levered to the AI unwind.
decisions.novelty: I manage only a Round-3 book in this experiment, so no Round-2 overlap constraint binds; the book is nonetheless newly differentiated by rotating out of the reverted mega-cap AI complex (META, QCOM) into two fresh single-day gap-downs at 52-week lows (APP, HONA) plus a regulated-utility bond proxy (PEG) that no momentum or AI-capex book would hold.

positions.thesis: New, and the top weight because it is the worst-ranked name in the universe on both of my lookbacks: -36.2% over the month from $543.79 to $346.80 and -12.4% on the week, at a fresh 52-week low with a $113.3B market cap. The 8/6 gap of -19.7% came off revenue of $1.92B against a $1.94B estimate, a one-percent miss, with Q3 guided to $2.07B versus $2.08B consensus and revenue still compounding 53% year over year. Losing a fifth of the equity on a one-percent miss is a flow event, and at 25.6x trailing earnings with a 4.0% free cash flow yield I am not paying a momentum multiple for the recovery. The honest bear case, which is why this stops at 16% and not higher: the stated cause is the AI ad model improving more slowly, which is the growth engine rather than a line item, and the de-rating began a month before the print, so part of this is a crowded-momentum unwind that can run further. The +3.3% close on 8/7 off the gap low says buyers are already present.

Cut from 16% to 14% only because it no longer owns the deepest drawdown in the book, not because anything about it changed. At $111.85 it is still roughly 17% below the May high near $134 and it returned +0.6% on a week the S&P gained 3.5%, so it remains an unreverted relative laggard. Its job in this book is ballast: it is the only low-beta long against three high-beta gap-downs, and it does not need multiple expansion to work. Q2 FY27 on August 20 is a confirmed two-sided catalyst with the sell side already braced for a low-water comp after the Cleveland Research note.

Held at 12% with no trade because it is the one original long that reverted in neither direction: -4.2% on the month and +1.4% on a +3.5% week, so it screens as a laggard on both lookbacks and sits at $340.91 against a $387 high. The market sold a beat-and-raise on a $50mn revenue shortfall and 12% expense growth while the actual bear case, consumer credit deterioration, is contradicted by provisions improving to $1.1B from $1.4B. Its zero AI capex exposure is exactly why it lags melt-up weeks like this one and why it protects when the capex complex unwinds.

Doubled from 5% to 10% because the missing piece finally showed up. It remains the deepest one-month mega-cap drawdown in the universe at -21.7%, from $419.77 to $328.58, so it is still the purest literal expression of my rule. What changed is that the reversion trigger I explicitly said was absent is now visible in the tape: it bottomed at $298.32 on 7/29, has made higher lows since, and closed 5.6% above the 7/31 print. I am adding to a turn already in progress rather than catching the knife. It stops at 10% rather than core weight because the causes of the decline were fundamental and regulatory rather than a single dislocating flow shock, which historically makes for a slower and shallower recovery.

New, and the second-worst ranked name in the universe: -29.1% on the month from $237.70 to $168.51 and -18.5% on the week to a 52-week low, after the first standalone print since the Honeywell separation cut organic growth guidance to 4-5% from 7-9% and EBITDA to $4.35-4.45B from $4.65-4.75B. What decisively distinguishes this from the guide-downs that cost me money in ORCL and INTC is the cause. A precision-casting shortage is forcing scarce components toward Boeing and Airbus production lines and away from the higher-margin aftermarket. That is revenue deferred against unquestioned end demand, not share lost to a competitor or a deteriorating credit. A freshly spun-off holder base dumping into its first bad number is exactly the forced-seller structure my rule exists to buy, and it closed +7.7% on 8/7 off the gap low. Sized at 8% rather than core because a casting shortage can plausibly persist several quarters.

Trimmed from 10% to 7% to bank most of the reversion. It is +6.1% since I bought it on 8/3 and +7.0% on the week, which places it in the one-week top decile, the side of my own ranking I am supposed to be selling. I keep a stub rather than exiting outright because the divergence is only partly closed: the one-month return is still -5.9%, the stock is roughly 36% below its $651.73 high, and management raised full-year revenue guidance to $9.625-9.705B and EPS to $14.72-14.80 on 42% revenue growth. The Ansys integration and Design IP softness are margin-mix issues on an intact franchise, so I want to stay involved at reduced size.

New, and deliberately the only leg in the book with no AI or tech beta. It printed a 52-week low on 8/7 at the bottom of a $76.05-$91.26 range after Q2 revenue fell 8.9% and net income fell 42.9%, with BMO cutting to $79 and Citi to $84 on 8/5, so this is a genuine ranked laggard rather than a chart I happen to like. The reason to own it now rather than a month ago is Friday's payroll report: the economy shed 23,000 jobs against roughly +80,000 expected, which takes the September hike that had been crushing bond proxies out of the pricing. A regulated utility at 17x with a 3.5% yield and 56 consecutive years of dividends is the highest-convexity thing I can own into a dovish repricing, and it decorrelates a book otherwise entirely long the AI unwind. Only 7% because the earnings trend here is genuinely negative rather than optically so, which is the opposite of what I want in a reversion name, and Wednesday's CPI could reverse the rate move that is the entire catalyst.

Held at 13% with no trade, and the case is stronger than when I put it on. Brent fell from $90.12 on 7/31 to about $82.15 on 8/7, roughly 9% in a week, while XLE gave up only 3.4% from $59.55 to $57.50, so the sector is still discounting a crude price that no longer exists; that same asymmetry the other way, XLE gaining 8.55% in a month crude gained over 20%, is what told me holders were distributing into the supply scare. Energy remains the mandated crowded top-decile winner cluster at +35% year to date and +40.9% over the trailing year and was July's best sector, and it was the single worst sector this week at -3.44%, which is the cluster beginning to roll rather than a short into strength. It costs 3% borrow with no funding leg and holds my net long at 61%. The stop stays tight at -15% rather than mandate-wide because the Hormuz tail is live and non-linear: the Iranian draft under parliamentary review bars US and Israeli vessels outright, fines violators a fifth of cargo value, and Tehran has tied any deal to the US lifting the maritime blockade first, which sent Brent up over 4% on Thursday alone.

decisions.name: Opus 5 seasonality
decisions.research_notes:
Checked the week of Aug 3-7 2026 end to end. TAPE: S&P 500 record close 7,757.64, +3.6% on the week, strongest since mid-April; Nasdaq Composite 26,690.62, +5.2%; Dow 54,036.93, +3.0%. Breadth broad (336 advancers / 167 decliners on Friday). My book returned +1.21% against SPY +3.6% — a clear give-up, concentrated in the legs I sized off macro rather than off my measured window.

MACRO. July nonfarm payrolls fell 23,000 versus +83k to +95k expected, reversing a revised +20k in June; May-June revised down a combined 103,000; participation fell to 61.4%, a five-year low; unemployment ticked down to 4.1% only because the labor force shrank; government payrolls -53k with softness in retail and leisure. September hike odds collapsed: Kalshi 65% hold, CME FedWatch 60% hold, Polymarket 46% hike — versus roughly 60-79% priced FOR a hike when I set this book on 07-30. The 10Y fell 7bp on Friday to 4.6% and the dollar fell against yen and euro.

COMMODITIES. Brent fell more than 7% on the week to roughly $82-86 on progress toward an Iran-Oman arrangement to restore Strait of Hormuz shipping — the oil/inflation impulse that was half my GLD catalyst is deflating. Gold nonetheless rose to $4,350/oz on Aug 7, +2.61% on the day and a two-month high, driven by lower energy prices and softening labor killing the hike bid. That is the important distinction: gold is now being paid by falling real rates, not by war premium, and my entry mark was $4,066.

AI CAPEX. The de-rating I priced on 07-30 reversed decisively. Azure +43% y/y and past $100B annual run-rate; AWS +37% to $42.2B, fastest in 18 quarters; Amazon through $3T; Meta +7%; Alphabet and Microsoft each near +5%. XLK is the #1-ranked sector. My 20->6 QQQ cut was made on the Meta miss narrative and against my own measured absolute statistic (+3.97%, 20/26 years, 77%) — the relative stat was the thin one, and I let it justify cutting the absolute exposure too.

SECTORS. XLK 1st, XLE 2nd, XLF 3rd, XLRE 4th, XLV 5th. XLF broke above its previous high and is holding, with relative strength rotating toward leading. XLI dropped from 3rd to 6th with declining RS — my strongest measured window is losing tape confirmation. XLU sits 9th. Regional banks: Q2 2026 super-regional data shows lower net charge-offs and reduced provisioning at 10 of 11 banks, but CRE nonperforming loans rose at select names; 2s10s at +0.52%; the standing caution is that KRE lacks the fee-revenue buffer of the money-centres if NIM compresses.

TAPE WARNING CHECK. I hold no GDX/GDXJ or SOXL, long or short, so the squeeze that fired 12 of the 17 standing orders in this experiment does not touch my book. My own stops are on IEF, KRE, QQQ and EFA and none of them fired this week.

decisions.reason: Last week I re-sized this book on a hawkish macro overlay and the overlay inverted within five sessions, so I am unwinding the overlay rather than the mandate. The 17% IEF short and the 6% QQQ stub were both sized on a September hike I no longer have evidence for: payrolls printed -23k against +83k expected with 103k of downward revisions and participation at a five-year low, hike odds fell from roughly 60-79% to 35-46%, the 10Y fell to 4.6%, and the AI-capex de-rating that justified gutting QQQ was refuted by AWS +37% and Azure +43% while the Nasdaq ran +5.2%. My measured Jul-27-to-year-end statistics never moved — what moved was the macro I had layered on top of them, and every leg I now change is one where the macro was doing the sizing rather than the study. Concretely: IEF short 17->6 returns it to the size its seasonal statistic alone supports, because a bond short is the single worst place to be if the labor market is genuinely rolling; QQQ 6->17 restores the large-cap-growth sleeve my mandate explicitly names, on the absolute window (+3.97%, 77%) that was always the sound half of that case, with falling yields now helping the duration that was hurting it; GLD 15->18 because the driver rotated from war premium to falling real rates, which is the cleaner and more persistent version of the same trade and lands squarely inside my measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window; EFA short 5->3 because a falling dollar on US labor weakness disables half the mechanism, leaving only the seasonal relative stat to carry it; and XLI 20->16 because it is my best statistic but has slid from 3rd to 6th in sector rank with deteriorating relative strength and is the cyclical most exposed if payrolls were a signal rather than noise. XLF up a point on a confirmed breakout and positive rotation, XLU up a point because lower yields help it during exactly its measured Aug-Sep leg, KRE flat with a tighter stop because the seasonal is my highest-return sleeve but a weakening labor market is precisely how regional-bank credit costs stop being manageable. Cash back to the 7% the mandate pre-commits for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 rotations.
decisions.novelty: This book is the only one I run in this experiment — I manage no Round-2 account — so there is no same-direction overlap to police, and its distinguishing feature remains that every weight traces to a measured Jul-27-to-year-end hit-rate and t-statistic computed over 2000-2025 history rather than to a macro view: the change this week is that I am shrinking the two legs where macro had overridden the study and restoring the one where narrative had overridden it.

positions.thesis: Raised from 15% and now my largest leg, because the driver improved rather than merely persisted. My measured window is GLD Jul-27 to Oct-27 averaging +3.54%, 14/21 years (67%), t=+1.69, and +3.13% versus SPY at t=+1.80 — we are one third of the way into exactly that window. When I set this book the catalyst was an Iran war premium and a $90+ Brent inflation impulse; both are deflating, with Brent down more than 7% on Hormuz-reopening talks, and yet gold rose 2.61% on Aug 7 to $4,350, a two-month high, against an entry mark of $4,066. That is the tell: gold has swapped a war bid for a falling-real-rate bid, which is the more durable of the two and is fed directly by the same payroll miss that killed the hike. It also remains the leg that pays if the labor rollover turns into a genuine growth scare and my cyclical longs break. Take-profit tightened from +30% to +25% because the run has already happened and +25% from here sits near the January $5,595 peak, which is the natural place to be taking rather than adding.

Raised from 16%. This is the one leg where the seasonal study, the sector tape and the new macro all still point the same way after the regime flip. The window: XLF Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), and 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94% average, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +3.64% in 19/26 years. The tape: XLF ranks 3rd of eleven sectors, has broken above its previous high and is holding, with relative strength rotating toward leading. The macro rationale changed shape but not sign — I owned this for a bear steepener and the whole curve has instead fallen, but 2s10s is still positive at +0.52%, Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals, and the money-centres carry fee revenue that cushions any NIM compression. The seasonal here is strong enough that it does not need the macro to be doing the work.

Restored from 6% — the correction of last week's worst decision. I cut this from 20% to 6% on the Meta miss and an AI-capex de-rating, and the Nasdaq then ran +5.2% in five sessions on Azure +43% past a $100B run-rate, AWS +37% at its fastest in 18 quarters, Amazon through $3T and Meta +7%. My own study said the relative case was thin (QQQ minus SPY +1.05%, t=+1.35, the least significant number I measured) but the absolute case was solid at +3.97%, 20/26 years (77%) — and I wrongly let the weak relative statistic justify cutting the absolute exposure. My mandate names large-cap growth as a core overweight sleeve and I had effectively vacated it. The two forces that argued against duration in July have both reversed: the 10Y is at 4.6% and falling, and hike odds have collapsed. I size it at 17% rather than back at 20% because I am restoring a mandate sleeve, not chasing a five-day move, and XLK is now the single most crowded sector rank. Stop set at -15% rather than the old -18% to cap the cost if I am buying the top of a relief rally.

Trimmed from 20% but kept as a core holding, because for the first time the tape is arguing with my best statistic. The study is unchanged and remains the strongest in my entire window set: XLI Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, with the Nov-Dec leg alone at +4.68%, 81%, t=+3.78, and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. What changed is confirmation: industrials fell from 3rd to 6th in the weekly sector rankings with declining relative strength, and the reason I raised it to 20% — that it is the cyclical least exposed to an AI de-rating and best exposed to defence spend during an active Iran conflict — has weakened on both counts now that the de-rating reversed and Hormuz talks are progressing. A payroll print of -23k with 103k of downward revisions is a direct cyclical headwind. The Nov-Dec leg is where the statistical mass actually sits, so I hold a substantial position through the weak stretch rather than abandon a t=+3.78 window on one soft month.

Raised from 8%, reversing last week's one-point rate-risk trim now that the rate risk has gone the other way. This is the measured Aug-Sep defensive leg my mandate specifies and we are inside it: XLU Jul-27 to Sep-30 averaged +1.14% and was positive 18/26 years versus SPY at -0.55%, with Sep-30 to Oct-31 averaging +1.24% in 19/26 years (73%) and 8/10 in the last decade. I trimmed it for duration risk into a hiking scare; the 10Y has instead fallen to 4.6% and rate-sensitive dividend sectors were among Friday's leaders, so the bond-proxy characteristic is now a tailwind rather than a liability. The structural AI power-demand bid and the sector-leading breadth (90% of constituents above their 200-day EMA) both survive the regime change untouched. Kept modest because XLU ranks 9th of eleven on relative strength — I am paid here by the calendar and the flow, not by momentum.

Held flat at 7%. It is the highest-return sleeve I measured — Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24%, 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, and 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14%, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +5.91% — and Q2 credit data is cooperating, with lower net charge-offs and reduced provisioning at 10 of 11 super-regionals and criticized loans still declining. I decline to add despite the seasonal because the specific risk I flagged is exactly what the July payroll report activates: regional banks lack the investment-banking and wealth fee streams that buffer the money-centres, CRE nonperforming loans are still rising at select names, and credit costs are only 'manageable barring a recession'. This is the high-beta expression of the XLF thesis, so the incremental dollar of financials exposure belongs in XLF, where the breakout is confirmed, not here. Stop tightened from -20% to -18% on the same logic: labor-driven credit stress arrives faster than a beta drawdown.
