Cut hard from 17% to 6% — the largest change in the book. The seasonal case is intact and is why I keep a position at all: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%, the most extreme statistic in my study. But 17% was never the seasonal size; it was the size the macro justified, and that macro is gone. I raised it on three FOMC dissents for a hike, 60-79% priced hike odds by September, Brent through $90 and long yields rising on a hold. Today hike odds are 35-46%, Brent is down over 7% on Hormuz-reopening talks, the 10Y fell 7bp on Friday to 4.6%, payrolls printed negative with 103k of downward revisions, and participation is at a five-year low. A short duration position sized on conviction is the single worst place to be if the labor market is actually rolling over, and I would rather be paid the small seasonal edge than defend an oversized macro bet I no longer believe. Stop tightened from -10% to -8% for the same reason — a bond rally of that size now means recession is being priced, and I want out before it correlates with my cyclical longs rather than after.

Trimmed from 5% to a residual. The seasonal statistic is still one of my better relative measures — EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65% average — and developed non-US equity is a short sleeve my mandate names explicitly, so I keep a token rather than vacate it. But the mechanism has degraded twice over. Half the case was dollar strength, and the dollar fell against both yen and euro on Friday as US labor weakness pulled yields down; a Fed that is no longer hiking while foreign central banks hold is the wrong rate differential for this trade. The other half was a US-led tech correction hurting the US more, and that correction just reversed with the Nasdaq +5.2%, which paradoxically flatters my QQQ leg while removing the divergence this short needs. Sized at 3% so that being wrong is an irrelevance and being right is a modest carry — the 3% borrow cost over five months is roughly 0.04% of NAV at this weight.

decisions.name: Opus 5 trend following
decisions.research_notes:
Checked the 3-7 Aug tape leg by leg against my two filters (price vs 50/200dma, 3m time-series momentum) and against the macro drivers I actually cited on 1 Aug.

THE EVENT: July payrolls, released Fri 7 Aug, printed -23,000 vs +80,000 expected — the first outright decline in months — with average hourly earnings +0.1% vs +0.3% and wage growth down to 3.2%. This is the exact opposite of the "JP Morgan now forecasts a December hike" premise on which I built three of my four short/dollar legs. CME FedWatch flipped from ~1-in-3 hold to 60% hold for September. Notably December hike odds are still ~75%, so the hiking cycle is not dead — which is why I exit these legs rather than reverse them.

PRICE CONFIRMATION (this is what governs, not the narrative):
- Gold $4,399.70 spot / GLD $398.47, +7% on the week from $4,043. I estimated the gold 50dma at ~$4,243 from my own 31 Jul reading (4.7% below); gold is now ~3.7% ABOVE it. Fast filter flipped. Gold is still ~1.7% below its 200dma, so it is a no-position, not a long.
- Silver $63.50, +10% weekly, six-week high; SLV $57.50. Still marginally under a ~$65.7 50dma but the counter-signal I said would kill the trade fired.
- URA $44.91 from ~$39 — up ~15% in a week, now through the ~$44.5 50dma I derived on 31 Jul. Materials/miners led the tape on lower rate-hike odds.
- EUR/USD $1.1560, a 7-week high; DXY -0.37% to 99.56. EUO $30.09 — if EUR is at a 7-week high, EUO is at a 7-week low, i.e. below its 50dma. Fast filter broken.
- WTI $78.18 vs $84.67 on 31 Jul (-7.7%); USO $117.98 from ~$128. That puts USO essentially back ON the ~$117 50dma with 3m momentum (only +1.5% a week ago) now negative. Goldman: Brent $80-90 until a US-Iran deal; Iran-Oman talks on reopening Hormuz are live. XLE $57.50 from ~$59.5, still ~2% above its 50dma and ~12% above its 200dma — the sector trend survived, the crude leg did not.
- BTC $64,940, +2.8% weekly, back above $65k and above its 50dma on the dovish print. Below the 200dma still, but the MA filter is now split.
- Survivors: XLV $165.68 (near $168.53 52wk high, YTD +29%), XLF $57.60 (fresh record vs $56.18 last week), DBA $27.62 (52wk high $28.84). All three still clear on both filters.
- S&P 500 record close 7,757.64, +3.6% on the week (best since April); Nasdaq +5.2%. SPY $773.26 against a $776.85 52wk high — the most established, lowest-volatility uptrend in my universe.

NEW CANDIDATES SCREENED: CPER $39.90, copper at a record high, 1yr +45.3%, both filters clearly positive — a genuine non-equity trend. IGV $102.69 (+3.29% Fri) rejected: 1yr return is -8.14%, this is a bounce off $73.93, not an established trend. SMH $582.70 rejected both ways: SOX is -15% since 1 July so it fails as a long, but 1yr +104% means it is far above its 200dma so it fails as a short — which is consistent with the SOXL short stop-outs on 7 Aug. EEM $65.64 rejected: 8% off its high, dragged by the same semi names. XLU $43.61 rejected: near the bottom of a $41.15-$47.80 range, a laggard, and shorting a bond proxy into a dovish repricing is fighting the catalyst. GDX/GDXJ deliberately not touched in either direction.

CONCLUSION: six of ten legs lost their signal in one week and almost nothing in my universe now screens short. The honest trend answer is a smaller, long-only book in the four survivors plus the two cleanest new uptrends, with the rest in cash at 4%.

decisions.reason: Six of my ten legs lost their price signal in a single week, and I refuse to defend a view after the filters that put me in the trade have flipped. The 7 Aug payrolls print (-23k vs +80k expected, wages +0.1%) inverted the rate path I explicitly cited as the driver for GLD, SLV and EUO, and — more importantly than the narrative — it moved price through my exit levels: gold cleared the ~$4,243 50dma I derived from my own 31 Jul reading, URA gapped ~15% through its ~$44.5 50dma, and EUR/USD at a 7-week high of 1.1560 puts EUO at a 7-week low under its 50dma. USO fell back onto its 50dma as WTI dropped 7.7% to $78.18 with 3m momentum turning negative, and BTC pushed back above its 50dma, splitting that filter. I applied exactly this standard to XLY on 1 Aug and to IWM before that for a 0.1% breach; consistency demands I apply it to legs that are costing me money, not just to ones I am indifferent about. I do NOT flip long gold or silver — both are still below their 200dmas, so they are no-positions, and I am not chasing a squeeze that stopped out twelve shorts. XLE is trimmed 19 to 11 rather than cut because the sector trend held (~2% above 50dma, ~12% above 200dma) even though the crude leg it rested on did not. The redeployment goes to the two cleanest uptrends I can find: SPY at a record 7,757.64 after the best week since April, and copper at an all-time high. Cash rises to 22% because when half my universe stops screening, holding 4% risk-free is a position, not a failure to act.
decisions.novelty: This is my only book in the experiment, but it is a deliberate break from the book it replaces: the short/hard-dollar sleeve that defined it — GLD, SLV, URA, BTC and EUO, 35.5% of gross — is gone entirely and replaced with a long-only trend set anchored by a broad-index core and an industrial-metal leg I have never held, so same-direction overlap with the prior book is limited to the four legs whose signals actually survived.

positions.thesis: New top weight and the single most established trend in my universe: a record close at 7,757.64, +3.6% on the week (best since April), price within 0.5% of the 52wk high of $776.85, clearly above both moving averages and 1yr +23.55%. I have been expressing equity trend only through sector bets, which meant my equity risk was a set of thematic opinions rather than the trend itself; with the broad index printing records this is the cleanest available expression and it carries the lowest volatility in the book (~13%), which is precisely why inverse-vol sizing puts it first. Wide -15% stop because index drawdowns of that size are regime changes, not noise, and weekly reassessment is my real exit.

Held and nudged up because it did what I bought it to do — $165.68 against a $168.53 52wk high, up on Friday, YTD +29.17% — and it did it without needing the defensive-rotation story I abandoned a week ago. It remains the strongest 3m time-series momentum of any low-volatility sleeve at ~18% vol, above both moving averages with the golden cross intact, and it is now my lowest-correlation equity leg against an index core plus two cyclicals. Nothing in the payrolls repricing touches the healthcare trend in either direction.

Raised modestly from 9.8 for a specific reason: I trimmed it last week because I was carrying it into a Fed that JP Morgan expected to hike in December, where higher-for-longer threatened credit and the multiple. That tail got smaller this week — September hold odds went to 60% and the 10yr fell 8.6bp to 4.657% — while the price trend extended to a fresh record $57.60 from $56.18, roughly 8% above its 50dma. It gave back 0.36% on Friday with energy as the sector laggards, which is noise against a trend this clean at only 13.2% vol.

Cut from 19 to 11 because the evidence that justified top weight decayed: Brent went from $90.12 to roughly $82 and WTI from $84.67 to $78.18 as Iran-Oman talks on reopening Hormuz replaced the 31 July tanker attacks as the live story, and Goldman now frames Brent at $80-90 absent a deal or a major escalation. Energy was the worst sector on Friday. I keep it rather than exit because the sector's own trend still passes both filters — ~$57.50, about 2% above its 50dma and ~12% above its 200dma with positive 3m momentum and 1yr +40% on record refiner margins — but it no longer earns a conviction overweight above its 24.4% volatility, so it reverts to roughly its inverse-vol baseline. Stop tightened from -25% to -22% to reflect a driver that is now diplomatic rather than physical.

New position and the book's replacement source of non-equity trend now that gold, silver and uranium have all stopped screening. Copper printed an all-time high this week with CPER at $39.90 against a $27.27-$40.97 52wk range and 1yr +45.3%, so it is unambiguously above both moving averages with strongly positive 3m momentum. The driver is supply-side and structural rather than a rate call — demand exceeding global supply on electrification, grid buildout and AI infrastructure, with the rally attributed to tight supply rather than a growth acceleration — which is exactly why it diversifies a book whose remaining legs are US equity beta. Sized at 10 on roughly 23% volatility, and it fell 2.11% on Friday, so I am not buying the print of the record itself.

Lifted from 8 to 10 and now the book's second non-equity leg. Trend is intact on its own terms — $27.62 against a $25.40-$28.84 range, above both moving averages, 1yr +10.11% — and the fundamental backdrop got fresher rather than staler with heavy rain disrupting the Brazilian coffee harvest and drought pressuring US growers. Its beta of 0.12 makes it the least equity-correlated thing I own, which matters more now that I have removed every short and my remaining risk is directional; at 13.3% volatility it is cheap risk to carry and inverse-vol sizing would justify more than I am taking.

decisions.name: Opus 5 unrestricted
decisions.research_notes:
Checked the packet first: NAV $966.96, -3.30%, max DD -3.92%, gross 89%, cash 17%, book entered 2026-08-03. No standing order fired — ERX -30%, MPC -25%, VLO -22%, JETS -20%/+30%, DOGE -50%/+90% all intact. So the drawdown is mark-to-market, not stop damage, and I needed to find where it came from.

MARKS (all 2026-08-07 close): ERX $88.24 (-2.26% on the day, 52w 50.06-110.78); XLE $57.50 (-1.13%, 52w 42.05-63.46, vs 58.38 when I wrote the book); MPC $301.01 (day range 293.73-303.33); VLO $298.31 (-1.54%, 52w high 320.24); XLV $165.68 (+0.75%, 52w high 168.53); JETS $32.54 (-0.31%, 52w 23.36-34.06); DOGE ~$0.070; BTC ~$64.3k; gold spot ~$4,315-4,350 at records; silver $64.10 (+4.16%); Brent $83.46 (+1.18% Fri, but -5% on the week from ~$90); WTI $78.05.

WHAT I LEARNED, in order of how much it changed my mind:

1. THE REFINING THESIS IS FALSIFIED BY MANAGEMENT ITSELF. MPC printed a monster Q2 on 8/4 — $5.1bn net income, $17.73 EPS vs $13.95 consensus (a 27% beat), $8.5bn adj EBITDA vs $3.3bn, R&M margin $36.33/bbl vs $17.58, record 112% capture, $2.8bn returned. And the stock is at $301, BELOW the ~$314 it traded at when I sized the leg. A 27% beat that the tape sells is the market telling me forward money is already out. Worse, the call itself gutted my sizing rationale: management said Q3 carries ~$290mn of turnaround expense and planned maintenance on conversion units — I had bought this on the premise that 40% of annual turnarounds were front-loaded into Q1 so they could run 2.99mb/d into this window. They also said Q3 is historically the most muted quarter (95% average capture 2023-25 vs the 112% just printed), that "margins are still good in early Q3 but not at Q2 levels," that the jet-to-diesel spread has narrowed, and that some Q2 derivative benefits were "not repeatable."

2. THE CRACK ITSELF HAS ROLLED. The 3-2-1 hit an all-time ~$70-72/bbl in July — that was the top, not a trend. NY Harbor diesel crack peaked 10 July at 84c/gal and has fallen to ~60c, now BELOW the 2020-24 five-year average. EIA expects "significantly narrower crack spreads in 4Q26" as inventories restock and driving season ends. Distillate exports hit an all-time weekly record 1.884mb/d, which is what a market clearing a shortage looks like. VLO has itself warned margins could fall 28% by 2027. Analyst consensus PTs now sit BELOW spot for the group ($309.79 avg on VLO at $298 is only 3.8% upside after a 20-24% July). I bought VLO five days ago specifically because "the binary event is behind it and the CEO already told me Q3 is better." The event is behind it and the stock fell anyway. That is new information I did not have when I bought, and it is the answer to the question I bought the position to ask.

3. THE LABOR MARKET CRACKED ON FRIDAY. July payrolls -23,000 against +80-83k consensus, with May revised 129k->63k and June 57k->20k — roughly 100k of retroactive destruction. Unemployment 4.1%, average hourly earnings +2c, 12-month wage growth 3.2%, the lowest since May 2021. Traders priced OUT a September hike. This is the single biggest new fact of the week and it changes the regime: an oil-driven inflation impulse on top of a labor market that is now contracting is stagflation, and it is demand-negative for the refined products my two biggest single-name longs sell.

4. GOLD AND SILVER ARE THE CLEAN EXPRESSION OF THAT REGIME. Gold held above $4,300 and climbed toward records on the payrolls miss; silver ripped 4.16% to $64.10, a six-week high, dollar to a two-week low, gold/silver ratio compressed 69->67. Drivers stack: rate-cut repricing, persistent oil-fed inflation, central bank buying, and a Hormuz safe-haven bid. Critically this is the only asset in my opportunity set that wins in BOTH tails of my own book — Hormuz escalation (haven bid) and Hormuz resolution into a weakening economy (rate cuts). Note on the tape warning: the GDX/GDXJ pain has been in SHORTS being squeezed, so long precious metals is on the correct side of that flow, and I am taking it in bullion ETFs rather than miners because I do not need the extra operating leverage on top of ERX.

5. ENERGY EQUITY DOWNSIDE CAPTURE HELD UP — THE ONE THESIS THAT PASSED. Crude fell ~5% on the week and XLE gave up only ~1.5%; XLE rose 1.48% on 8/7 while the S&P fell 0.2% and the Dow lost 0.9%. Energy remains the best-performing US sector. That is direct confirmation of the asymmetry I built ERX on. But the de-escalation path is now more concrete than a headline: an Iran-Oman draft accord is in the Iranian parliament (restricting US/Israeli vessels, cargo penalties), even as Iran struck targets near Qeshm Island and the draft's terms are stricter than markets expected. Unresolved, both ways.

6. JETS: my short is roughly flat (32.54 vs ~31.86 entry) and it will not fall — it sits near a 52w high of 34.06. The demand half of the thesis improved a lot on Friday (payrolls weak, leisure and hospitality specifically soft). The cost half is deteriorating: crude -5% on the week, and I have the June precedent that falling fuel costs lifted AAL +7%, UAL +6%, JBLU +5% in a single session. The $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo ask with a federal equity stake is still live and still my gap risk.

7. DOGE: $0.070, range 0.0686-0.0702, still stuck below $0.08 with the crypto fear index at 25 and FXStreet describing the sell-off as "unstoppable despite renewed retail interest." Nothing changed. Risk noted: the dovish repricing lifts high-beta risk assets, and DOGE amplifies both directions.

decisions.reason: I am exiting refining entirely because the thesis was falsified by the people who run the companies. I sized MPC at 16% on the specific premise that management front-loaded ~40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 to run flat-out into this window, and I added VLO at 10% because its CEO had guided Q3 margins above Q2 with the binary print already behind it. On the 4 August call MPC told me Q3 carries ~$290mn of turnaround expense plus planned conversion-unit maintenance, that Q3 historically averages 95% capture against the 112% just printed, that early-Q3 margins are 'not at Q2 levels', that the jet-to-diesel spread has narrowed and that some Q2 drivers were 'not repeatable'. That is my sizing premise reversed by the issuer. The tape says the same thing louder: a 27% EPS beat ($17.73 vs $13.95, $5.1bn net income, margin doubled to $36.33/bbl) and the stock closed 8/7 at $301, below the ~$314 where I bought it. When a print that good cannot lift a stock, the forward money has already left. The commodity confirms it — the 3-2-1 crack's all-time $70-72 was a July peak, NY Harbor diesel has fallen from 84c on 10 July to ~60c and is now below its five-year average, distillate exports set an all-time weekly record, and EIA looks for significantly narrower cracks in 4Q26. Holding a token position with a dead thesis is worse than holding none, so both go. Second, Friday's payrolls print (-23k vs +80k, with ~100k of downward revisions to May and June, wage growth at a 2021 low) is a genuine regime break: an oil-driven inflation impulse landing on a contracting labor market. That is demand-negative for exactly the refined products I just sold, and it re-prices the Fed from a possible hike to cuts. The asset that wins in both tails of my own book is precious metals — it gets the haven bid if Hormuz escalates and the rate-cut bid if the strait reopens into a weakening economy — so gold becomes my largest single position at 20% with silver at 7% for beta to the same call. I take this in bullion, not miners: GDX/GDXJ have been squeezing shorts violently, which tells me the direction is right and the entry is extended, and I do not need levered operating gearing stacked on top of a 2x energy fund. Third, I keep the energy core because it is the one leg the week actually confirmed — crude fell ~5% and XLE gave up only ~1.5%, XLE rose 1.48% on Friday against a down tape, and energy is still the best-performing US sector. But 26% of a 2x fund is a 52% effective single-sector bet, and the de-escalation path is no longer a headline, it is a draft accord sitting in the Iranian parliament. Trimming to 20% keeps 40% effective XLE as my largest risk exposure while the labor data resolves. XLV goes up rather than down because the defensive rotation is now the trade and not merely the ballast — it closed 8/7 at $165.68 near a 52w high of $168.53, +29% on the year, 0.56 beta, and it is explicitly being bought as the haven for money leaving tech. JETS comes down to 6%: the demand half of the short improved on Friday but the cost half is going the wrong way, and I have the June precedent that a fuel-price drop puts 6-7% into airline stocks in one session. It is a labor-rollover short now, not a fuel-cost short, and it is smaller because it stays directionally additive to whatever energy exposure I still carry. Total turnover is roughly 65% one-way at ~2bps a side, about 1.3bps of NAV — cheap enough that being wrong for another week costs far more than the trade does.
decisions.novelty: This book pivots the mandate's engine from the refining crack — where the trade is now demonstrably peaked, with management guiding Q3 down and a 27% beat closing below its pre-print price — to precious metals as the expression of the same supply shock, on the view that after Friday's -23k payrolls the oil shock is transmitting through inflation and a cracking labor market rather than through refiner margins; refining goes from 26% of NAV to zero and gold/silver from zero to 27%.

positions.thesis: New largest position, and the reason it earns that slot is that it is the only asset I own that wins in both tails of my own book. If Hormuz escalates, gold takes the haven bid alongside ERX. If the Iran-Oman draft accord passes and the strait reopens, crude collapses and ERX halves the move twice over — but that resolution lands on a labor market that just contracted 23,000 jobs against a +80k consensus with ~100k of downward revisions to May and June, and the Fed repricing from a possible September hike to cuts is exactly what gold is built for. Every other leg I have needs one of those two worlds. Spot held above $4,300 and pushed toward records into Friday's close with the dollar at a two-week low, and the bid is layered rather than single-source: rate-cut repricing, an inflation impulse that oil keeps feeding even as employment weakens, sustained central-bank buying, and a geopolitical premium from the same Hormuz situation that drives my energy leg. I am taking this in bullion rather than GDX/GDXJ deliberately. The miners have been squeezing shorts hard, which tells me the direction is right but the entry is extended, and stacking mining operating leverage on top of a 2x levered energy fund would concentrate variance in precisely the thing I am trying to reduce. At ~15% annualised vol a 20% weight carries materially less portfolio variance than the 26% ERX position it partly replaces. The -18% stop is set wide on purpose: it caps the leg at 3.6% of NAV and is far enough out that a headline-driven spike will not shake me out of a hedge, but it is close enough that a genuine break of the record-high structure — which would mean the rate-cut thesis died — takes me out.

Raised from 20% because its job has changed. I bought healthcare as ballast to make an energy concentration carryable — negative correlation to XLE, 0.22 to SPY, 13.7% vol — and it has done that job, closing 8/7 at $165.68 (+0.75% on a day the Dow lost 0.9%) near a 52-week high of $168.53, +29% over the year. But after Friday's payrolls the defensive rotation stops being insurance and starts being the trade: a contracting labor market with a Fed pivoting to cuts is the textbook regime for low-beta defensives, and the sector is already being bought explicitly as the haven for money leaving tech, with State Street's Q3 upgrade to positive on drug-pipeline wins giving it institutional sponsorship. Adding five points here is how I redeploy part of the refining capital into something whose thesis the week strengthened rather than broke. Still deliberately unlevered rather than 3x CURE — the point of the largest equity leg in a book that also runs a 2x energy fund is to not add variance. No stop: this is the position I want to still own if everything else in the book is wrong, and a stop on my lowest-beta leg would only ever fire in a market-wide flush, which is the exact moment I would want to be holding it.

Trimmed from 26 to 20, and the trim is a sizing decision rather than a change of view, because this is the one leg the week actually confirmed. The asymmetry I built it on held under live test: crude fell roughly 5% on the week and XLE gave up only about 1.5%, closing $57.50 against a 52-week high of $63.46, and on 8/7 XLE rose 1.48% while the S&P fell 0.2% and the Dow lost 0.9%. Energy equities still discount crude far below an $83 Brent that itself sits well under where a closed Hormuz should price it, and equities cannot hand back a move they never made — that unconverged discount is simultaneously my upside and my cushion. Energy remains the best-performing US sector. What has changed is that the de-escalation path is no longer a headline I can dismiss: an Iran-Oman draft accord is sitting in the Iranian parliament, and while its terms are stricter than markets expected and Iran struck targets near Qeshm Island in the same week, a written proposal is a different order of risk than a rumour. Meanwhile a labor market that just contracted is demand-negative for crude at the margin. Holding 26% of a 2x fund is a 52% effective single-sector bet, and I am not willing to run that into an unresolved binary while the macro deteriorates. At 20% this is still 40% effective XLE and still my largest directional risk exposure — the mandate's core survives intact. Stop tightened from -30% to -28%, capping the leg at 5.6% of NAV, roughly a -14% XLE break.

The higher-beta leg of the same precious-metals call, sized small because it is genuinely more volatile than gold. Silver ripped 4.16% to $64.10 on Friday, a six-week high, and the move compressed the gold/silver ratio from about 69 to 67 — silver outrunning gold on a dovish repricing is the classic pattern, and it did it on the same catalyst that drives the GLD leg, a jobs contraction that knocked the dollar to a two-week low and unwound rate-hike bets. A ratio still near 67 leaves room for further catch-up. Silver also carries an industrial demand component that gold lacks, which cuts against it in a labor-market slowdown — that ambivalence is exactly why this is 7% and gold is 20%, not the reverse. The instrument's own history in this cycle demands respect: it traded as high as the mid-$80s in February and is now $64, a drawdown that would have taken out any tight stop. The -22% stop caps the leg at 1.5% of NAV and is set wide enough to survive normal silver noise while still ending the position if the reflation trade genuinely fails.

Cut from 8% to 6% and re-founded on a different driver. When I put it on, this was the mirror of my refiner longs — the record crack the refiners captured was the cost airlines paid — and I have now sold the refiners, so that pairing is gone. Two things replace it, one better and one worse. Better: Friday's payrolls print showed the economy shedding 23,000 jobs with leisure and hospitality specifically called out as soft and roughly 100k of downward revisions to prior months. Discretionary air travel demand is a direct function of exactly that, and this becomes a labor-rollover short. Worse: the cost half is now working against me, with crude down about 5% on the week, and I have a live precedent from June that a fuel-price drop alone put AAL +7%, UAL +6% and JBLU +5% into the tape in a single session. The position also refuses to work — it closed 8/7 at $32.54 against my ~$31.86 entry and sits near a 52-week high of $34.06. Two of my three original pillars have weakened, so the size comes down rather than the position coming off, because it remains my only equity-market hedge and the one thing in the book that pays if the indices break. Squeeze risk is unchanged and specific: the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a government equity stake is still live even though Transportation Secretary Duffy publicly said private funding is preferable and there is no need. It is an ETF, so no single-name earnings gap. 3% APR borrow on 6% is about 18bps a year. Stop tightened from -20% to -18%, capping the leg at 1.1% of NAV, take-profit lowered from +30% to +25% because I want a smaller, faster exit on a thesis I now hold with less conviction.

Held completely untouched, because nothing about it changed and resizing a 3% leg would cost more in attention and fees than it could earn. The engine asymmetry that justifies it is structural rather than a market view: short perps pay zero funding while long perps pay leverage times 10% APR, so this 3x is genuinely free carry. DOGE closed the week around $0.070 in a 0.0686-0.0702 range, still stuck below $0.08, still the worst cross-sectional performer in the asset class, with the crypto fear index at 25 and the sell-off described as unstoppable despite renewed retail interest, while BTC sits at $64.3k. The one honest risk I will name: the same dovish repricing that makes my gold leg work also lifts high-beta risk assets, and DOGE amplifies market moves in both directions — it followed the tape higher after the jobs miss. That is why this stays 3% and 3x rather than anything larger. Loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin, the -50% stop caps it at 1.5% of NAV, and the +90% take-profit corresponds to DOGE down roughly 30% for about 1.8:1.

decisions.name: Opus 5 vol regime
decisions.research_notes:
WEEK IN REVIEW (2026-08-03 to 08-07). The tape went vertical: S&P 500 +3.58% to a record 7,757.64, Nasdaq +5.19%, Dow +2.96% through 54,000, Technology sector +7.2% and Materials +4.8%. My book made +0.97%. That gap is the finding, not the noise.

WHY IT RALLIED. July payrolls printed -23,000 against ~+80,000 expected, with May revised 129k->63k and June 57k->20k (-103k combined) and participation at 61.4%, a five-year low. Unemployment 4.1%. AHE +3.2% y/y vs +3.5% expected. Equities rallied on this because Warsh's Fed had a live HIKE on the table for 15-16 Sep (July hold at 3.50-3.75% carried hawkish dissents); the soft print cut hike odds from 57% to 44%. A market that makes an all-time high on a contracting labour market, purely through the rate channel, has inverted its good-news/bad-news polarity. 44% is still a coin flip on a hike.

VOL STATE. VIX closed 15.15 (-4.2% on the day), the lowest reading in this experiment. SPY 20d close-to-close realized was 13.49% at 31-Jul; SPY IV rank 12.49 at 03-Aug. So the volatility risk premium is roughly 15.15 - 13.5 = ~1.7 points, versus the ~7 points I sized the (now closed) SVXY leg against and a ~3-4 point historical norm. There is no compensation left for being short index vol, and long index vol at VIX 15 is close to fair on realized alone.

CORRELATION IS THE REAL SIGNAL. Cboe implied correlation is at 23-year lows: COR3M ~9-10 with a 52-week range of 9.29-11.95, COR1M prints as low as 8.7-9.93, DSPX in a 26.46-50.40 range and elevated. Expected average single-stock correlation ~23%. Correlation is bounded below and mean-reverting; at a 23-year low it is a one-way option. Index variance is roughly average constituent variance times correlation, so long index vol here pays if EITHER realized rises OR correlation normalises.

CARRY IS CHEAPER THAN I PRICED IT. The VIX curve is in compressed contango, VX6/VX1 at 1.062 versus a 1.15-1.20 historical average, with the 2024-26 slope averaging ~6%. I entered VIXY assuming ~43.8%/yr bleed. Compressed contango cuts the front-month roll cost to roughly a third to a half of that. Cheap level plus cheap carry plus a free correlation option.

CATALYST CALENDAR INSIDE THE HORIZON. July CPI 12-Aug (June headline 3.5%, first decline in five months, energy +15.7% and gasoline +26.7% y/y still running hot). Hormuz: Brent ~$80 (down from $100) on an Iran-Oman draft to open the strait for 60 days fee-free, but talks stalled Friday over Iran wanting 5-7% transit fees vs Oman's 3% vs Washington's zero, and the draft bans US/Israeli transit. Binary both ways. Then FOMC 15-16 Sep with a live hike. Three dated binaries against VIX 15.

MY CORE, HONESTLY ASSESSED. USMV +5.21% YTD vs SPLV +9.98%; 1yr SPLV +8.28% vs USMV +6.48%. I was 46/32 tilted toward the YTD laggard. More importantly, I have been conflating two different things under the word "vol". Vol targeting scales exposure to the index by the INDEX's realized vol. Owning low-volatility STOCKS is a different trade: it buys low vol by surrendering expected return and by concentrating in rate-sensitive sectors (SPLV ~25.4% utilities into a 44% hike probability). The index buys its low vol from diversification, which is free, and diversification is at a 23-year maximum right now. At COR3M ~10 the S&P delivers 13.5% vol while its average constituent delivers far more. That makes the index, not the low-vol factor, the cheapest carrier of equity risk available to me in this specific regime. My effective beta was ~40 SPY-equivalents against a low-vol index tape - materially under-deployed by my own rule.

PAYOFF CHECK ON THE NEW SHAPE. Calm state (SPY +2%/mo, VIXY -3%/mo): ~+0.86%/mo vs ~+0.65% on the old book. Shock state (SPY -8%, VIX 15->30, VIXY +45%): ~+0.36% vs ~-0.55% on the old book. Moderate scare (SPY -4%, VIXY +22%): ~+0.12%. The new book dominates the old one in all three states because buying cheap convexity is what LETS you carry beta, and I had been paying for the insurance without using the permission it bought.

TAPE WARNING NOTED: I am short nothing, so the GDX/GDXJ/SOXL squeeze that fired 12 of 17 standing orders is not my problem this week. All legs long, no leverage, no crypto, no perps, no margin.

decisions.reason: Two things moved enough to force this, and they point the same way. First, the volatility risk premium has closed: VIX 15.15 against SPY 20d realized 13.49% is ~1.7 points, versus a ~3-4 point norm, so index vol is no longer expensive - and Cboe implied correlation sits at a 23-year low (COR3M ~9-10, 52-week range 9.29-11.95), which is a bounded, mean-reverting quantity that can only normalise upward. Long index vol therefore pays if realized rises OR correlation normalises, and the compressed contango (VX6/VX1 1.062 vs a 1.15-1.20 norm) means I pay a third-to-half the carry I underwrote at entry. Cheaper insurance against a denser calendar - CPI 12-Aug, a stalled Hormuz fee dispute with Brent at $80, and a 15-16 Sep FOMC where a Warsh hike is still 44% priced after payrolls printed -23k with 103k of downward revisions. Second, and this is the correction I owe myself: I have been conflating vol targeting with owning low-vol stocks. Vol targeting scales exposure to the INDEX by the index's realized vol. USMV and SPLV buy their low vol by surrendering expected return and by parking 25% of SPLV in utilities ahead of a live hike; the index buys its low vol from diversification, which is free and is at a 23-year maximum precisely because correlation is at a 23-year low. At COR3M ~10 the S&P realizes 13.5% while its average constituent realizes far more - that makes SPY the cheapest carrier of equity risk in my universe right now, not USMV. My book was carrying only ~40 SPY-equivalent betas into a low-correlation, low-index-vol tape and made +0.97% while the index made +3.58% and tech made +7.2%. The fix is not to abandon defence, it is to take the permission the insurance already bought: raise index beta and raise the hedge together. Modelled across three states - calm melt-up, moderate scare, and a VIX-doubling shock - the new shape beats the old one in every one, because more cheap convexity is what makes more beta affordable rather than a substitute for it.
decisions.novelty: This book is a low-correlation index-carry expression - long the S&P itself as the diversification-cheapest vehicle for equity risk while implied correlation sits at a 23-year low, financed against an upsized long-index-volatility leg bought at a 1.7-point risk premium with compressed contango; the low-vol factor sleeve is demoted from the core to residual ballast rather than being the thesis, which inverts the construction I ran for the prior three weeks.

positions.thesis: The new core, and the point of the whole rebalance. Cboe implied correlation is at its lowest in at least 23 years - COR3M ~9-10 against a 52-week range of 9.29-11.95, COR1M printing 8.7-9.93, expected average single-stock correlation ~23%. Index variance is approximately average constituent variance times correlation, so at these readings the S&P realizes 13.49% (20d, close-to-close) while its average member realizes far more. That is diversification benefit at a two-decade maximum, and it is free. Every other way I have owned equity in this book paid for its low volatility: USMV pays in surrendered expected return (+5.21% YTD vs SPLV's +9.98% and an index at record highs), SPLV pays by concentrating 25.4% in utilities. SPY pays nothing for it. In a genuinely high-dispersion regime the correct long-only expression is to own the index rather than its components, because dispersion is exactly what makes the wrapper safer than its contents - and I had been drawing the opposite conclusion from the same data, buying low-vol stocks when the dispersion I identified was an argument for the index. Sized at 40% rather than higher for two reasons: the melt-up ran on a jobs contraction, which is the rate channel doing the work rather than earnings, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC still carries a 44%-priced hike under Warsh. The -18% stop is deliberately wide - it is a regime-break brake, not a trading stop, because VIXY is the actual hedge and stacking a tight stop on top of a convex hedge is double-paying for the same protection and inviting a whipsaw out of the position at the worst moment.

Cut from 46% to 22% but kept, because the evidence I gathered for it is still good and only its role changed. What survives: MSCI's min-vol optimizer explicitly excludes high-volatility constituents, so the 31.82% technology label sits in low-beta software, services and payments rather than semiconductors - demonstrated on 29-Jul when USMV fell 0.21% against SMH -4.79% and SPY -1.54%, a ~14% downside capture no fund with real semi exposure could post. 20d realized 9.97%, issuer 3yr beta 0.49, 6.96% utilities so the least rate-sensitive of my defensive sleeves with the 10y at ~4.68%. What no longer holds: that this deserves to be the single largest line. It is +5.21% YTD against an index at a record high, and the low volatility is bought with foregone return, whereas SPY's is bought with correlation that is at a 23-year low and therefore unusually generous. So USMV moves from being the thesis to being ballast - the sleeve that keeps working if a soft-landing rotation punishes beta without a volatility event, which is the one state where neither SPY nor VIXY helps me. The -14% stop is unchanged and now caps this leg near -3.1% of NAV rather than -6.4%.

Cut hardest, from 32% to 12%, because it is the leg whose bull case is most dependent on a rate path the calendar may not deliver. The reason to own it is unchanged and still real: 1.78% technology against USMV's 31.82% makes it the only genuinely tech-free sleeve I have, and it fails in different states than USMV, which is why owning a little of both is actual diversification rather than duplication. But ~25.4% utilities is a direct short-rates position, and the Fed under Warsh held in July with hawkish dissents pushing to tighten and still carries a ~44% market-implied probability of a hike on 15-16 Sep even after a -23k payroll print. SPLV's +9.98% YTD lead over USMV was earned in a window where that risk was not being priced, and it now trades within ~1% of its 52-week high, which is where the crowded defensive trade lives. I am not willing to keep a third of the book in a single rate expression I cannot hedge, so I keep the diversification and shed the concentration. The stop stays wide at -16% for the original reason: ordinary rate noise in the utility sleeve must not knock me out of a position I hold specifically for its tech-free composition.

Upsized from 6% to 11% because every input that sets the price of this hedge improved at once. Level: VIX closed 15.15, the lowest print of this experiment and ~9% below where I last added. Value against realized: SPY 20d realized is 13.49%, so the risk premium I am paying is ~1.7 points against a ~3-4 point historical norm - insurance is close to fair on realized alone, which almost never happens. Carry: the curve is in compressed contango at VX6/VX1 1.062 versus a 1.15-1.20 historical average, so the roll cost is a third to a half of the ~43.8%/yr I underwrote at entry, and my single largest objection to this leg has weakened materially. And the free option: Cboe implied correlation at a 23-year low of ~9-10 means index vol is being suppressed by dispersion rather than by calm, so I get paid if realized vol rises OR if correlation simply reverts, and correlation at the bottom of a 23-year range can essentially only revert upward. Against that, three dated binaries inside the horizon: CPI on 12-Aug with energy still +15.7% y/y, a Hormuz negotiation that stalled Friday over a 5-7% vs 3% vs zero transit-fee dispute with Brent at $80, and a 15-16 Sep FOMC with a live hike at 44%. This is what makes the 40% SPY line affordable - convexity bought cheaply is a permission to carry beta, not a substitute for it, and last week I paid for the insurance without using the permission. Take-profit widened from +50% to +60%: off a VIX-15 base a +50% move now corresponds to a smaller absolute dislocation than it did at VIX 20, and I want this to survive a moderate scare intact and only convert to cash on a genuine one. No stop, for the same reason as always - stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the single thing insurance must never do.

decisions.name: Opus Momentum
decisions.research_notes:
Checked the 2026-08-07 session and the week's tape for both books.

MACRO — the week's dominant event was the July jobs report: US nonfarm payrolls unexpectedly LOST 23,000 jobs against consensus of +80,000. The market read it dovishly rather than as a growth scare: S&P 500 closed at a record 7,757.64 (+0.62%), Nasdaq Composite at a record 26,690.62 (+1.30%), Dow +0.28%, Russell 2000 +1.10%, with 336 S&P names advancing — broad participation, not mega-cap-only. 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.64%. Gold rose sharply on a safe-haven and lower-real-rate bid. Brent +1.3%.

SEMIS — the complex split in two. Broad semis and leveraged semis ripped: SOXX up double digits on the week, SMH high single digits, SOXL up sharply (a near-perfect 3x day of +18.55% against SOXX +6.30% on the Tuesday), and semiconductor ETFs topped weekly fund flows for the first time. That is exactly the confirmation my 2026-08-01 reversal call needed. But MEMORY broke away from it: on 08-07 Western Digital fell 17%, Sandisk 9.1%, Seagate 3.9%. Citigroup cut its Micron target 18% from $1,400 to $1,150 (keeping Buy), with Atif Malik writing "we see both DRAM and NAND prices decelerating Q/Q in the next four quarters" and naming rising Chinese DRAM and NAND production as the primary long-term risk. MU itself held up far better than peers — down only ~1.2% to roughly $854-871 with an 8%+ intraday range — because ~40% of its DRAM bits are locked under long-term contracts worth $22bn of commitments.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO ME SPECIFICALLY — my MU thesis was written on one explicit, checkable claim: DRAM rose 90% in Q1 with suppliers guiding a further 10-20% per month into year-end and shortage beyond 2026. Citi's four-quarter deceleration call plus a 17% single-session drop in a direct peer is the first genuine contradiction of that claim, and it postdates my reasoning. The rest of my mandate's universe simultaneously made new highs. That is a split inside the sleeve, not a market-wide de-risking.

TAPE NOTE ON SQUEEZES — the desk flags that 12 of 17 standing orders ever fired were shorts in gold miners and SOXL being stopped out, five on 08-07 alone. I am long both complexes' direction (SOXL long, GLD long), so the squeeze is a tailwind, not a hazard, for how I am positioned. I did not build any new short leg into it.

CRYPTO — my Round-2 mandate contemplates short BTC/ETH/SOL perps as funding. I have no fresh crypto data this week and, independently, a dovish-Fed repricing with indices at record highs is not a tape for opening leveraged short risk-asset exposure. Declining to re-open that sleeve on an information gap rather than guessing at it.

CARRY BOOK — the single premise on which I cut all long duration on 2026-07-30 was that the Fed on hold against three dissents, with Warsh talking hawkishly, meant I was taking rate risk without being paid term premium. A -23,000 payroll print inverts that premise and the bond market agreed the same session (10y to 4.64%). The same reversal applies to the reason I trimmed gold: I cited a hawkish Fed and rising real rates as the headwind, and both just flipped. Conversely, a contracting labour market is the fundamental that high-yield credit spreads are genuinely short, so credit carry is the sleeve that now deserves less weight, not more.

decisions.reason: The one checkable claim under my largest position was contradicted this week and nothing else in the mandate was. My MU thesis rested on DRAM pricing accelerating 10-20% per month into year-end; Citi cut its target 18% on an explicit call that DRAM and NAND decelerate quarter-over-quarter for four straight quarters on Chinese supply, and the peer group confirmed it violently with WDC -17% and Sandisk -9.1% in one session. Over the same week the rest of the complex did the opposite: SOXX and SMH rallied hard, semis ETFs topped weekly fund flows for the first time, and the Nasdaq closed at a record 26,690 after a -23,000 payroll print repriced the Fed dovish and pulled the 10-year to 4.64%. So this is not risk-off to be hidden from, it is one sub-sector breaking while the mandate's core is being confirmed, and the honest momentum response is to move weight out of the falsified driver and into the trends actually making new highs. MU goes from my top weight to a residual tail rather than to zero, because it fell only ~1.2% while peers fell 17% - 40% of its bits sit under $22bn of long-term contracts, so it is the relative-strength survivor of a broken sub-sector, which is worth a small position and not a large one. I add TQQQ because the record high was Nasdaq-wide and rates-driven, not chips-only, and my mandate names that instrument. XLV comes down because it was ballast bought when the semis reversal was still unconfirmed and that doubt has now been resolved; VZ goes entirely because carry ballast is a worse buffer than the 4% cash I already hold. XLE is trimmed because a labour market shedding jobs is a demand-side negative that leaves the leg resting on supply premium alone.

positions.thesis: The clean, low-idiosyncratic expression of the mandate, and now the one confirmed by tape rather than argued from news: broad semis rallied high single digits on the week, semis ETFs led all weekly fund flows for the first time on record, and the Nasdaq closed at an all-time high. Made the top weight precisely because the memory blow-up showed that single-name chip risk inside this complex is real and idiosyncratic - owning the index is how I stay long the confirmed trend without betting on which sub-sector's pricing curve breaks next.

Custom AI silicon is the non-memory half of the semis story and it is untouched by the DRAM/NAND pricing problem - Broadcom sells design and logic against hyperscaler capex guided above $400bn, not commodity bits into a decelerating price curve. Raised from 7% with capital taken directly out of MU because it is the same complex minus the specific driver that just got falsified.

Post-earnings-announcement drift on the strongest print of the quarter - revenue $200.6bn (+20%), operating income +43%, AWS accelerating to 37% with $496bn of RPO - and the drift is still running with the Nasdaq at a record. A falling 10-year at 4.64% is a direct multiple tailwind for long-duration mega-cap cash flows, which is a second, rates-driven leg to the thesis that did not exist when I entered.

Post-earnings breakout reinforced by live escalation around Hormuz, and the reason to keep it at full size this week is that it is the only sleeve here with zero exposure to the AI capex debate. If the -23,000 payroll print turns out to be the start of a growth scare rather than a dovish gift, order-book momentum backed by government budgets is what keeps working when semis stop.

Kept as the low-beta anchor but cut from 13% because its job has changed. I sized it up when the semis reversal was one session old and unproven; the reversal is now confirmed by a week of record highs and leading fund flows, so paying momentum-book capital for defensive breadth at that size is no longer justified. Nine percent keeps a genuine anchor without dragging on the mandate.

One of the two prints that broke the capex-fear narrative, with Azure converting AI spend into recognised cloud revenue and a 16% single-session move behind it. Nudged up because software and AI names specifically drew the institutional buying on the 08-07 record-high session as yields fell - the drift and the rates tailwind are pushing the same way.

The mandate's named leveraged instrument, pointed the right way into a confirmed uptrend - it printed a clean +18.55% day against SOXX +6.30%, and the desk's own record shows repeated short stop-outs in this name, meaning the pressure is on the other side of my position. Raised only from 5% to 7% and both brackets kept: daily-rebalanced 3x decays hard in chop, so I want more convexity but with the downside still defined.

Fresh post-earnings trend with real backlog visibility and the same geopolitical reinforcement as RTX. Paired with RTX it forms a sleeve whose correlation to the AI cycle is near zero, which is the whole point of holding it in a book that is otherwise long one macro factor.

Cut from 13% to a residual because the pricing claim that justified the size is now contested - Citi projects DRAM and NAND decelerating quarter-over-quarter for four quarters on rising Chinese supply. Not cut to zero because MU fell only ~1.2% on the day WDC fell 17% and Sandisk 9.1%: roughly 40% of its DRAM bits are locked under $22bn of long-term contracts, so it is the contracted, defensible end of a sub-sector that is being repriced. Stop tightened from -18% to -15% - I no longer want to sit through the full noise band of a name whose fundamental driver is under revision.

Trimmed from 7% because a labour market that shed 23,000 jobs is a demand-side negative for crude, which leaves this leg standing on the Hormuz supply premium alone rather than on the two-sided case I entered. Kept at 5% because that premium is live and it remains the only position that pays off if inflation, not employment, turns out to be the binding problem.

New leg, and the mandate's other named leveraged instrument. The 08-07 record high was Nasdaq-wide with 336 S&P names advancing and the 10-year down to 4.64% - the driver was falling rates lifting all long-duration growth, not a chips-only move, and my book had no instrument that expressed that broader leg. Sized at only 4% with a wide stop because 3x index beta on top of an already-long book is where a growth-scare reinterpretation of the payroll print would hurt fastest.

decisions.reason: I cut all long duration on 2026-07-30 for one stated reason: the Fed on hold against three dissents with Warsh hawkish meant I was carrying rate risk without being paid term premium. The July payroll print at -23,000 against +80,000 expected inverts that premise, and the bond market repriced the same session with the 10-year at 4.64%. The identical reversal applies to gold - I explicitly trimmed it citing a hawkish Fed and rising real rates as headwinds, and both of those just flipped, with gold bid sharply into the bargain. So the two sleeves I cut for a hawkish Fed go back up, which is what a term-premium and diversification mandate is supposed to do when it finally starts getting paid. Moving the other way, high-yield comes down: a contracting labour market is the fundamental that credit spreads are genuinely short, and collecting a 7% coupon into the first real crack in employment is the exact mistake this book exists to avoid. XLRE is raised because a 4.64% ten-year feeds directly into rent-carry valuations and REITs are the sleeve most levered to the rate move. Duration is added mostly in the belly, with only a satellite position at the long end, because cuts get priced into the belly first while the long end still carries unrewarded fiscal term premium - I want the Fed reaction function, not the deficit.
decisions.novelty: This book overlaps the Round-2 momentum book by a single 5% XLE leg out of 92% gross - it is long intermediate and long duration, gold, REITs and defensive dividend carry precisely where the momentum book is long leveraged semis, Nasdaq beta and defence, so the two express opposite readings of the same -23,000 payroll print and one of them works whether it resolves as a dovish gift or a growth scare.

positions.thesis: Raised from 13% and made the top weight. This is the sleeve that gets paid first when the Fed's reaction function turns, and a payroll print at -23,000 against +80,000 expected is the cleanest turn signal available - the market moved the 10-year to 4.64% within the session. The belly rather than the long end because rate cuts are priced into 7-10y paper without also taking the fiscal term-premium risk sitting at the back of the curve, and it remains the only asset here that rallies if this resolves as a genuine growth scare.

The core equity-risk-premium sleeve and the lowest-volatility asset in the basket, so inverse-vol weighting keeps it near the top. Trimmed two points only to fund duration and gold, not because anything about it deteriorated - a min-vol equity book is exactly what I want owning the equity premium into a tape where the bullish catalyst was a contracting labour market.

Raised from 9% because the specific reason I trimmed it has reversed. I wrote that a hawkish Fed and rising real rates were a genuine headwind and that I wanted insurance rather than a directional bet; falling real rates and a Fed pushed toward cuts remove that headwind, and gold rallied sharply on the print. It stays the book's low-correlation real asset and its best hedge against an AI-credit tail. Stop widened to -12% because the complex has just been through a violent short squeeze and post-squeeze mean reversion would take out a -10% stop on noise alone.

Raised from 7% because REITs are the carry sleeve most directly levered to the move I am underwriting - rent yields are valued off the long rate, and the 10-year just fell to 4.64% on a Fed repricing. It supplies a cash-flow stream distinct from both equity beta and credit, which is what a cross-asset carry book is for, and it had already been quietly working at +13.2% on 6m.

Cut from 11% to 8%. High-yield carry pays roughly 7% and spreads still have not widened, but the thing credit is genuinely short is employment, and employment just contracted by 23,000 jobs. Combined with an AI complex that is debt-funded and already showing stress in NVDA CDS and Oracle at 200bp, I would rather hold less of the coupon than be paid to stand in front of the first labour-market crack. Tight -6% stop retained.

Low-volatility equity built on a pure realised-vol screen rather than USMV's optimisation, so the two hold materially different names and diversify each other while keeping portfolio variance down. Trimmed a point alongside USMV purely as funding for the duration and gold adds.

Reinstated as a satellite after being cut entirely on 2026-07-30. My mandate names term premium as a target and I refused it while the Fed was on hold against three dissents; a -23,000 payroll print is the event that changes what I get paid for holding rate risk. Deliberately 6% and not more - the long end also carries fiscal supply risk that no amount of Fed dovishness fixes, so this is a position on the reaction function with the belly, not the back end, doing the heavy lifting.

Consumer staples as the defensive dividend-carry sleeve, taking the bond-proxy income role with similar yield and beta to utilities and none of the AI-datacenter-power exposure. Modestly trimmed as funding; its case is unchanged and it is precisely the equity exposure that holds up if the payroll number is read as recessionary rather than dovish next month.

Trimmed from 7% for the same reason as in the momentum book - a contracting labour market is a demand-side negative for crude, so the leg now rests on supply premium alone. Kept at 5% because it is this book's only inflation-linked sleeve and pays real dividend and FCF carry, and I do not want a portfolio whose every position needs rates to keep falling.

The single-name expression of defensive dividend carry with the strongest trend of any staple - +14.4% 3m and +22.7% 6m on a stable dividend. Trimmed one point as funding; it remains where low-beta money is actually going and benefits alongside every other bond proxy as the discount rate falls.

Telecom yield carry with momentum on regulated domestic cash flows and essentially no correlation to the AI capex cycle. A high-dividend, rate-sensitive payer is a direct beneficiary of the 10-year moving to 4.64%, which is the same trade as the duration adds expressed through equity rather than bonds.

decisions.name: Opus Broadening
decisions.research_notes:
WEEK TAPE (through 2026-08-07 close): S&P 500 +3.6% to a record 7,757.64; Nasdaq Composite +5.2% to a record 26,690.62; Dow +~3%. Strongest week for the majors since mid-April. Treasury yields FELL.

MACRO — the decisive item. July nonfarm payrolls printed -23,000 against +80,000 expected (range 10k-140k). Local government education -50k, retail -19k, leisure/hospitality -40k (World Cup roll-off), health care +22k. Revisions were worse than the headline: May cut 129k -> 63k, June cut 57k -> 20k, ~103k removed between them. CME FedWatch: September hike odds fell 57% -> 44% within hours; hold-in-September rose to 56.1%. This is the direct inversion of the hawkish premise (three hike dissents, 30-yr at 5.22%/2007 highs) that I underwrote my Round 2 book on seven days ago.

ENERGY — premise decayed. WTI $77.08 on 8/7 (-0.27%), Brent $82.15. Iran and Oman are negotiating over the Strait of Hormuz; the Jordan-strike war premium that justified taking energy to 25% of Round 2 has largely come out. Breadth internals weak too: only 33% of XLE/XOP/OIH holdings above the 10-day SMA, 38% of XLE names on a Buy technical.

SEMIS — squeeze became structure. SOXQ $97.20, +123.4% over one year. SMH $571.82 (8/6). Semi ETFs surged up to 19% on the week. The driver is now supply, not a short squeeze: SK Hynix chairman guides global memory supply ~20% BELOW demand through 2030, Micron HBM sold out through 2027, Kioxia's entire 2026 NAND output committed, global semi sales a record $120.6B in May (+104% y/y, 15th straight record month). BofA reiterated $1,550 on Micron. This is confirmation of the reversal I acted on last week.

MY ROUND 3 NAMES. SNOW $330.49 (+3.93% on 8/7) against a 52-week high of $331.40 — 99.7% of range, an outright momentum leader; Wells Fargo raised PT to $500; Cortex AI Gateway launched; earnings moved OUT to 2026-09-02, so no print inside my window. PANW $363.86, 52wk $139.57-$376.98 = 94% of range, market cap +157% YTD, BofA to $420; China opened a formal security review (analysts treat as noise); earnings moved to 2026-09-01. ORCL $147.02, 52wk $114.50-$345.72 = 14% of range but UP ~16% off its 7/29 close (one +9% session) on a Google Cloud/Gemini tie-up, a $7B defense contract and Oracle Health expansion; fundamentals unchanged and ugly (-$23.7B FCF, $97.6B net debt, S&P cut to BBB-, ~$40B FY27 raise planned, Burry re-shorting). HOOD ~$90.71 close, 52wk $63.52-$153.86 = 30% of range, 41% below its high despite record Q2 ($1.3B rev +32%, $22B net deposits); Cantor cut PT $130 -> $115.

FINTECH SCREEN — no leader exists. NU $13.84 on a $11.20-$18.98 range = 24% of range, 27% below its high. AFRM $75.25 on $42.10-$100.00 = 57% of range. HOOD 30%. Under a cross-sectional momentum mandate that names fintech, the honest read is that the sector supplies a short, not a long. I am not forcing a fintech long.

ROUND 2 NAMES. RSP $220.09 against a 52-week high of $221.09 — equal weight is at a record and net inflows are accelerating; the anti-concentration long is working even though the anti-concentration SHORT is not. XBI $157.37, 52wk $84.52-$165.71 = 90% of range, +83.6% over one year, +2.87% on 8/7, equal-weighted by construction. Russell 2000 +20% YTD, best year since 2003; ~40% of constituents carry floating-rate debt, which is exactly why a payroll miss that kills hike odds is a small-cap catalyst.

CANDIDATE I REJECTED: MU $877.57 — 12-1 momentum is enormous (from $110) and forward P/E is 6.1, but it sits 30% below its $1,255 high, took a hit on SanDisk guidance, and I already own it inside SMH. Adding it is concentration with single-name gap risk, not new signal.

STANDING-ORDER TAPE CHECK: 12 of 17 fills ever were shorts in GDX/GDXJ and SOXL being stopped out, five on 8/07 alone. I am short neither complex — I am LONG semis via SMH — so that warning cuts in my favour rather than against me. None of my own stops fired this week.

decisions.reason: The three-legged macro premise I wrote this book on seven days ago has inverted on two legs and decayed on the third, so holding it would be holding a view I no longer have. (1) I took energy to 25% of the book because an Iranian strike on a US base in Jordan put a live supply shock into crude; crude is now back at $77.08 WTI / $82.15 Brent with Iran and Oman negotiating over Hormuz, and only a third of the XLE/XOP complex is above its 10-day average. I am paying a war premium that has already left the price, so XLE goes 17->8 and XOP goes to zero. (2) I sized IWM 15->13 and XBI 11->7 specifically because the 30-year was at 2007 highs and three Fed officials were dissenting toward a hike. July payrolls printed -23,000 against +80,000 expected with 103,000 revised away from May and June, yields fell, and September hike odds went 57%->44%. That is the single most direct input to small caps, where roughly 40% of the Russell carries floating-rate debt, and to biotech, the longest-duration asset I own and now at 90% of its 52-week range at +84% over a year. Both trims rested on a premise that no longer exists, so I reverse them: IWM 13->19, XBI 7->12. (3) The QQQ short is the one leg where the market told me I was wrong rather than that the world changed: Nasdaq closed at a record and LED the week at +5.2% against the S&P's +3.6%, so the equal-weight-over-megacap spread ran against me. My mandate requires an anti-concentration short, so I halve it to the mandate minimum rather than abandon it, and I note RSP itself is at 99.5% of its 52-week range - the long side of the pair is still working, only the short side is not. Separately I am fixing a mandate gap: my mandate says TNA-amplified and I have never owned TNA. A rate-cut repricing off a weak labour print is the highest-torque moment there is for 3x small-cap, so I take a stopped 6% starter rather than leave the mandate unexpressed. RSP and ETH are left untouched at exactly their current weights so I pay nothing to restate positions I still believe.

positions.thesis: Unchanged at 19 and deliberately not traded. RSP closed at $220.09 against a 52-week high of $221.09 - equal weight is making records and net inflows into the strategy are accelerating. The anti-concentration thesis is being expressed by the long leg, not the short leg, so this is where the size belongs. +22.4% over one year at a 0.92 beta.

Restored 13->19, reversing a trim I made for a reason that has since evaporated. I capped it a week ago because 30-year yields at their highest since 2007 are a headwind to floating-rate small-cap borrowers; payrolls at -23,000 with 103,000 revised away pulled September hike odds to 44% and sent yields down. Roughly 40% of Russell 2000 constituents carry floating-rate debt, so this is the most mechanically rate-sensitive long in my universe, and the index is already having its best year since 2003 at +20%.

Restored 7->12. I cut this to 7 explicitly because it is the longest-duration asset I own and the 30-year was at 5.22%; yields fell on the payroll miss, so the stated reason for the trim is gone. It also satisfies the equal-weight half of my mandate by construction, sits at 90% of a $84.52-$165.71 range, is +83.6% over one year, and rose 2.87% on 8/7 - a leader, not a laggard I am hoping recovers.

Nudged 9->11. Industrials are cyclical breadth with no semiconductor supply-chain exposure and no crude beta, which is exactly what I want more of as I take energy down by two thirds. Lower discount rates and a Fed pushed back to hold help capital-intensive domestic cyclicals; a softening labour market is the offsetting risk, which is why this is a nudge and not a large add.

Up 8->10. I trimmed this last week partly because 20-year-high long yields mark down bank securities portfolios; yields fell this week, which reverses that specific drag. Regional banks are also small-cap financials, so they are levered breadth rather than a separate bet. Held to 10 and no higher because -23,000 payrolls with heavy negative revisions is a credit-quality signal, and banks are where a labour-market crack shows up first.

Cut hard, 17->8. I made this my largest long a week ago on a live supply shock after strikes on a US base in Jordan sent crude up over 6%. Crude is back at $77.08 and Iran and Oman are negotiating over the Strait of Hormuz - the shock has been priced out, and only 33% of the energy complex is above its 10-day average. I keep a residual 8% because energy is a genuine cyclical sector inside my breadth mandate and Hormuz risk is reduced rather than resolved; I do not keep a position sized for a war premium that has left the tape.

New, and it closes an open mandate gap - my mandate literally says TNA-amplified and I have never held it. The reason to open it now rather than at any point in the past four weeks is that 3x small-cap needs a catalyst to justify its decay, and a payroll miss that cuts September hike odds from 57% to 44% is that catalyst, landing on the most floating-rate-levered index in the market. Started at 6% with a -25% stop because 3x daily compounding punishes chop, so this leg has to be small enough that a sideways month is an annoyance rather than a hole.

Held at exactly 3% so I pay no crossing cost. The regime moved my way - a Fed pushed back from hiking and record equity highs beat the three-dissent tape I trimmed into - but it is still down roughly 49% over a year, which is a laggard on any horizon that matters. Token speculative tail per mandate, stopped at -30%, and at 35bps a side it is not worth resizing on a view this marginal.

Halved 12->6. I upsized this leg because QQQ was 11.6% below its high while RSP was 1.1% below its; this week QQQ made a record close and LED at +5.2% against the S&P's +3.6%, so the spread I said was paying me reversed and this was the largest single drag on the book. My mandate requires a small anti-concentration short and I will not abandon a mandate leg over one bad week, but a mandated hedge running against me belongs at the small end of small. Kept live rather than closed because a labour market shedding jobs is the setup where richly-priced megacap multiples eventually get questioned.

decisions.reason: Two problems, both mine rather than the market's. First, ORCL. I upsized the short 5->8 on the argument that a capex boom hurts the one participant who has to borrow to build. Within days it went from roughly $126 to $147 - one +9% session, about +16% against me on the week - on a Google Cloud and Gemini integration, a $7B defense contract, Oracle Health expansion and new logo wins. It is now within a few points of my -20% stop. The mandate case for keeping it is real and unchanged: at $147 on a $114.50-$345.72 range it is at 14% of range, free cash flow is -$23.7B, net debt $97.6B, S&P has it at BBB- and it needs ~$40B of FY27 financing - on twelve-month-minus-one-month momentum, the construction my mandate uses, it is bottom decile and this bounce is precisely the recent-month reversal that construction skips. But a thesis that draws a 16% counter-move inside a week has earned a smaller position, not the bigger one I gave it. I cut it to 4%, where the stop caps the leg at 0.8% of NAV, and I stop pressing a loser to prove a point. Second, I was carrying 40% cash under a mandate that says winners keep winning, through the strongest week for the indices since April, and every one of my three longs got stronger while I sat in T-bills. That is the mandate not being expressed. SNOW closed at $330.49 against a 52-week high of $331.40 and its earnings moved out to Sept 2, so the event risk I sized my stop for is not in my window. PANW is at 94% of its range with its print also moved to Sept 1. Semis are no longer a squeeze I got lucky on - SK Hynix now guides global memory supply ~20% below demand through 2030, Micron HBM is sold out through 2027 and Kioxia's whole 2026 NAND book is committed, which is a multi-year shortage, and SOXQ is +123% over one year. I press all three and add PLTR, where a +30% post-earnings move on 79% trailing revenue growth is the freshest momentum ignition in my universe with the print already behind it. I add no fintech long on purpose: I screened NU at 24% of its range, AFRM at 57% and HOOD at 30%, and a sector with no leader supplies a short, not a long - which is where my fintech exposure already sits. I keep 23% cash rather than going flat out, because -23,000 payrolls with 103,000 revised away is a real crack and this is a book of 150x-to-350x-earnings names at record index highs.
decisions.novelty: Round 3 shares zero symbols with Round 2 and the two books are structurally opposed rather than merely different: Round 3 is 67% long concentrated megacap-adjacent AI software and semis, while Round 2 is short QQQ and long equal-weight, small-cap, biotech, industrials, banks and energy - same-direction gross-weight overlap is 0%, and the one place they touch the same theme they touch it on opposite sides.

positions.thesis: Pressed 20->24 and still the largest position. The reason to add is that the basis of the trade changed from technical to structural since I opened it: what I bought as a violent reversal off an SK Hynix miss is now underwritten by SK Hynix's own chairman guiding global memory supply roughly 20% below demand through 2030, Micron HBM sold out through 2027, Kioxia's entire 2026 NAND output committed, and record global semi sales of $120.6B in May, the fifteenth consecutive monthly record. SOXQ is +123% over one year, first in my universe on twelve-month-minus-one-month momentum. Still taken via the diversified ETF at 2bps rather than Micron at $878 after a $110-$1,255 annual range, because I want the sector and not the gap risk. Stop stays wide at -18% because the complex still trades in 15-20% weekly swings.

Up 14->18. Closed at $330.49 against a 52-week high of $331.40 - 99.7% of its range, the best relative-strength reading in my universe and the literal definition of the signal my mandate trades. Two things improved since I set the weight: the earnings date moved from Aug 26 to Sept 2, so the print my stop was sized against is no longer inside my holding window, and Wells Fargo took its target to $500 on agent adoption. Cortex AI Gateway extends the consumption story that lets me own the AI capex cycle through software rather than hardware. Stop stays at -22% because a name at 156x forward and 100% of its range has no valuation floor to land on.

Up 12->15. At $363.86 on a $139.57-$376.98 range it sits at 94% of range with market cap up 157% year to date, and BofA, Barclays and Oppenheimer all raised targets. The specific unlock is that earnings moved from Aug 17 to Sept 1, which removes the print I was explicitly holding size back for. China's formal security review is the live negative and the reason this is a 15 and not a 20; the sell-side reads it as noise against AI-driven security demand, and security budgets are the least discretionary line in enterprise software when the labour market is cracking. Stop stays real at -20% against a 352 trailing P/E.

New. Rose 10.32% on 8/7 to $172.01 and is up roughly 30% since Q2, on trailing revenue of $6.16B growing 79% with EPS up 288%, driven by commercial AI acceleration rather than government renewals alone. A large positive post-earnings move on an accelerating fundamental is the cleanest fresh momentum ignition available to me, and post-announcement drift is the same effect my mandate is built on. It adds a driver I do not already own - defense and government AI software, uncorrelated to both memory pricing and enterprise data consumption - so it is diversification inside the mandate rather than more of SMH. Sized at only 10% because at 65% of a $106-$208 range it has not reclaimed its high, it carries a 147 P/E, and a 1.56-beta name that just moved 30% can give a third of it back without anything being wrong.

Unchanged at 6% and untraded. At roughly $90.71 on a $63.52-$153.86 range it is at 30% of range and 41% below its high despite a record quarter - $1.3B revenue up 32%, $22B net deposits - and Cantor cut its target from $130 to $115 anyway. A name that cannot hold a bid on a blowout print, through a week when the Nasdaq made a record high and the whole retail-risk complex should have carried it, is a laggard confirming itself; that non-participation in this specific week is the new evidence. Kept small with a wide -25% stop because it is a high-beta retail and crypto proxy that squeezes hardest in exactly the melt-up my longs need.

Cut 8->4, reversing last week's upsize. The fundamental case is intact and arguably worse: -$23.7B free cash flow, $97.6B net debt, S&P at BBB- one notch off junk, ~$40B of FY27 debt and equity financing needed, all against a $638B backlog worth 1.6x the market cap that still has to convert to cash, and at $147 on a $114.50-$345.72 range it remains a bottom-decile twelve-month momentum name. What changed is the tape, not the balance sheet - a Google Cloud and Gemini tie-up, a $7B defense contract and Oracle Health expansion took it up roughly 16% in a week, one session of it +9%. My mandate wants two persistent laggards and this is still one, and the reversal is the recent month that momentum construction deliberately ignores. But being right slowly at 8% with a -20% stop a few points away is a coin flip on timing, so I hold the view at a size where the stop costs 0.8% of NAV.

decisions.name: Opus Picks-and-Shovels
decisions.research_notes:
PRICES/EVENTS CHECKED (through 2026-08-07 close, via stockanalysis.com quote pages):

Round 2 names — ANET $188.67 (-1.90% Fri): reported Q2 on Aug 4, revenue >$3B, +37.7% y/y, FY26 guide RAISED to $12.6B (~+40% growth); consensus Strong Buy, avg target $238.63, Barclays high $289; stock still -12% below its $214.89 high.
