VRT $272.40 (-1.01%), -28% from its $379.94 high after a July 29 Q2 revenue MISS ($3.27B vs $3.38B) that management called a timing/supply issue; fwd PE 34.9, target $338.

Tape/macro — SPY $773.26 (+0.61%), basically at its record $776.85, but commentary flags the move as options-positioning-driven; Burry publicly warning of a 1987-type top. SOXX $543.27 (+2.02%) still -17% below its $655.95 high — semis are the laggard complex, not the extended one. SOXL $140.25 (+5.99%) but -54% from its high on 3x decay. Decisive macro event: a soft US payrolls print cut Fed hike expectations — GLD $398.47 (+2.26%), gold at seven-week highs near $4,300/oz; GDX $89.89 (+7.11%); GDXJ $117.62 (+7.51%); UUP $28.07 (-0.43%).

Round 3 names — XLE $57.50 (-1.13%), the ONLY leg down on the dovish day, +40% 1y, 2.64% yield, -9% from high. COPX $88.03 (+2.25%), +104% 1y, PE 18.5. EWZ $35.34 (-1.31%), PE 9.81, 4.14% yield, 25% US tariffs live but Brazil's central bank still cutting. EZU $71.57 (+0.76%) at its 52-week high, PE 17.6, Stoxx 600 at records with ~20.8% earnings growth. EWJ $96.90 (+1.75%) at its 52-week high, PE 18.6, 3.68% yield.

WHAT I LEARNED THAT CHANGED MY MIND: (1) My SMCI short thesis is being contradicted by the issuer itself — SMCI pre-announced strong prelims and the street raised targets; I was holding a squeezing 9% short into a positively pre-announced Aug 11 print, in a tape where 12 of 17 standing orders that ever fired were shorts getting stopped out. (2) ANET, not MU, produced the week's actual fundamental confirmation, and it is my most under-weighted leg. (3) SK Hynix capex is bullish the tool vendor (AMAT) and bearish the commodity (MU) — the shortage is now inducing supply. (4) The hawkish-Warsh-Fed premise on which I cut my dollar short to 3% last week was falsified by the payroll miss.

decisions.reason: Two things broke my book's logic this week and both point the same way. First, my 9% SMCI short is a negative-expectancy trade I can identify in advance: the company itself pre-announced a strong preliminary fiscal Q4, analysts raised targets on it, the street's $37.81 target sits ABOVE the $31.13 spot, and it closed +5.96% Friday — I would be carrying a squeezing short into a positively pre-announced Aug 11 print, in a tape that has stopped out shorts 12 times out of 17 firings. The margin-compression thesis may still be true in a year; it is not tradeable through Tuesday, so I cover before the print rather than after. Second, ANET delivered the only hard fundamental confirmation of the week — revenue >$3B, +37.7% y/y, full-year guide RAISED to $12.6B/+40% — and it was my smallest long at 8%, while MU, which delivered nothing, was 12%. MU is now below its 50-day ($877 vs $971) precisely because SK Hynix announced heavy capex, which is the supply response that ends memory shortages; that same news raises wafer-fab-equipment demand, so the memory dollar belongs with the tool vendor I already own, not the commodity. I therefore cut MU to a 5% stub (kept only because forward PE 6.1 and a $1,502 target make a full exit reckless), take ANET to 15%, add 1pt to AVGO on the genuinely new $200B Samsung AI-chip partnership, and open a 7% VRT leg — datacenter power and thermal is the same electrons-are-the-bottleneck thesis as GEV but 28% off its high after a Q2 revenue miss management attributes to project timing, which is the discounted entry GEV no longer offers. I deliberately do NOT re-establish a leveraged semis kicker despite my mandate permitting one: SOXL closed +5.99% on Friday and my max drawdown is already -14.61%, so buying 3x semis after a 6% day is exactly the risk my mandate caps. Net long rises 70%-to-85% because covering the short mechanically adds exposure and because the evidence is one-directional, but I hold 15% cash at 4% rather than the 8% I would run if SPY were not at a record on admittedly options-driven mechanics with semis still 17% below their high.

positions.thesis: GE Vernova remains the power-generation bottleneck feeding $720-745B of 2026 hyperscaler capex — Q2 orders +88% y/y, $176B backlog, 30GW gas-turbine target by 2030. Trimmed 1pt purely as funding: at $990.32 it is flat since my fill, PE 28.3, and its $1,231 consensus target implies 24% upside, less discount than the two legs I am adding to. It stays my largest position because it is the only leg whose supply constraint is physical rather than cyclical.

Applied Materials sells the tools, not the commodity, and SK Hynix's newly announced capex is a direct order-book event for wafer-fab equipment — the supply response to the memory shortage spends through AMAT. $539.14, forward PE 35.8 against a $629 target, freshly added to Goldman's US Conviction List. Held at 20% and deliberately NOT increased into the Aug 13 Q3 print: I want the exposure I already have, not an added bet on a binary three sessions out. Wide -22% stop so an earnings gap cannot mechanically stop out a thesis that is about 2027 orders.

Raised 16-to-17 on genuinely new information: a ~$200B AI-chip partnership with Samsung that widens Broadcom's custom-silicon manufacturing capacity, the binding constraint on a business whose accelerator bookings have been stacking faster than it can ship. Rising memory and system costs make custom ASICs the cheaper compute-per-dollar answer, not a casualty. $427.76, forward PE 27.1 against a $527.88 target, still -14% from its $495 high. Earnings Sept 2 sits outside the near window.

Raised 8-to-15, the largest add in the book, because Arista is the only holding that produced hard confirmation this week: Q2 revenue above $3B, +37.7% y/y, and a full-year guide RAISED to $12.6B implying ~40% growth, with targets lifted broadly afterward (consensus $238.63, Barclays $289). At $188.67 it is -12% from its high and fell 1.9% on Friday despite the beat — the market has not repriced it. PE 59.7 is the risk, but it is the cheapest way I have to own compute-fabric growth of 40% and it diversifies me away from a book that is otherwise semiconductors and turbines.

New leg. Vertiv is datacenter power distribution and liquid cooling — the same physical-bottleneck thesis as GEV, but available at a 28% discount to its $379.94 high because Q2 revenue missed ($3.27B vs $3.38B) on what management calls project-timing and supply-chain slippage. Timing slippage in a capex cycle running at $720-745B is deferred revenue, not lost revenue. Forward PE 34.9 against a $338 target and 28 analysts at Strong Buy. Wider -25% stop because I am buying a name that has already been marked down for an execution stumble and needs room to prove the miss was temporary.

Cut 12-to-5. The memory shortage is real, but SK Hynix's capex announcement is the supply response that historically ends it, and the tape agrees — $877.57 is below the $970.95 50-day moving average, so the stock is in a downtrend while my other legs make new ground. Forward PE 6.1 and a $1,502 consensus target are why I keep a stub rather than exiting: memory cyclicals are cheapest at the top, but they are also occasionally just cheap. Tightened to a -20% stop from -28% because I no longer want catastrophe-insurance width on a position I have already reduced to a stub; next earnings is Sept 22.

decisions.reason: The single macro event of the week was a soft US payrolls print that cut Fed hike expectations, and it moved four of my seven legs in a way that says my current weights encode last week's regime, not this one. Gold went to a seven-week high near $4,300 (GLD +2.26%), GDX +7.11% and GDXJ +7.51% in a single session, and the dollar fell — while XLE was the ONLY leg in the book that fell (-1.13%). That is the whole rebalance. XLE goes 26-to-20: it was sized as my anchor on a geopolitical-supply-and-inflation premise, but if the Fed is now easing because the labour market is cracking, energy demand is the leg most exposed to that crack, and Friday's tape already showed energy trading as a growth asset rather than a real asset. UUP short goes 3-to-7: last week I explicitly cut it to a 3% token because a hawkish Warsh Fed with September hike risk favoured the near-term rate differential — that exact premise was falsified on Friday, so I restore the leg rather than pretend the reason still holds. COPX goes 12-to-15 because copper is the one holding levered to all three of a weaker dollar, an easing Fed and electrification demand simultaneously. I am NOT adding to GDX despite it being my best performer: the desk note that a dozen short stops fired in the gold complex tells me a large part of Friday's 7% was a crowded-short unwind, and unwind fuel exhausts, so I hold 22% and let the position work rather than chase it. EWZ, EZU and EWJ are untouched — Brazil at PE 9.8 with a 4.1% yield gets the classic EM tailwind from Fed easing that offsets the 25% tariff drag, and Europe and Japan are both sitting at 52-week highs with the Stoxx 600 at records on ~20.8% earnings growth, which is a reason to leave them alone rather than to trade around them. Cash to 7%; at a 4% APY there is no case for holding more when every real-asset leg just got a monetary tailwind.
decisions.novelty: Round 3 shares zero names and zero same-direction gross weight with my Round 2 book: Round 2 is 85% long US AI-infrastructure equities (power generation, semi-cap, custom silicon, networking, datacenter thermal) with no shorts, while Round 3 is 86% long non-US and real-asset exposure (energy, gold miners, copper miners, Brazil, eurozone, Japan) plus a 7% short dollar leg — the two books have no overlapping ticker and are driven by opposite macro inputs, since Round 2 wants nominal growth and Round 3 wants a falling real rate and a weaker dollar.

positions.thesis: Gold miners as the levered Fed-credibility trade, and now the book's anchor. Friday's soft payrolls cut hike expectations and took gold to a seven-week high near $4,300; GDX rose 7.11% to $89.89 yet still trades -23% below its $117.18 high at PE 13.6 with miners earning record margins at this gold price. Held at 22% rather than raised, because part of Friday's move was a crowded short base being stopped out and that fuel does not repeat. No take-profit, so I am not forced out of a monetary thesis by a price target; stop tightened to -18% from the new level to protect the gain.

Trimmed 26-to-20 and demoted from anchor. Energy remains genuine real-asset carry — +40% over the year, 2.64% yield, -9% from its high, supported by Middle East supply risk, refiner margins and AI power demand — but it was the only holding that FELL on the dovish payroll day, which tells me the market is now pricing it as a demand-cyclical rather than an inflation hedge. If the Fed is easing because employment is deteriorating, this is the leg that owns that deterioration, so it should not also be my largest position.

Raised 12-to-15. Copper miners are the only leg simultaneously levered to all three of what just changed: a weaker dollar, a Fed pivoting from hikes toward cuts, and physical tightness meeting grid electrification and datacenter buildout demand. $88.03 (+2.25% Friday), +104% over the past year, PE 18.5, 2.2% yield, still short of its $99.99 high. This is the industrial-real-asset counterpart to the monetary bet in GDX.

Held at 10%. Brazil at PE 9.81 with a 4.14% dividend yield is the cheapest carry in the basket, and a Fed that stops hiking is historically the single strongest input for EM equity while Brazil's own central bank is already cutting into moderating inflation. The 25% US tariff on Brazilian goods is why this is 10% and not 15%, but Vale and Petrobras give it commodity leverage that benefits from the same weaker dollar driving the rest of the book.

Held at 10%. Eurozone value at PE 17.6 with a 2.57% yield, sitting at $71.57 against a $71.82 52-week high with the Stoxx 600 at records on roughly 20.8% projected earnings growth. A non-US, non-AI earnings stream with no exposure whatsoever to the hyperscaler capex argument my Round 2 book is making. Left untouched because a leg making new highs on broadening earnings is not a leg that needs managing.

Held at 9%. Japan's governance-reform and buyback story is still compounding — $96.90 (+1.75% Friday) against a $97.52 high, PE 18.6, 3.68% yield, +33% total return over the past year. A dollar that weakens on Fed easing firms the yen, which adds to dollar-based returns here, so this leg and the UUP short reinforce each other.

Raised 3-to-7, reversing last week's cut. I reduced this leg to a token specifically because a hawkish Fed with September hike risk made the near-term rate differential favour the dollar — Friday's soft payrolls repriced hike expectations away and UUP fell to $28.07, so the reason for the cut no longer exists. The structural fiscal-credibility case was always intact; what was missing was the near-term catalyst, and the labour data supplied it. Sized at 7% rather than the original 8% because UUP still sits in the upper half of its $26.40-$28.60 range and one payroll print is one data point. Tight -8% stop: this is a macro expression, not a conviction position.

decisions.name: Opus Quality Defensive
decisions.research_notes:
WEB SEARCH BUDGET WAS EXHAUSTED (200/200) before I could use it, so I rebuilt the tape from primary price data (Yahoo chart API, pulled fresh through 2026-08-07 into /tmp/.../scratchpad/w4px/) plus targeted WebFetch on stockanalysis.com quote/news pages. Local repo price files (px.csv, universe_px.csv) were stale at 2026-07-24 and unusable.

THE MACRO EVENT: The July employment report printed a LOSS of 23,000 payrolls. Markets repriced the Fed toward cuts. Consequences visible across every asset I hold: dollar down, Treasury yields down (TLT +1.0% wk), gold broke out to ~$4,350 spot (seven-week high, plus the PBoC's largest monthly purchase since 2023), and equities put in "the best week since April with a record close" on the S&P. This is the exact opposite of the regime both my books were positioned for on 7/31 (rotation OUT of AI-capex INTO cheap defensive cash-flow).

WEEK-ENDING 2026-08-07 NUMBERS I PULLED (1w / 1m / 3m / 12m / vs50d / vs200d):
- SMH +7.80 / -4.64 / +11.48 / +103.32 / -2.1 / +27.8. SOXX +7.60 / -6.55 / +12.59 / +125.97 / -4.1 / +33.0. The semis "bust" was a -20% one-month drawdown that got bought violently. Long-term trend emphatically intact.
- GDX +21.31 in ONE WEEK, +19.01 1m, +67.8 12m, +14.6 above its 50d. GLD +7.25 / +5.69 / -4.73 / +29.63, now +4.2 above 50d but still -3.2 below 200d (recovering from a -10.5% six-month correction). Consistent with the desk note that 12 of 17 fired standing orders were gold-miner and SOXL shorts stopping out.
- Defensives (mine): XLV +1.93 / +3.01 / +14.53 / +23.52, +5.1 vs 50d, +9.0 vs 200d — still the best 3m sector I own. SCHD +1.28 / +4.63 / +7.83 / +28.64. USMV +2.75 / +2.93 / +6.86. XLP +0.08 / +1.19 / +1.96 / +7.34 — the clear laggard, barely participating. XLU -1.67 / -3.96 (glad I own none).
- Energy/commodities BROKE, and this is the finding I did not expect: USO -8.66% on the week and -13.69% over two weeks, -18.17% 3m, now below its 50-day — while the news flow was maximally bullish (Iran/Strait of Hormuz tension, record refinery margins, XOM and CVX Q2 profits surging on higher crude). A sector that cannot rally on its own best headlines has a finished trend. XLE -3.44 wk / -2.58 3m. PDBC -1.77 wk, -3.90 2w, -7.21 3m (still +10.3 above 200d). DBC -1.83 wk. A contracting labour market is demand-negative for oil, which reconciles the price action with the headlines.
- Trend candidates I screened for Round 3: EFA +2.81 / +4.04 / +8.06 / +23.71, +4.6 vs 50d, +10.0 vs 200d — the most consistent uptrend across every horizon on my screen, and a weak-dollar regime is structurally its tailwind. IWM +3.56 / +1.88 / +6.98 / +35.79, +13.3 above 200d, outperforming the S&P YTD. XLF +1.16 / +3.39 / +12.04, +5.2 vs 50d. JEPI +0.91 / +2.10 / +4.00 / +9.52 — materially better than last week's read; it has reclaimed its 200-day (+4.1) so the carry leg now passes the trend filter it failed on 7/31. DBMF flat (+0.03 wk) — CTAs got whipsawed as commodities and the equity short both reversed, but it holds above both MAs. MTUM still -2.4 below its 50d. SLV +9.82 wk but -9.8 below its 200d (squeeze, not trend). KRE screens well (+3.2 vs 50d) but I rejected it: regional-bank credit into a shrinking payroll count is the wrong risk.
- Crypto: ETH +4.06 / +7.28, +6.7 above 50d but -6.7 below 200d and -55% 12m. BTC +3.50 / +1.82, +2.6 above 50d but -7.5 below 200d and -44% 12m. Both remain broken primary trends; ETH is the stronger.

WHAT I CONCLUDED: The AI-infra-overextension short is a losing hedge in a rate-cut liquidity regime — it stopped hedging my longs and started correlating against them. And a -23k payroll print is genuinely bad economic news that the market is trading as good news; that argues for MORE defensive quality and MORE gold, not for chasing the melt-up, but it also argues against being short the highest-beta thing in a Fed-cut tape and against owning cyclical energy demand.

decisions.reason: The July payroll print (-23,000 jobs) flipped the regime my 7/31 book was built for, and it did so in a way that hurts one leg and helps the mandate everywhere else. Two changes follow from that, and I am deliberately not touching the rest. First, the semis short: my thesis was 'AI-infra overextended,' the bust actually happened (-20% in a month), and it was bought back with both hands the moment the Fed turned dovish — SMH +7.80% in a week, +103% over twelve months, still 27.8% above its 200-day. Insurance that pays out against my longs falling is worth carrying; insurance whose losses are driven by the same rate-cut impulse that lifts my longs is not insurance at all, it is an uncorrelated short in the market's highest-beta index. I cut it in half and tighten the stop so a full stop-out from here costs 32bp instead of ~1%. This is also the complex where 5 of 17 standing orders died on 8/07 alone; I am sizing to survive a squeeze rather than to be right about it. Second, my mandate names a gold diversifier and my book has had none — an omission the tape just punished. Gold broke out on soft jobs, a weaker dollar, falling real yields and record PBoC buying; bullion is the low-volatility way to own that, unlike the miners which just went up 21% in five sessions. I fund it by trimming XLP, which is the only defensive sleeve failing to participate (+1.96% over three months). Crucially I am NOT retreating from the defensive stance: a shrinking labour market is precisely the environment where healthcare, quality cash-flow and min-vol earn their keep over the next several quarters, so XLV stays the conviction position at a third of the book.

positions.thesis: Still the conviction position and untouched in substance. Healthcare leads my defensive set on the horizon that matters (+14.53% 3m) and on the year (+23.52%), trades 5.1% above its 50-day and 9.0% above its 200-day, and the leadership stays broad across LLY, JNJ, ABBV, MRK and managed care rather than one drug. A 0.56 beta with earnings that do not depend on the payroll count is exactly what I want owning going into a labour market that just shed 23,000 jobs. I trimmed two points only to make room for the mandated gold sleeve, not because the view weakened.

The quality-factor sleeve, screening on return on capital, free cash flow and low leverage without QUAL's ~30% technology weight. It keeps compounding through the regime flip: +4.63% 1m, +7.83% 3m, +15.56% 6m, +24.27% YTD, and 13.1% above its 200-day. Dividend cash-flow quality also holds its value better than most equity factors if the Fed is cutting because the economy is genuinely deteriorating rather than because inflation is solved.

Min-vol ballast, and it quietly did its job this week — +2.75%, ahead of XLP and SCHD, while sitting 4.0% above its 50-day and 6.4% above its 200-day. I keep preferring it to SPLV because SPLV's utilities concentration is a live drag (XLU -3.96% 1m, below both moving averages) even now that yields have come down.

Trimmed from 13% because it is the one defensive leg not participating: +0.08% on the week and +1.96% over three months, versus +14.53% for XLV. I am not abandoning it — staples remain the truest low-beta cash-flow ballast and it still holds above both moving averages — but it does not deserve a weight comparable to sleeves compounding six times faster, and it is the natural funding source for the gold position.

New, and it repairs a gap: my mandate specifies a small gold diversifier and the book had none through exactly the week gold broke out. Spot reached ~$4,350 on soft payrolls, a weaker dollar, falling real yields and the PBoC's biggest monthly purchase since 2023, putting GLD 4.2% above its 50-day (+7.25% on the week, +5.69% 1m). It is still 3.2% below its 200-day after a -10.5% six-month correction, so I am buying a trend that is turning rather than one that is finished, which is the better risk. I choose bullion over the miners deliberately: GDX rose 21% in five sessions and that is a squeeze, not an entry. Stop below the breakout, take-profit near the next major extension.

Halved from 8% and demoted to a token. The overextension case is intact on the long horizon — 44.7x earnings, +103% over twelve months, 27.8% above its 200-day — and SMH is still 4.6% below where it was a month ago and below its 50-day, so I will not claim the view is dead. But the market just told me the timing is wrong: a -20% drawdown was fully bought within days of the Fed repricing dovish, and in a rate-cut regime long-duration growth gets a bid regardless of capex discipline. At 4% with a stop 8% away, the worst case from here costs 32bp, which is what a speculative hedge should cost a defensive book. Take-profit unchanged so I still get paid properly if the bust resumes.

decisions.reason: This is a trend-stacking mandate and the cross-asset trend set genuinely changed, so re-racking is the discipline, not churn. Three trends I owned rolled over and two I did not own turned up. The clearest signal of the week was not in my P&L, it was in oil: USO fell 8.66% in five sessions and 13.69% in two weeks, through its 50-day, while the headlines were as bullish as they get — Hormuz disruption, record refinery margins, supermajor profits surging on crude. A trend that cannot rally on its own best news is over, and a shrinking payroll count explains why. So XLE goes to zero and PDBC is cut from 24% to a residual. Second, I close the SMH short outright. Last week I wrote that I was applying the trend filter honestly; applying it honestly today means admitting that a name up 103% over twelve months, 27.8% above its 200-day, that just rose 7.8% in a week, is not a downtrend a trend book gets to be short. The intermediate dip was the countertrend, not the trend, and I was on the wrong side of my own rule. Third, the redeployment. EFA is the cleanest uptrend on my entire screen — positive on every horizon from one week to twelve months, above both moving averages — and a Fed cutting into a weak dollar is the structural tailwind for ex-US equity, so it becomes a core leg. IWM gets the equity-momentum slot: 13.3% above its 200-day and beating the S&P year-to-date, and small caps are the most direct expression of the rate-cut repricing. XLF adds trend plus dividend carry with far better credit quality than KRE, which I screened and rejected because regional-bank credit into a contracting labour market is the wrong risk to be paid for. JEPI is upgraded from a grudging stub to a real weight because it now clears the filter it failed on 7/31 — it has reclaimed its 200-day (+4.1%) and option-writing income is exactly the right carry to own if this melt-up turns choppy. DBMF stays the structural core even though it went nowhere this week; the whole point of a managed-futures sleeve is that it re-positions across the regime turn without my having to call each leg. BTC is cut to zero and only ETH keeps a crypto stub: both are still below their 200-days and down 44% and 55% on the year, and if I only get to hold one broken trend it should be the one 6.7% above its 50-day rather than 2.6%.
decisions.novelty: Zero name overlap with my Round 2 defensive book and zero same-direction gross-weight overlap: Round 2 owns US defensive quality and bullion (XLV, SCHD, USMV, XLP, GLD) plus a residual semis short, while Round 3 owns international and small-cap equity trend, financials, option-premium and managed-futures carry, a commodity residual and a crypto stub (EFA, IWM, XLF, JEPI, DBMF, PDBC, ETH) — and where the two books touch the same idea they take opposite postures, with Round 2 holding gold as a defensive hedge and shorting semis while Round 3 holds neither and instead expresses the same dovish-Fed impulse through high-beta cyclical and ex-US trend legs.

positions.thesis: The mandate's structural core: cross-asset managed-futures trend that re-positions itself when the regime turns, which is precisely what just happened. It went nowhere this week (+0.03%) because CTAs were long commodities and short equities and both reversed — that whipsaw is the cost of the sleeve, not evidence against it. It still holds above both moving averages (+0.4% vs 50d, +4.7% vs 200d) and is +26.0% over twelve months. I own it so that the next trend turn gets captured without my having to be early on every leg by hand.

New core trend leg and the single most consistent uptrend on my screen: positive over one week (+2.81%), one month (+4.04%), three months (+8.06%), six months (+9.46%) and twelve (+23.71%), sitting 4.6% above its 50-day and 10.0% above its 200-day. Unlike the US momentum complex it never had the AI-capex air pocket, so there is no unwind overhanging it. The macro fits the mandate too: a Fed cutting into a softening labour market weakens the dollar, and dollar weakness is a direct, mechanical tailwind to unhedged developed-international returns — trend and a currency carry in one line.

Promoted from an 8% stub because the facts changed. On 7/31 I kept it grudgingly since it sat below its 200-day and had returned +0.1% over twelve months; it now trades 4.1% above its 200-day and 3.0% above its 50-day, at +4.00% over three months and +9.52% over twelve. That means the covered-call income sleeve my mandate requires finally clears the same trend filter I apply to everything else, so it earns a real weight rather than a token one. Written-call carry is also the right thing to own if a record-high melt-up on weak economic data turns into a choppy, low-drift tape.

New, and it fills the equity-momentum slot I emptied when I sold MTUM. Small caps are outperforming the S&P year-to-date, up 35.8% over twelve months, 13.3% above the 200-day and 2.7% above the 50-day, and they rose 3.56% this week. I prefer IWM to MTUM here because MTUM is still 2.4% below its own 50-day — it remains the crowded AI trade in a repair phase — whereas the Russell is the cleanest, most direct beneficiary of the rate-cut repricing that soft payrolls just triggered. Sized below my core legs because small-cap earnings are the most economically sensitive thing I own and the payroll print was genuinely weak, so the stop matters.

Cut from 24% to a residual, which is the biggest single change in the book. The roll-carry structure is unchanged and PDBC still holds above both moving averages (+1.4% vs 50d, +10.3% vs 200d) at +29.9% year-to-date, which is why it is not zero. But its dominant exposure just cracked: crude fell 8.66% in a week and 13.69% in two, through its 50-day, against the most bullish supply headlines available. Three-month return is now -7.21%. A contracting labour market is demand-negative for energy, so I treat the past month's strength as the tail of a trade rather than the start of one and keep only enough to stay in the commodity-carry sleeve my mandate names.

New, and it does two jobs the mandate wants at once: a confirmed uptrend (+12.04% over three months, 5.2% above its 50-day, 9.4% above its 200-day) and dividend carry. Falling front-end rates with a steepening curve is the classic setup for financials to earn wider net interest margin while capital-markets activity picks up on the record-volume tape. I chose XLF over KRE, which screened comparably, on purpose: money-centre banks, insurers and exchanges are far better collateral than regional-bank loan books if the -23,000 payroll print is the start of real credit deterioration rather than a one-month blip.

The crypto sleeve survives as a single stub rather than two. ETH is +7.28% over a month and 6.7% above its 50-day, the strongest short-horizon crypto trend available, and it participated in the risk-on week at +4.06%. But it is still 6.7% below its 200-day and -55% over twelve months, so the primary trend remains down and a trend mandate cannot justify size here just because crypto is a headline sleeve. Held spot rather than as a perp to avoid paying 10% APR funding to be long a broken trend. Wide stop so ordinary crypto volatility does not take me out, take-profit set where a 50-day reclaim would have become a genuine base.
