GDX $89.89 (+7.11% on the day), +57.73% 1yr, vs a $117.18 52-week high; GDXJ $117.62 (+7.51%), +68.91% 1yr — I chose GDX over GDXJ for liquidity and lower volatility at equivalent distance from the high. SPLV $76.21 (-0.07%), only +6.48% over 1yr, beta 0.54 — the weakest sleeve in either book by a wide margin. TLT $82.76 near its $81.89 52-week low with the 30yr brushing 5%, so the high-rate regime persists and is not a reason to add duration-sensitive assets. Cross-checked the desk note that 12 of 17 standing orders ever fired were shorts in GDX/SOXL being stopped out: I hold no shorts anywhere, so that tape is a signal to me rather than a risk.

decisions.reason: The book is up 4.55% because the software-dislocation call worked, and the right response to a thesis that worked is to bank the leg where the gap has actually closed and press the leg where new fundamental evidence arrived — not to hold everything because it is green. Adobe is the specific case: it is up about 10% from entry and the 40-analyst consensus target of $269.61 now sits above the $265.21 price with Morgan Stanley at Underweight, so the mispricing I bought has been paid out and what remains is a value trap argument rather than a value argument. ServiceNow is the mirror image: I bought it as a starter explicitly saying I would average in rather than anchor on one bounce, and this week supplied the confirmation I asked for — 23% subscription growth and AI ACV crossing $1bn with a ninefold rise in deployments — while the stock is still 36% below its high, so the discount is intact but the terminal-decline premise is now falsifiably wrong. On crypto, my own thesis last week said Ethereum was the only major showing genuine mean-reversion and Bitcoin had no near-term catalyst; a month of ETH +25% against BTC +4.8% is that statement being scored, so I shift weight toward the one that is actually reverting instead of paying carry on the one that is not. Gold I add to for the reason I originally bought it: it printed a seven-week high near $4,293 with the 30-year brushing 5% and TLT pinned at its lows, which is strength against its worst macro headwind, and GLD itself remains far below its high so it is a discounted hedge rather than a chase. UNH, CRM and XLV are untouched — UNH's Q2 and raised targets have not been contradicted by a 2.8% drift, and XLV near its 52-week high vindicates the stub I nearly deleted.

positions.thesis: Held at 18% and still the highest-conviction line. Q2 adjusted EPS of $6.38 beat $4.91 and JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and Goldman all raised targets afterward; 27 analysts now average $475.23 against a $407.08 price. The stock is down about 2.8% since I sized it while XLV sits at a 52-week high, which is a divergence between a company whose numbers improved and a sector that re-rated without it — that is a wider discount than I entered at, not a broken thesis, so the weight stays.

Raised 13->15. Spot gold made a seven-week high near $4,293 and GLD rose 3.95% in a session while TLT sits at $82.76 against an $81.89 52-week low and the 30-year brushes 5% — gold advancing into its single worst macro headwind for a second consecutive week is the confirmation I said I was waiting for. It is also still well below its $509.70 52-week high, so I am adding to a discounted hedge rather than chasing an extended one, and it remains the only position in this book that pays off if the Hormuz de-escalation talks fail.

Held at 13%. Up about 9.5% from my $176 entry to $192.74 with net income +29.3% on revenue +11.0% at 22.4x earnings, and 53 analysts still average $241.72. I deliberately do not add ahead of the 2026-08-26 print: the mean-reversion is compounding on its own and adding size into a binary event would convert a valuation thesis into an earnings bet, which is not what this mandate is.

Raised 6->9. I sized this as a starter and said I would average in only if the bounce were confirmed rather than anchor on one day, and the confirmation is fundamental rather than tape-based: Q2 subscription revenue grew 23%, AI ACV crossed $1bn and customer deployments rose ninefold, which directly refutes the terminal-decline pricing. At $124.88 it is still 36% below its $194.73 high on 22.2% revenue growth, so the dislocation survives even after a 16.7% week. Not taken to core weight because a 27.6x forward multiple is the most rate-sensitive duration in this book and long yields are not falling.

Raised 8->9 and still the crypto core. Up 24.99% over the past month to $1,964 while still down 49% on the year — deeply oversold but actually turning is the exact setup this mandate is written for, and the Ethereum ETF remains the only institutional catalyst in the complex. The add is one point rather than five because a 35bp round trip plus a 25% one-month move means I am no longer buying the bottom, only confirming it. Stop stays at -25% because oversold assets can still trend down.

Held at 8%. Last week I cut this because July sector data showed healthcare at -0.78% and I could not find the rotation I had bought it for; at $165.68, within a point of its $168.53 52-week high and +29.17% over a year on strong Q2 results across the majors, the rotation has arrived. I do not raise it because the stub already does its job of diversifying UNH single-name risk, but the evidence that would have justified deleting it has reversed.

Cut 12->7 to bank a thesis that worked. I bought this as the most extreme valuation dislocation in profitable quality software at $241; at $265.21 the 40-analyst consensus target is $269.61, which is 1.66% of upside, and Morgan Stanley has moved to Underweight on multiple simultaneous transitions. A contrarian mandate exits when the gap it identified closes. The forward PE of 10.23 is the only part of the original argument still standing, and net income growth decelerating to 5.2% against revenue +11.5% is the margin compression the AI-disruption bears predicted, which is why the residual is small.

Cut 6->4. I wrote last week that Bitcoin had no near-term catalyst while Ethereum did, and a month of BTC +4.8% against ETH +25% is that judgment being scored against the tape rather than an opinion I am revising after the fact. It stays in the book at reduced size because at $64,860 it is roughly half off its $126,198 high and the mandate is to own deeply oversold assets, but weight belongs where reversion is observable, not merely available. Stop stays at -25%.

decisions.reason: This book is flat at +0.02% while every trend I claim to follow has been running, and the reason is that its two largest allocations point at things that are no longer trending. XLE was sized at 16% on a specific stated driver — crude up more than 20% in July to roughly $85 WTI and $88 Brent on Hormuz attacks — and that driver has reversed to $78.18 and $83.55 with Iran and Oman reported near a landmark deal to manage the Strait and traders described as staying bearish through the disruptions. The commodity leads the equity, so a trend follower cuts on the divergence rather than waiting for a 15% stop to convert a working trade into a loss; XLE also fell 1.13% on a day the broad tape and every other sleeve rose. SPLV is worse in mandate terms: it has returned 6.48% over a year against SPMO's 29.7%, GDX's 57.7% and XLV's 29.2%, so a 10% weight in the single weakest thing I can measure is not risk management, it is a momentum book paying to be short momentum. The volatility-regime argument I used to justify it — a 65% one-month collapse in a 3x semi fund — has resolved, with SOXX now +130% over twelve months and rising again this week, which also means my read that the semi bounce was mere short covering was wrong. Redeploying into SPMO returns me to my own mandate's purest instrument at a weight that matters, and GDX is the strongest verified relative-strength signal available anywhere in my universe. Alphabet I trim rather than hold flat because losing both the DeepMind CEO and the chief scientist in one week degrades the quality half of quality-momentum in a way the stock's 0.96% decline has plainly not priced.
decisions.novelty: This book shares no symbol with my Round-2 book and selects on the opposite criterion in the two sectors they both touch: precious metals are expressed through miner relative strength (GDX, +57.7% over a year) rather than Round 2's discounted bullion hedge, and technology is expressed through demonstrated leadership (SPMO, AMZN, GOOGL) rather than Round 2's beaten-down software value names (CRM, ADBE, NOW) — the same sectors reached from strength here and from dislocation there.

positions.thesis: Held at 12%. Rising long yields remain a mild headwind to dividend carry with TLT at its 52-week low, but this sleeve exists to dampen drawdown while I make larger changes elsewhere in the book, and this is the week I am making them. Cutting ballast in the same session I add a 10% miner position and double momentum would stack two decisions into one bet; keeping it paid keeps the changes survivable if I am early.

Held at 12%. With TLT pinned at $82.76 against an $81.89 low and the 30-year brushing 5%, high return-on-equity businesses carrying little leverage are the part of the equity complex least damaged by a permanently higher cost of capital, because they do not need to raise any. It keeps me inside the factor mandate without rebuilding the high-beta exposure that hurt this book earlier, and nothing in the rate picture changed this week.

Raised 6->12. I held this at a token 6% because I distrusted the semiconductor bounce as short covering rather than demand; SOXX at +130.37% over twelve months and up another 2.02% this week is no longer a squeeze, it is a completed re-rating, and SPMO's top weights are exactly that complex — Micron 10.1%, NVIDIA 8.2%, Broadcom 6.9%. At +29.69% over a year it is the second-strongest sleeve I can hold and it is the literal instrument of my mandate, so a 6% allocation to it was the drift, not the correction. Its index reconstitution also rotates me out of fading leaders mechanically, which is the cheapest way to run trend without forecasting.

Trimmed 13->11. The momentum half is fine — 17.8x earnings, a $4.33T cap, and a $25bn bond raise that pulled $115bn of orders — but the quality half took a hit the 0.96% price move has not registered: Demis Hassabis stepped down as DeepMind CEO and chief scientist Jeff Dean departed in the same week, with commentary that the lab has lost its independence. Losing the two people most identified with the asset that justifies the AI premium is the kind of degradation this mandate should act on early rather than after the multiple compresses. A trim rather than an exit because search and cloud cash generation is untouched by it.

Raised 8->10. I entered small with a deliberately tight stop because I was buying immediately after a 15% gap and gaps retrace; a week later it sits at $274.48 having held and edged higher rather than filling, which is the specific confirmation the small size was waiting for. Trailing net income is up 91.6% on revenue +15.8%, market cap is up 24.9% over a year, and consensus is Strong Buy at $324.94. It expresses AI through cloud monetization rather than the hardware cycle, which is why it complements rather than duplicates the semiconductor weight I am adding via SPMO. Stop stays at 12%.

New 10%. This is the strongest verified relative-strength signal in my universe: +57.73% over twelve months, +7.11% in Friday's session alone, with spot gold at a seven-week high near $4,293 and silver +4.10% alongside. The corroboration is unusually hard — the desk's own order record shows shorts in this complex being stopped out repeatedly, including several on 2026-08-07, which is what a real trend looks like from the inside rather than a chart I am interpreting. At $89.89 against a $117.18 high this is a trend that has resumed, not one that is terminally extended. I chose GDX over GDXJ despite the junior index's higher one-year return because they sit the same distance below their highs and GDX carries less single-name and liquidity risk. The 15% stop is wider than my equity sleeves because miners run roughly three times bullion's volatility and a tighter stop would only be noise-triggered.

Held at 10%. Written-call premium is richest when realized dispersion is high, and this week produced another round of it — a 7.5% move in ServiceNow, mid-single-digit swings across software, gold miners up 7% and crude down. The carry improves precisely as my directional sleeves get noisier, which is the counter-cyclical property I hold it for, and since I am raising directional risk elsewhere in this book I want that offset intact rather than trimmed to fund it.

Halved 16->8 with the stop tightened from 15% to 10%. I sized this on a named driver — crude up over 20% in July to roughly $85 WTI and $88 Brent on Iranian attacks on escorted tankers — and wrote that a geopolitical premium can unwind on one ceasefire headline. WTI is now $78.18 and Brent $83.55, Iran and Oman are reported near a landmark deal to manage the Strait, and traders are described as bearish through the disruptions. The commodity leads the equity, and XLE falling 1.13% into a broad rally says the divergence is already visible. I keep half because one-year total return is still +39.97%, refiner margins hit a record and the PE is 20.9 with a 2.6% yield — the fundamentals are good even where the trend is not, and this remains the only sleeve that hedges an inflation re-acceleration.

Cut 10->7. I bought this as a volatility-regime hedge after a 65% one-month collapse in a 3x semiconductor fund; that regime resolved upward, with SOXX now +130% over twelve months. Meanwhile SPLV has returned 6.48% over a year against 29.7% for momentum and 57.7% for miners, making it by far the weakest thing I own, and a trend-following book cannot justify a double-digit weight in its own worst performer. The residual stays because a 0.54 beta genuinely cushions the miner and momentum risk I am adding, but it is now ballast rather than a position.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet deep value
decisions.research_notes:
Checked every line plus the macro since my 2026-08-03 fill; prices through the 2026-08-07 close.

COMPANY NEWS. PFE reported Q2 on 8/4: adjusted $0.77 against $0.68 consensus, a ~13% beat, and it raised the low end of the revenue outlook. Stock $26.76, +2.14% on 8/7, still only 9.64x forward with a 6.43% yield and a $28.64 consensus. Supporting news: positive Phase 3 LITFULO data in vitiligo, FDA priority review on a prostate-cancer combination, EU authorisation of the updated COVID formula. This is the only line in the book whose company-specific case got stronger this week. CVX $186.56 (-1.41%), 12.21x forward, 3.82% yield, $216.96 consensus, record quarter confirmed ($12.1bn net income vs $2.5bn). C $135.00 (+0.88%), 11.56x forward, $154.50 consensus. VZ $47.06, 9.28x forward, 6.01% yield, $51.56 consensus, but a new headwind: SpaceX claiming it can build wireless capability without heavy network investment, which pressured telecom. VLO $298.31 (-1.54%) against a $320.24 52-week high, 7.82x forward, refining margins described as "at extreme," but consensus $309.79 is only 3.85% above spot. MO $68.35, forward PE 11.86 (better than the 13.1x I had carried), 6.20% yield, beta 0.50, Q2 showed adjusted EPS and OCI growth, FY26 guidance narrowed to $5.61-5.72.

THE MACRO FACT THAT MATTERS. Nonfarm payrolls unexpectedly DECLINED by 23,000, and May and June were revised down by a combined 103,000. Odds of a September hike fell from 58% to 42% in a day. The 10-year dropped ~7bp to 4.65% and the 30-year to 5.20% from 5.28%. This inverts the rate premise I wrote into three separate theses last week. I explicitly sized VZ at 12% and MO at 5% because "a 6% bond proxy is the wrong duration against a 5.28% 30-year with a hike being priced," and I explicitly justified part of C on "two-thirds odds of a September hike priced - a direct NIM tailwind." Both premises moved against what I wrote, in opposite directions for the two sleeves.

ENERGY. Brent is $83.55, down more than 7% on the week, on reporting of a potential Iran-Oman agreement to restore Strait of Hormuz shipping. I raised CVX from 13% to 16% eight days ago explicitly citing "Brent around $88-90, up more than 20% on the month, with Iran attacking tankers in the Strait of Hormuz." That specific premium is deflating, and a negative payroll print is demand-negative for crude on top of it. Note the refiner cuts the other way: cheaper feedstock with cracks still at extremes is the favourable combination for VLO, which is why I treat CVX and VLO differently rather than cutting "energy."

THE SHORT. SMH $582.70, +1.96% on 8/7, with SOXL +5.99% the same session and five shorts in the leveraged-semi and gold-miner complexes stopped out on that one day. Semis carry a 44.71x P/E, which still makes SMH the most stretched cohort I can actually name (ARKK is flat over twelve months and shorting it is not shorting something stretched), so the mandate's hedge stays - but a falling rate path is a tailwind for the exact duration I am short, which is a second reason beyond the already-falsified capex catalyst to keep it minimal.

decisions.reason: One new fact reprices three of my own stated premises, so I am rotating within deep value rather than trading the tape. Payrolls fell 23,000 with 103,000 of downward revisions and September hike odds went 58% to 42%, taking the 30-year to 5.20%. I had explicitly sized VZ at 12% and MO at 5% BECAUSE a 6% bond-proxy yield was a thin spread against a 5.28% long end with a hike being priced; that headwind has reversed, so consistency requires sizing them up. Symmetrically, I raised CVX to 16% eight days ago explicitly on Brent at $88-90 and Iran attacking Hormuz tankers, and Brent is now $83.55 after a 7%-plus weekly fall on Iran-Oman talks to reopen the strait, with a negative payroll print adding demand risk - so the macro add comes off while the company holding stays. C gets a modest trim for the same reason in reverse: the hike-driven NIM leg weakened, and a cracking labour market is a credit-cost signal for a bank with a large US cards book, though a dovish front-end repricing steepens the curve in its favour, so I trim rather than exit. The proceeds go to PFE, the only line whose own fundamentals improved this week (13% beat, guidance floor raised, still 9.64x with a 6.43% yield and zero cyclical or AI-capex exposure). Net effect is a deliberate tilt from economically-cyclical value toward defensive FCF value at the moment the labour data turns, which is what the mandate is for.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so this book carries no overlap constraint; its distinguishing feature remains the labour-data-driven rotation from cyclical value (energy, banks) into rate-sensitive defensive value (pharma, telecom, staples) at high single-digit forward multiples, with the growth short kept deliberately vestigial rather than expressed as a directional bet.

positions.thesis: Raised from 18% on a print that post-dates my fill and validates the thesis. Q2 on 8/4 delivered adjusted $0.77 against $0.68 consensus, a fifth consecutive beat, and management raised the low end of the revenue outlook - the pattern I sized into. At $26.76 it is still 9.64x forward against a 19x industry, yields 6.43%, and sits ~7% below the $28.64 consensus target and well under its $28.75 peak. The pipeline news is additive rather than load-bearing: positive Phase 3 LITFULO data in vitiligo, FDA priority review on a prostate-cancer combination, EU authorisation of the updated COVID formula. Critically, this is the one holding with no AI-capex duration and no economic cyclicality, and its 6.4% yield gets MORE attractive as the long end falls on a negative payroll print - the same repricing that hurts my cyclical sleeve helps this one. Keeping the -18% stop wide so a valuation thesis is never converted into a stop-out by a single bad tape day.

Raised from 12% because the precise reason I gave for keeping it small has reversed. I wrote that a 6% bond-proxy yield was a thin spread against a 5.28% 30-year with a September hike being priced; payrolls fell 23,000 with 103,000 of downward revisions, hike odds dropped 58% to 42%, the 10-year fell 7bp to 4.65% and the 30-year to 5.20%. Short-duration contracted cash flows re-rate on a dovish repricing. The fundamentals are unchanged and good: 9.28x forward, a 6.01% dividend covered by free cash flow, beta 0.24, buyback target raised to $4.5bn, raised 2026 guidance, and the $1bn+ Google dark-fiber deal that makes the AI buildout pay Verizon rent instead of costing it multiple. The reason this is 15% and not 20% is a genuine new negative: reporting that SpaceX believes it can build wireless capability without massive network investment pressured the group, and direct-to-cell is a real long-run terminal-value question I cannot dismiss.

Trimmed from 15%. Part of my case was explicitly two-thirds odds of a September hike as a direct NIM tailwind; those odds are now 42%, and a labour market printing negative payrolls with 103,000 of downward revisions is a forward credit-cost signal for a bank whose US Personal Banking and cards book is consumer-levered. Partially offsetting, a dovish front-end repricing steepens the curve, which is the larger NIM driver, so this is a trim and not an exit. What still holds is the valuation: at $135.00 it is 11.56x forward, the cheapest large-cap US bank, with Q2 net income of $5.8bn on $24.77bn revenue, ROTCE at 13%, and a $154.50 consensus implying ~14% upside. And I keep my own correction on the record - at $100.89 TBVPS this is ~1.34x tangible, not the sub-book story I once claimed, so there is no buyback-accretion kicker here. The $127 no-news flush I bought has fully mean-reverted, so the specific dislocation is harvested; what is left is an ordinary cheap bank, worth 13% and not 15%. Stop stays wide at -20% because the rate debate will keep the group volatile in both directions.

Cut from 16% - I am unwinding the macro add, not the value holding. I raised this to 16% eight days ago explicitly citing Brent at $88-90, up 20% on the month, with Iran attacking tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent is now $83.55 after a decline of more than 7% on the week on reporting of a potential Iran-Oman agreement to restore Hormuz shipping, and a negative payroll print adds demand-side risk. The premium I paid up for is deflating, and I should not keep an oversized position justified by a catalyst that is reversing. The company leg is genuinely excellent and is why I keep a real 11%: record Q2 with $12.1bn net income against $2.5bn a year ago, production up 20% on Hess and the Permian, record US refinery throughput, a 20-year Microsoft data-centre power agreement, 12.21x forward, a 3.82% yield, beta 0.49 and a $216.96 consensus 16% above spot. Brent at $83.55 is still up 25% year over year, so this remains a sub-market-multiple FCF payer and the book's inflation hedge - just at a size set by the business rather than by a headline.

Held flat, and deliberately not cut alongside CVX because the crude move helps this line rather than hurting it. A refiner buys crude and sells product: Brent falling more than 7% while refining margins are described as at extreme levels is the favourable configuration, feedstock cheapening before cracks follow it down. Q2 confirmed the operating leverage - $3.7bn net income, adjusted $12.54 against $10.22 consensus, refining operating income $4.5bn against $1.3bn a year ago, renewable diesel swinging to $717m of operating income, $2.6bn returned at a 59% payout. But that print was already in my 7/31-close entry and is not a reason to add, and at $298.31 against a $320.24 high with the market cap already doubled, consensus sees only 3.85% upside. So it earns its 9% at 7.82x forward and no more. The +20% take-profit harvests a distillate-crack blowout without my having to time the exit, and the -18% stop covers the reversal case where crude stops falling and cracks compress.

Raised from 5% on the same duration logic that lifts VZ, plus a correction to my own numbers. I had been carrying this at 13.1x forward; it is actually 11.86x, with a 6.20% yield and beta 0.50, and Q2 showed adjusted EPS and OCI growth on smokables plus an expanding smoke-free portfolio with FY26 guidance narrowed to $5.61-5.72. I sized this at only 5% explicitly because a ~6% bond proxy was the wrong duration against a 5.28% 30-year with a hike priced; with the 30-year at 5.20%, hike odds at 42% and payrolls outright negative, near-zero-beta contracted carry is worth more, not less. It stays capped at 7% for the reason I gave before and which has not changed: at $68.35 against a $77.06 high and a $70.64 consensus target, the deep-value discount here is largely closed, so this is ballast and carry rather than a discount trade.

Trimmed 6% to 5% and kept deliberately vestigial. The mandate requires a small short in the most stretched growth cohort, and at a 44.71x P/E with the fund 21.7% NVIDIA, SMH is still honestly that cohort - ARKK is flat over twelve months and shorting it would not be shorting anything stretched. But I have now lost the argument twice over. First the catalyst: hyperscaler capex doubt inverted into ~$650bn of confirmed 2026 spend with semis as the direct recipients. Now the discount rate: a negative payroll print and hike odds falling to 42% lower the discount rate on exactly the long-duration cash flows I am short. And the tape is hostile in a measurable way - SMH +1.96% on 8/7 with SOXL +5.99% the same session, and five shorts in this and the gold-miner complex stopped out on that single day. That is a live squeeze and I am on the wrong side of it, so I size for survival, not for a view: 5% of NAV with a -22% stop risks about 1.1% of the book, and 3% borrow with no funding cost on shorts makes the carry negligible. It stays as insurance against a broad de-rating that would hit my long book, not as a bet that semis fall.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet dividend growth
decisions.research_notes:
WEB SEARCH BUDGET WAS EXHAUSTED (200/200) BEFORE I STARTED, so all research was done via WebFetch on stockanalysis.com quote/fund pages, which carry 2026-08-07 closing marks, TTM fundamentals, consensus targets and recent-news digests. Coverage was complete: I pulled every one of my ten holdings plus three replacement candidates and three market/sector benchmarks.

MARKET BACKDROP (8/7 close): SPY $773.26, +0.61% on the day, 52wk high $776.85 — the index closed within 0.5% of its all-time high, YTD +23.55%, with news flow citing record options activity and "S&P to 8,000 before year-end" chatter. That is a melt-up tape, not a defensive one, which explains why my book returned only +1.15% on the week. Sector split is the important finding: XLV (healthcare) +29.17% 1yr, beta 0.56, described in coverage as "a haven for investors" on earnings momentum and rotation out of tech; XLP (staples) only +7.18% 1yr. Both halves of my "defensive staples/healthcare" mandate are permitted, but one is compounding at 4x the other. That asymmetry drives most of what follows.

CORE INSTRUMENT CHECK: SCHD $33.90, +31.73% 1yr total return, 3.09% yield, 0.06% fee, $105.7B AUM (up from $100B), 103 holdings, top names ABT 4.64%/AMGN 4.61%/HD 4.31%. I benchmarked it against the two alternatives: DGRO +25.21% 1yr at a 1.86% yield, NOBL +16.32% 1yr at a 1.99% yield and a 0.35% fee. SCHD beats both on return AND yield AND cost, so the anchor stays SCHD and gets bigger rather than diversified across wrappers.

WHAT RESOLVED WELL: ABBV reported adj EPS $3.65 vs $3.61 consensus, called it "another excellent quarter," RAISED FY26 revenue guidance to ~$67.6B from $67.3B, flagged Skyrizi momentum, and added EC approval for Rinvoq in alopecia areata plus FDA acceptance of a supplemental Botox Cosmetic filing — yet the stock sits at $246.04 against a $273.39 target (+11.1%) and a 2.81% yield. The coin-flip print I refused to upsize into last week landed on the right side and the price went the wrong way. JNJ $259.24 (+0.88% on the day): the talc overhang is now a settled $5.5B number, OTTAVA launched, Rybrevant Faspro got FDA priority review, multiple targets were raised — the guidance-cut fear I trimmed on did not compound.

WHAT DETERIORATED: (1) PG $145.79, sitting near its 52wk low of $137.62 against a $167.25 high. Q4 missed, organic sales missed, HSBC AND Argus both cut to Hold, management blamed "rising input costs" and "economic and geopolitical uncertainty," and Q1 EPS is guided to decline 5%+. On top of a decelerating core they are spending $3.8B on Thorne, a supplements maker — capital leaving the core franchise while the core is shrinking. (2) ADP $271.32, consensus now HOLD with only 5.66% upside. The decisive item is that ADP's own National Employment Report shows US businesses added just 44,000 jobs in July, the smallest in six months. ADP bills on pays-per-control, so its own published data is a leading indicator against its own revenue line. (3) MCD reported 8/4: value-menu rollout execution failure, weak deal promotion, a pullback in digital offers, an outright drop in visits, and a new US president (Skye Anderson) installed to fix it. Multiple targets cut. (4) ABT $107.81 at 34.9x trailing with only 9.84% upside, and coverage flags Abbott investigating cyber incidents affecting cancer diagnostics and internal systems — a live operational unknown.

ENERGY: CVX $186.56, 3.82% yield, 12.21x forward, net income $12.1B vs $2.5B a year ago, consensus $216.96 (+16.3%). XOM $153.04, 2.69% yield, Q2 earnings $14.5B on $23.6B operating cash flow from Guyana/Permian, TD Cowen to $168, but only ~10% upside. Same sector, same driver — CVX pays 113bps more yield for 6pts more upside at a cheaper multiple. Both rest on a Middle East geopolitical premium and CVX fell 1.41% on a day the tape rose 0.61%, plus coverage notes political pressure on pump prices, so this is the leg I keep stopped rather than upsized aggressively.

REPLACEMENT SOURCED: MDT $87.16, a 48-consecutive-year Dividend Aristocrat, 3.30% yield — the highest-yielding healthcare aristocrat I could find — trading in the lower third of a $73.31-$106.33 range, consensus Buy at $98.44 (+12.9%), beta 0.57, FY26 revenue +8.43%, with Affera mapping/ablation CE Mark expanded to ventricular arrhythmias and SPR Therapeutics plus Scientia Vascular closed. Critically, it does not report until Sep 1, so it carries no near-term earnings binary.

NOT APPLICABLE TO ME: the tape warning on GDX/GDXJ/SOXL short squeezes is irrelevant here — this book is long-only equity with zero gold, zero leveraged ETFs, zero crypto and zero perps.

decisions.reason: Three names have had their theses actually falsified by news this week and one had its thesis confirmed while the price fell, so I am reallocating along the evidence rather than sitting still. PG goes to zero: a 68-year raise streak does not offset a Q4 miss, missed organic sales, two fresh downgrades to Hold, guided Q1 EPS down 5%+, and a $3.8B Thorne acquisition that spends shareholder cash outside the core while the core decelerates — and XLP at +7.18% over a year against XLV at +29.17% says the entire complex is dead money. ADP goes to zero on the cleanest signal I found all week: ADP's own employment report shows July job creation of 44,000, the weakest in six months, and ADP bills per employee on client payrolls, so its own data is a leading indicator against its own revenue, with consensus already at Hold and only 5.66% upside. MCD goes to zero because the Aug 4 print was precisely the binary I sized it as a call option on, and it came in badly — value-menu execution failure, a drop in visits, the US president replaced — so the option expired and I take the small gain instead of paying to find out whether the turnaround works. Against those cuts I add ABBV, which beat at $3.65 vs $3.61 and RAISED FY26 revenue guidance yet trades 11% below target, because a resolved-favourably earnings event that leaves the stock cheaper is the exact setup I underweighted for last week. I open MDT, a 48-year aristocrat at a 3.30% yield and 0.57 beta in the bottom third of its range with no print until Sep 1, which buys back the defensive ballast PG was supposed to provide but does it in the sector that is actually working. I tilt energy toward CVX over XOM because CVX pays 113bps more yield at 12.2x forward with 16.3% upside versus 10% for the same oil-price driver. Finally I lift the SCHD anchor to 36% and carry 10% cash: with three single names removed, pushing weight into the one instrument that out-yields, out-returns and out-costs both DGRO and NOBL cuts idiosyncratic risk without giving up the factor, and holding dry powder at 4% risk-free while the index closes within 0.5% of its all-time high amid record options activity is the mandate's own cash sleeve doing its job.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book in this experiment, so the <50% same-direction overlap constraint has no counterparty to bind against; what distinguishes this book on its own terms is that it is the only long-only, zero-leverage, zero-crypto sleeve here whose entire edge is 25+ year dividend-raise streaks bought at consensus discounts, and this week it deliberately rotates staples weight into healthcare aristocrats — cutting P&G and McDonald's outright to fund AbbVie and Medtronic — rather than joining the gold-miner and leveraged-semi squeeze trades that dominated the tape.

positions.thesis: Core anchor, raised from 33% to 36%. Head-to-head against its two rivals this week SCHD wins on every axis that matters to this mandate: +31.73% trailing 1yr total return versus DGRO's +25.21% and NOBL's +16.32%, a 3.09% yield versus 1.86% and 1.99%, and a 0.06% fee versus 0.08% and 0.35%. It now holds $105.7B across 103 quality-screened dividend growers. I am removing three single names this week, and routing part of that weight into the diversified basket rather than into another single name lowers idiosyncratic and earnings-date risk while keeping the quality-income factor exposure fully intact. Deep 12% stop is portfolio-level protection only, not a trading stop on a 103-name basket.

Upsized from 8% to 11% and now my largest single name. Last week I explicitly refused to add because the Jul 31 print was a genuine coin flip; it landed on the right side — adj EPS $3.65 versus $3.61 consensus, management calling it 'another excellent quarter,' FY26 revenue guidance RAISED to ~$67.6B from $67.3B, Skyrizi momentum in immunology, EC approval for Rinvoq in alopecia areata and FDA acceptance of a supplemental Botox Cosmetic filing. Yet the stock sits at $246.04 against a $273.39 Buy consensus, +11.1%. A 53-year raise streak at a 2.81% yield where the event risk is banked and the price is lower than before the event is the single best risk-adjusted setup in my universe. The stop widens from 10% to 12% precisely because the earnings binary that justified the tight stop no longer exists.

Upsized from 8% to 9% and now the larger of my two energy legs. A 38-year raiser yielding 3.82% — the highest yield in the entire book — at 12.21x forward earnings, with quarterly net income of $12.1B against $2.5B a year ago and a $216.96 consensus implying 16.3% upside. Against XOM's identical oil-price driver it pays 113 basis points more income for six more points of upside at a cheaper multiple, so if I want energy I want it here. Held to single digits rather than pushed harder because the earnings are levered to a Middle East geopolitical premium that can deflate overnight, it fell 1.41% on a day the S&P rose 0.61%, and there is active political pressure on the company to cut pump prices. The 10% stop stays because this is the one leg whose thesis has a genuine one-headline reversal risk.

Trimmed from 13% to 9%. The company is doing nothing wrong — 5% volume and 6% organic revenue growth, FY guidance raised, EPS +18% year over year, FIFA World Cup engagement, and a 62-year King's streak intact. What changed is the price: at $87.05 against a $94.70 consensus the upside has compressed from roughly 17% at entry to about 9%, it trades at 26.2x for a 2.44% yield, and it sits close to its $90.92 52-week high while the staples complex it belongs to has returned only 7.18% over a year. This remains the best staple I own and I keep a real weight in it, but it no longer earns a 13% slot when the reward per unit of risk has more than halved. The take-profit drops from +20% to +12% because a +20% target was never going to fill from here.

New position, funded by the P&G exit. A 48-consecutive-year Dividend Aristocrat yielding 3.30% — the richest yield available among healthcare aristocrats — with a 0.57 beta, FY26 revenue up 8.43% to $36.36B, and a Buy consensus at $98.44 against $87.16, or 12.9% upside. It trades in the bottom third of a $73.31-$106.33 range, so I am buying defensive quality on sale rather than chasing. Pipeline is moving: expanded CE Mark for the Affera mapping and ablation system into ventricular arrhythmias, plus closed acquisitions of SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular. Decisively, it does not report until Sep 1, so unlike every other name I own this quarter it carries no near-term earnings binary — it is pure ballast. This is how I replace P&G's defensive role while moving it into the sector that is actually compounding, XLV +29.17% against XLP +7.18%.

Trimmed from 9% to 7%. The fundamental case is unchanged and good — a 53-year raiser that beat with adj EPS $1.31 and raised FY EPS guidance, with FDA clearance to commercialize the SimpleScreen blood-based colorectal test opening a new diagnostics market, and the DOJ criminal probe into the formula facility now closed, which removes a legal overhang. I trim rather than hold flat for two specific reasons: at 34.9x trailing the consensus offers only 9.84% upside to $118.42, and Abbott is currently investigating cyber incidents affecting its cancer diagnostics business and internal systems, which is a live operational unknown with no quantified cost. I also already own it indirectly at 4.64% of SCHD, my largest position, so 7% direct is closer to 9% effective exposure. The take-profit comes in from +18% to +15% to sit nearer where the sell-side actually is.

Trimmed from 7% to 6% and deliberately kept behind CVX. The quarter was excellent in absolute terms — $14.5B of earnings on $23.6B of operating cash flow driven by Guyana and Permian volumes, with TD Cowen raising its target to $168 from $155 — and it remains a 40+ year raiser with enormous free cash flow. But it yields 2.69% against Chevron's 3.82% and offers roughly 10% upside against Chevron's 16.3% off the identical crude-price driver, so within a fixed energy budget every dollar is better spent next door. I keep a real position rather than exiting because I want diversified energy exposure across two operators, not a single-company bet on one asset base. Total energy sits at 15%, unchanged in size but improved in mix.

Held flat at 5%. I trimmed this to half size last week on the FY26 EPS guidance cut and the talc exposure, and that fear has not compounded: the $5.5B talc settlement is now a settled and quantified number rather than an open liability across roughly 76,000 suits, the stock closed up 0.88% at $259.24, OTTAVA robotic surgery has launched, Rybrevant Faspro received FDA priority review, and multiple analysts have raised targets. I do not add back, because at a $272.50 consensus there is only 5.12% upside left and Goldman has pulled it from its conviction list while keeping the Buy. This is a 63-year Dividend King held as low-beta ballast, sized for what it is. No take-profit attached — with the consensus this close, a TP would simply fire on noise and cost me the ballast I am holding it for. Wide 12% stop for the same reason.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet price momentum
decisions.research_notes:
Pulled point-in-time quotes and 52-week ranges through the 2026-08-07 close for every position I hold plus every mandate theme I do not.

WHAT I OWN. XLE $57.50, -1.13% on the day, +39.97% 1yr, but now 9.4% below its 52-week high of $63.46 (it was 7.6% below when I sized it to 36% on 7/31). XOP $166.40, -0.39%, +37.63% 1yr, 12.6% below its $190.36 high. ERX $88.24, -2.26% on the day, +77.14% 1yr, 20.3% below its $110.78 high. The underlying is worse than the equities: USO $117.98 is 23.4% below its $154.08 52-week high, and the tape shows crude dropping 8% on unconfirmed Hormuz diplomacy between Iran and Oman, with two-way headline risk still live. XLV $165.68, +0.75%, +29.17% 1yr, only 1.7% off its high. KRE $76.21, +31.48% 1yr (up from +26.1% a week ago), 2.7% off its high. XBI $157.37, +1.86% on the day, +83.55% 1yr (up from +71.6%), and it has closed the gap to its high from 10.7% to 5.0%.

WHAT I DO NOT OWN. This is the finding that matters. SPY $773.26 (+0.61%) is 0.46% off its all-time high; the 29 July hawkish-Fed/oil shock has been fully round-tripped by the index. IWM $301.56 (+1.11%), +38.15% 1yr, is 0.5% from its 52-week high — small caps are making new highs, and TNA $74.68 (+3.25%, +113.63% 1yr) sits only 2.8% below its own high, meaning the 3x vehicle has almost no accumulated decay gap versus the unlevered index. SMH $582.70 (+1.96%), +103.93% 1yr, 13.3% off its high and re-accelerating. QQQ $723.03 (+1.17%), +28.06% 1yr, 3.4% off its high. LABU +5.69% on the day, +350% 1yr but 16.7% below its high; SOXL $140.25 +5.99% but 53.6% below its $302 high — both 3x vehicles carry a decay gap two-to-six times wider than TNA's, which is why I take my leverage in small caps and not in biotech or semis.

WHAT I CONCLUDE. Every theme my mandate actually names — semis, biotech, tech, small-caps — is intact and re-accelerating, and the one theme I concentrated 54% of the book into last week is the only one rolling over. My -1.47% in a week when SPY printed a record is entirely energy. On the cross-sectional test I am supposed to run, XLE ranks below XBI, IWM, XLV, KRE, SMH and QQQ on distance-from-high, and XOP and ERX rank last on the board. I also note the tape warning on stopped-out shorts in GDX/GDXJ and SOXL: I carry no shorts in either complex, so it does not constrain me, but it corroborates that the squeeze is in beta, not defensives.

decisions.reason: Two independent things broke against last week's book at once, and both point the same way. First, the energy trade decayed on its own terms: crude is 23% off its high after an 8% one-day break on Hormuz diplomacy, XOP is now 12.6% below its high and ERX 20.3%, and XLE fell 1.13% on a day the S&P closed within half a percent of a record. A price-momentum book cannot hold 54% of NAV in the one theme whose relative rank is falling on every horizon. Second, the shock I repositioned around on 30 July did not persist — SPY has fully round-tripped it and IWM is printing new highs — so the reason I gave for cutting small-cap beta has been falsified by price, which is the only evidence my mandate lets me weigh. Meanwhile the themes my mandate explicitly names all improved while I was underweight them: XBI went from 10.7% to 5.0% below its high with its 12-month return rising from +71.6% to +83.6%, SMH is +104% over a year and turning up, and IWM is at highs. Holding would mean staying long a decaying theme and short my own mandate. I am rotating gross exposure rather than raising it: gross stays at 89% and cash stays at 11%, so this is a change of what I own, not how much risk I run. I keep a 7% XLE residual precisely because it is the leg that pays if Hormuz escalates instead of settling — that is real diversification against a book that is now overwhelmingly long risk-on beta — but XOP and ERX go to zero because a high-beta and a 2x expression of a theme I no longer rank first is exactly the leverage the mandate tells me to remove when the trend stops working. I take my one levered position in TNA rather than SOXL or LABU because TNA trades 2.8% below its own 52-week high against 53.6% for SOXL and 16.7% for LABU: the decay gap is the measurable evidence of whether daily rebalancing has been eating the trend, and only in small caps is it not. Turnover is roughly 55% one-way at 2-5bps a side, about 1.5bps of NAV, which is immaterial against the dispersion I am repositioning for.
decisions.novelty: I manage only a Round-3 book, so there is no Round-2 overlap to police, but this book is now deliberately distinct from the energy-and-defensives posture it replaces: the two largest legs, XBI and IWM, express biotech and small-cap breadth rather than commodity beta, and the single levered leg is 3x small-caps chosen on decay-gap evidence rather than 2x energy.

positions.thesis: The strongest intact trend on my board and the core of the mandate. +83.6% over twelve months, up from +71.6% a week ago, and price has closed from 10.7% below its high to 5.0% while rising 1.86% on the session. I halved this to 7% on 30 July on the argument that a Fed with hike dissents punishes long-duration small-cap biotech; the index answered by accelerating, and equal-weight biotech is being bid by large-cap pharma M&A rather than by rate expectations. Restored to top weight. The 12% stop is wide because this is a high-volatility equal-weight index where an 8% stop is noise, not trend damage.

The cleanest breakout available: 0.5% from its 52-week high with +38.2% over twelve months, outperforming the S&P year to date, and up 1.11% on the day. Small-caps are a theme my mandate names and I owned none of them after last week. I take the exposure unlevered here so that the levered leg can be sized small and stopped tight independently.

Semis have the highest twelve-month return of any unlevered theme I can own, +103.9%, and turned up 1.96% on the session. The 13.3% distance from its high is the reason this is a third-weight position rather than a first: the trend is intact on the twelve-month test and recovering on the daily one, but it has not yet reclaimed leadership on the drawdown test the way XBI and IWM have. Sized to participate in the recovery without pretending it is confirmed.

Held from the prior book with a modest trim, because nothing about it deteriorated: 1.7% below its 52-week high with +29.2% over twelve months and a positive session on a mixed tape. It is the highest-quality trend I own on the distance-from-high test and it is the ballast that lets me carry TNA and SMH, since large-cap pharma is bid by the same defensive rotation that would break a risk-on book.

Large-cap tech, the fourth theme my mandate names, +28.1% over twelve months and 3.4% below its high after a 1.17% session. This is the low-volatility way to hold the AI complex alongside SMH: if the concern about AI capex sustainability that is pressuring semis proves right, the megacap index absorbs it far better than a 26-stock semiconductor basket does.

Kept because it strengthened rather than faded: its twelve-month return improved from +26.1% to +31.5% and it sits 2.7% below its high at a 13.4 P/E. Regional banks are the natural beneficiary of both a steep curve and a small-cap tape making new highs, so this leg and IWM reinforce each other rather than duplicate. Trimmed from 10% only to fund the mandate themes.

Cut from 36% to a residual, not eliminated. The twelve-month trend is still +40% and price is only 9.4% below its high, so this does not fail the momentum test outright the way XOP and ERX now do. I keep it because it is the one leg in the book that profits from a Hormuz escalation, which is the specific headline that would hit small-caps, semis and biotech simultaneously. Sized so that being wrong on oil costs me a rounding error instead of the year, with a 9% stop that exits if the decay continues.

The mandate's select-leverage clause, and the only levered vehicle that currently earns it. TNA is 2.8% below its own 52-week high with +113.6% over twelve months and +3.25% on the session, versus SOXL 53.6% below its high and LABU 16.7% below theirs; that gap is the direct measure of how much daily rebalancing has eaten each trend, and in small-caps it has eaten almost nothing. Sized at 6% rather than the 8% I cut last week, so effective exposure is 18% and the 15% stop triggers on roughly a 5% move in IWM, which would be a genuine failure of the breakout rather than a shakeout.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet quality compounders
decisions.research_notes:
Round-3 book only (I run no Round-2 book). NAV $1,076.54, +7.65% in the first week, max DD -1.83%, gross 94% / cash 6%. No stops fired. WebSearch budget for the session was exhausted, so I pulled marks and news directly via WebFetch on each name.

Marks at 2026-08-07 close: NVDA $223.96 (+2.27% on the day, 52wk range $164.07-$236.54, fwd PE 22.43, 61 analysts Strong Buy, target $302.83 = +35%). MSFT $499.99 (fwd PE 25.41, FY26 revenue $331.84B +17.8%, net income +31.3%, EPS $17.95 +31.6%, target $563). GOOGL $354.30 (-0.96%, 52wk high $408.61 so still ~13% below, trailing PE 17.78 / fwd 26.67, target $428 = +21%). MA $562.95 (-2.26%, fwd 26.48, beta 0.73, 2025 revenue +16.4% and net income +16.3%, target $664 = +18%). V $362.50 (-2.15%, fwd 25.07, near 52wk high $373.97, FY25 revenue +11.3% but earnings growth moderated to 2.04%, target $414 = +14%). COST $947.82 (fwd PE 43.25, July net sales +10.7% / comps +8.9%, but FY25 EPS growth ~10%).

Tape: the pullback I bought into has been fully retraced. SMH $582.70 +1.96% on the day and back near highs after the late-July "chip stocks enter bear-market territory" scare; SPY $773.26 and QQQ $723.03 with QQQ +28% trailing year and the S&P pressing records. NVDA-specific catalysts since entry: up to $3B into Blackstone-backed power developer Lancium, and SpaceX committing to build its AI infrastructure exclusively on NVIDIA silicon. NVDA's Aug 26 print is still ahead.

What that changes: NVDA re-rated from 19.1x to 22.4x forward and went from 20% below its high to ~5% below, but earnings grew into it — it remains the cheapest line in the book on forward PE with by far the highest growth, so the screen still points at it and I am not trimming into a re-rating that the fundamentals earned. What did break on the screen is COST at 43x forward for ~10% earnings growth — that is the one holding that fails my own quality-at-a-discount test, and V/MA already supply the low-beta ballast COST was there for. Within payments, MA is now clearly the better half: 16% revenue and earnings growth and a clean Q2 beat versus V's 2% FY25 earnings growth, plus more consensus upside, so I am flipping their relative weights. GOOGL is the only mega-cap still carrying a visible discount to its own high and holds the largest net-cash pile ($122B); the offset is senior AI-leadership departures and a new bond raise to fund infrastructure, which is why the add is 2 points, not 6. No shorts anywhere in the book, so the GDX/GDXJ/SOXL squeeze that stopped out twelve orders in this experiment is not a risk I carry.

decisions.reason: One leg failed my own screen and one pair is mis-ranked; everything else is working and stays untouched. COST goes to zero because at 43x forward for ~10% earnings growth it is the only holding that contradicts the mandate's quality-AT-A-DISCOUNT premise, and the recession ballast it was bought for is already supplied by two payments names with sub-0.8 beta. Inside payments I flip the ranking toward MA: 16% revenue and net income growth and a clean Q2 beat versus Visa's FY25 earnings growth moderating to 2.04%, with V additionally sitting within 3% of its 52-week high. GOOGL gets 2 points because it is the only mega-cap left trading ~13% below its own high while carrying the biggest net-cash balance, so the mark-down gap my entry thesis was built on has still not closed — sized modestly rather than aggressively because senior AI-leadership departures and a new bond raise to fund datacenters both cut against the story. NVDA stays at full 26% deliberately: it re-rated from 19.1x to 22.4x forward, but earnings grew into the move and it is still the cheapest line in the book against the highest growth rate, so selling it purely because it went up would be reacting to price rather than to the screen. Cash to 8% is the small concession to the fact that the pullback I bought is gone and NVDA prints on Aug 26. Total turnover is 8 points at ~2bps a side — a repricing of two ideas, not a rebuild.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so this Round-3 book has zero same-direction overlap with any other book of mine by construction; within Round 3 the novelty this week is dropping the defensive retail sleeve entirely and expressing all non-AI exposure through the payments duopoly, tilted toward the faster-growing half.

positions.thesis: Still the cheapest line in the book on forward earnings (22.4x) against the fastest growth, so the re-rating from 19.1x was earned by numbers rather than by multiple expansion alone. ROIC ~105%, +$40B net cash, $119B FCF at 47% margin, 74% gross margin. Demand signal strengthened since entry: up to $3B into Lancium power infrastructure and SpaceX committing to build its AI buildout exclusively on NVIDIA. Consensus target $302.83, +35%. Aug 26 print is the catalyst and the risk; the -30% stop is a catastrophe brake set wide enough to survive a normal semis correction without being shaken out.

The AI-monetization question answered in its favour and now confirmed in the full year: FY26 revenue $331.84B +17.8%, net income +31.3%, EPS $17.95 +31.6%, Azure through $100B annualized with $175B of CY26 capex maintained. 25x forward, 28% ROIC, net cash. Held below NVDA only because part of the capex math still leans on extending datacenter depreciation from 15 to 25 years.

The last mega-cap in the book still visibly discounted to its own tape at ~13% below the 52-week high, with the largest net-cash balance in the portfolio (~$122B) and Search/YouTube monopoly economics at 17.8x trailing. Being marked down for the same AI capex Microsoft is now being paid for; that gap is the trade, and consensus at $428 agrees by 21%. Added only 2 points rather than more because senior AI-leadership departures and a bond raise to fund infrastructure both chip at the moat-plus-fortress-balance-sheet case.

Promoted to the senior half of the payments sleeve: 2025 revenue +16.4% and net income +16.3%, a clean Q2 beat that drew multiple target raises, beta 0.73, minimal capital intensity, and the widest consensus upside in the book outside NVDA at +18%. The BVNK acquisition plus Borderless and Fiserv partnerships buy optionality on stablecoin rails without paying up for it. A toll road whose volumes do not depend on datacenter capex.

Kept as low-beta ballast (0.76) on ~90% gross margins with the same duopoly economics, but cut to the junior slot because FY25 earnings growth moderated to 2.04% against Mastercard's 16%, and the stock sits within 3% of its 52-week high with only 14% consensus upside. The 2,600-role reduction and the $2.4B BioCatch fraud-detection deal are both margin- and moat-supportive, which is why the position stays rather than closing.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet small/mid-cap growth
decisions.research_notes:
Checked every line in the book plus the small-cap tape. WebSearch budget for the session was exhausted, so all work was done via direct fetches of stockanalysis.com quote and statistics pages (prices are 2026-08-07 close).

EVENTS THAT RESOLVED THIS WEEK — all three prints I was carrying came in bullish:
- NET (6 Aug): standout Q2, revenue growth accelerating on AI demand, FY26 revenue and EPS guidance raised. Stock +5.57% on 7 Aug to $300.27, a new all-time high. Morgan Stanley, BTIG and Scotiabank raised targets by $50-90. Launched Kitesurf, a browser for AI agents. The 209x-forward de-rating risk I sized down for did not happen — it re-rated up. But statistics page: forward PE 203.6, P/S 42.6, P/FCF 313, GAAP net loss of $206m ttm, and the 34-analyst average target of $317.81 is only 4.8% above spot. Beat is real; the upside to consensus is thin.
- DDOG (Q2): revenue +36% to $1.12bn, beat, FY26 guide raised to $4.45-4.47bn. Closed $233.93 (+2.02%). Initially sold on "lower usage from a major AI customer" — the customer-concentration overhang is the live issue, not growth. PE 473, consensus target $281.94 (+20%).
- HOOD (Q2): record quarter. Prediction markets is now the fastest-growing business in company history, revenue up 10x in the quarter; UK crypto approval; Ventures Fund II. Analyst reaction split — BofA to $140, Goldman down to $118. Closed $93.29 (+2.84%) but is still -11.7% over 52 weeks and 39% below its $153.86 high. Forward PE 39.5, beta 2.32, short interest 4.24%.

NO-EVENT NAMES:
- CRDO $249.89, +8.45% on 7 Aug. Revenue +205.7% ttm, fiscal 2026 earnings +800%. Fresh target raises: Barclays $300, BofA $340, Stifel $350; Strong Buy, average $279.29. Critically, the statistics page shows forward PE 40.8 against 52.7% projected three-year revenue growth, net margin 35.4%, current ratio 10.2, debt/equity 0.01. That is the best valuation-to-growth in the book, not the most speculative line. Next earnings 2 September — no event in this window. Beta 3.23 is the constraint.
- CRWD $214.42, +3.39%. Fal.Con 2026 sold out at record pace, Cerebras partnership, Frost & Sullivan award, Morgan Stanley to $227 and Loop initiating at $230. But the 53-analyst consensus target is $193.13 — spot is ~11% ABOVE the average target, the only name in the book where that is true. Up ~80% in six months. Earnings 26 August.
- NU $13.84, -1.98% on the day, the only red line. Forward PE 16.3, consensus $17.98 (+30%). Banco Porto Real acquisition for the Brazilian licence, Mexican banking authorisation, $1bn buyback. Earnings 13 AUGUST — the one event inside the coming week.
- XBI $157.37, +1.86%, +83.6% over one year. Reporting frames healthcare as "a haven for investors ditching tech," with biotech dealmaking accelerating. Equal-weight, 157 holdings, the ballast is working.

TAPE: IWM closed $301.56 (+1.11%) against a 52-week high of $303.06 — small caps are within 0.5% of their high and have outperformed the broad market this year. The regime break I repositioned for on 30 July (Fed hike dissents, long-end yields, hyperscalers punished for capex) did not broaden. Cloudflare's print specifically reversed the "AI disrupts software" fear. I could not reach Reuters or CNBC (403/fetch blocked) so I have no fresh read on yields or Fed speak this week; I am treating that as a known gap and keeping a real cash buffer rather than assuming the macro all-clear.

I hold no shorts and no crypto, so the GDX/GDXJ/SOXL squeeze that stopped out twelve short legs across the experiment does not touch this book.

decisions.reason: The insurance I bought on 30 July expired unused and is now costing me. I sized this book for a capex scare broadening into an opex scare, and instead all three prints I was carrying resolved bullish — NET beat, raised and closed at an all-time high, DDOG beat and raised FY guide to $4.45-4.47bn, and IWM finished within 0.5% of its 52-week high — so small-cap and software leadership is intact rather than broken. Two lines were built for the scenario that did not arrive and must shrink. CRWD was explicitly held as the defensive line if software budgets got cut; that call was wrong, and it now trades ~11% ABOVE its 53-analyst consensus target of $193 after an 80% six-month run, which is the worst forward risk/reward in the book regardless of how good the business is. NU is cut not on thesis but on calendar: it is the single name with a print inside the coming week (13 August) and I do not want 16% of NAV riding one Brazilian quarter when I cannot control the gap. The proceeds go where the event risk has already been paid for and the price is still defensible. CRDO is the biggest add because the statistics undercut my own prior framing of it as the speculative leg — 40.8x forward against 52.7% projected three-year growth, 35% net margins, essentially no debt, Strong Buy with fresh $300-350 targets, and no earnings until 2 September. NET gets only a small add rather than a large one precisely because the beat was so good: at 203x forward, a GAAP loss and 4.8% upside to consensus, adding aggressively into an all-time high is chasing, so I take the validation and tighten the stop instead. DDOG and XBI each rise modestly — DDOG because the print is behind it with 20% left to consensus, capped only by the AI-customer concentration flag, and XBI because the rotation into healthcare gives me the one genuinely low-correlation growth line I own. HOOD comes down two points and stays the joint-largest: it is the only name my rate view helps rather than hurts and prediction-market revenue just went up tenfold, but it is -11.7% over 52 weeks and I will not keep adding to a persistent laggard on a story. Cash goes 18% to 13% because 4% on idle money is a poor trade against a confirmed uptrend, while still leaving a real buffer given I could not verify this week's rates and Fed news and the book has already seen a -10.29% drawdown.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to manage, but the novelty within my own history is directional rather than cosmetic: this is the first week I have stopped paying for downside insurance inside a long-only mandate — the two positions whose entire rationale was defensive (CRWD as budget-proof software, and an 18% cash drag) are cut in favour of names whose binary events have already cleared, which converts the book from a hedged bet on a regime forecast into an unhedged bet on post-earnings fundamentals I can actually read.

positions.thesis: Still the only line my macro helps rather than hurts — roughly a third of revenue is net interest, so higher-for-longer compounds it while volatility feeds the options franchise. Q2 was a record and prediction markets grew revenue tenfold in the quarter, which is a genuinely new engine rather than a re-telling of the old story. Trimmed two points because it is -11.7% over 52 weeks, sits 39% below its high, and the sell-side is openly split (BofA $140 against Goldman $118): I will hold it at conviction size but I will not keep feeding a laggard. Beta 2.32 justifies leaving the stop wide rather than tightening it into the noise.

Promoted from smallest active line to joint-largest because the numbers contradict my earlier framing of it as the speculative leg: 40.8x forward against 52.7% projected three-year revenue growth, 35% net margin, current ratio 10 and debt/equity 0.01 is the best valuation-to-growth in the book, not the frothiest. Revenue tripled, Strong Buy with fresh Barclays $300, BofA $340 and Stifel $350 targets, and no earnings until 2 September means no binary inside this window. Capped at 15% rather than higher purely because beta 3.23 makes it the dominant risk contributor at any larger weight, and it keeps the widest stop in the book for the same reason.

The AI-consumption thesis was validated rather than merely survived: growth accelerated on AI demand, FY26 revenue and EPS guidance went up, and the print specifically reversed the market-wide fear that AI disrupts software. Added only two points because the good news is now in the price — 203x forward, 42x sales, a GAAP loss and an average target of $317.81 leave just 4.8% to consensus at an all-time high. Taking the validation but not chasing it, and cutting the stop from -22% to -15% so the earnings gap I just earned is protected rather than round-tripped.

Beat with revenue +36% and raised the FY26 guide to $4.45-4.47bn, so the event I was underweight ahead of is now behind it with roughly 20% still open to the $282 consensus. Added three points on that clearing. The cap on the size is customer concentration, not growth: the stock sold off initially on lower usage from one large AI customer, which is a real single-counterparty overhang on a name at 473x earnings, so this stays a middleweight rather than a top-three position.

The ballast is outperforming rather than merely diversifying — up 83.6% over a year, +1.9% on Friday, with dealmaking accelerating and money rotating into healthcare as a haven from tech. Equal-weighted across 157 names, so it carries no single-drug or single-print risk, which is exactly what a book with three high-multiple software lines needs. Added four points because it is the only genuinely low-correlation growth exposure available inside my mandate, and the stop is tightened to -15% since a good deal of the one-year gain is now embedded in the entry price.

Cheapest thing I own and the thesis is unchanged — 16.3x forward for mid-30s revenue growth, a $1bn buyback, the Banco Porto Real acquisition securing the Brazilian licence and Mexican banking authorisation, with 30% upside to the $18 consensus and a LatAm penetration story insulated from both US long-end rates and AI sentiment. Cut from 16% to 11% purely on calendar: this is the only position with earnings inside the coming week (13 August), and the correct control on gap risk I cannot hedge is a smaller position, not a tighter stop that would simply be jumped through.

Demoted to the smallest line because the reason I owned it has expired. It was bought as the defensive line if the capex scare broadened into an opex scare; that scare did not broaden, so I am paying a premium for protection I no longer need. After an 80% six-month run it is the only name in the book trading above its own consensus target — $214 spot against a 53-analyst average of $193 — which means the sell-side thinks the next move is down even as the business itself compounds fine on Falcon consolidation and the Cerebras partnership. Kept rather than cut to zero because the platform story is intact and the 26 August print could re-rate it, but sized so a bad print is an irritant, with the tightest stop in the book to enforce that.
